UNFINISHED STILL. . A baby's boot and a skein of wool, Faded and soiled and s"oft ; Odd things you say, and I doubt you're right, Round a seaman's neck, this stormy night, Up in the yards aloft. Most likely it's folly; but, mate, look here! When first I went to sea, A woman stood on yon far-off strand With a wedding ring on her small soft hand Which clung close to me. My wife—God bless her !—the day before Sat she beside my foot; And the sunlight kissed her yellow hair, And the dainty fingers deft and fair Knitted a baby's boot. The voyage was over; I came ashore; What think you I found there? A grave the daisies had sprinkled white A cottage empty and dark at night, And this beside the chair. The little boot, 'twas unfinished still; The tangled skein lay near; But the knitter had gone away to her rest, With the babe asleep on her quiet breast. Down in the churchyard drear.

Repent of evil that's past; avoid that which may come. He who knows most grieves most for wasted time.— Lawton A walking stick creates much less excitement than a . walking match. Poverty may excuse a shabby coat, but it is no excuse for shabby morals. It is rather strange that so many people who have no object in life persist in living. The man who is always behind with his shoemaker can't really say his sole's his own. It will be no use trying to organise a gun trust. You can never trust a gun in some men's hands. - An inventor has patented an electric contribution box for church use. Whenever a button or piece of tin is de- posited in the box an electric bell rings and informs the Do-gregation of the fact. Freddy had been repeatedly told he must not ask people for money. One day he met Mr. Williams, who could never resist an appeal from the small boy. "Mr. Williams," said Freddy, "do you ever give pennies to little boys what do not ask for 'ism?" He got the money. ' "And what are you going to be, my little man ?" asked the minister, as he patted the boy on the head, "what are you going to be when you grow up ?" "I am going to be a waiter, sir ?" "A waiter? Well, that is not a very lofty ambition. Let me ask you, my little man, why you are going to be a waiter?" "Because, sir. I've heard papa say that all things come to him who waits." Tne GOLD FF,VEM—MANLY Giess.—The gold diggings at Ballarat had just been discovered, and everyman was rushing off from Melbourne in that strange and almost mad excitement of hope which the discovery of gold alone can create. The gold mania seized upon the sailors of he emigrant ship Nerthumberland, and they every one deserted, even to the very boys. The outfit for a gold-seeker at Ballarat was so very simple and inexpen- sive that it was not to be wondered at that the fever for gold-finding attacked all working men. All that a man wanted was a tin bowl, with which to scoop up the sand in the bank of the river or stream, and in which to wash away the sand from the gold particles which were found in it. In the early days of Ballarat 6' diggings" an ordi- nary gold-washer found four or five ounces of gold a week. This fever of gold-finding was, however, a very bad thing for the Northumberland, which lay in the har- bour. her remaining passengers eating out her store of provisions, and with only the captain, the doctor, and a men with a wooden leg, who had been a sailor, to take her on to Sydney. All the men passsngers, as well as thg sailors, had left her. The captain and the doctor held a consultation, and they appealed to the matron and the sixty-three emigrant girls to help them. If these girls were willing to take their turns as "hands' in navi- gating the ship they might go on. The girls unani- mously agreed, and under the guidance of the captain, the doctor, the man with the wooden leg, and the two hired boys, those girls carried the Northumberland safely from Melbourne to Sydney, a distance of 700 miles, with- (nit harm or accident of any kind. When nearing Sydney they fen in with a pilot boat, which took them safe into port Such an instance of "brave work by a party of girls has seldom been recorded."—"..Ks Sayings and Doings," by the Rev. W. Quekett. " Brtansaaw" us 1844.—Quite as characteristic as the growth of the "Guide" are the changes which have taken place in railway habits and customs. Thus at this time we find trains described as "first-class," "second-class," "mixed," "fast," and "mail," the term " express " not having come into use. Stations, too, were classified as "first-class or otherwise," certain trains calling only at "first-class stations." On the London and Birmingham Railway there was a curious method in practice of classifying the fares, which seemed to be regulated by the number of persons in a compart- rqent, and varied according as it was day or night. Thust the charge from London to Birmingham by first-class was 32.5. 6d., but if four travelled inside by day, or six by night, it was reduced to 305.; if six travelled inside by day, the second-class carriage was charged 255„ "closed by night," but 20s. "open by day." It was an- nounced with an almost axiomatic gravity that " first- class trains stop at first-class stations," as though there , was a fixed relation between them. Little or no account indeed was taken of the " waggon " or "open carriages" as the phrase went, companies in these times seeming to hold the third-class passenger in horror. We find RIRD allusions to what were called "glass coaches." The tickets were described as "check tickets" or "passes," and this important caution is laid down, that "the check ticket given to the passenger on payment of his fare will be demanded from him at the station next before his arrival at London or Birmingham, and if not then produced he will be liable to have the fare againdemanded." Further, "No smoking is allowed at the stations or in the corn- ,pany's carriages." An annual subscription ticket to s Brighton and back was fixed at the startling prohibitive figure of £100! There were mime railway phrases then introduced which were inexpressive enough, and which have given place to much more telling forms. Places were " booked "as in the way-bill of a coach, and you were asked the place to which you were "destined," the place itself being your "destination." The carriages were always described as the "coaches," while " voyagers " " rode "in their "coaches." As to the luggage, "passengers are especially recommended to have their names and address or destination legibly written on each part of their luggage," when it will be placed on the top of the " coach " in which they "ride," If the passenger be "destined for Manchester or Liver- pool and has booked his place through, his luggage will be placed on the Liverpool or Manchester coach, and will not be disturbed until it reaches its destination."— Cornhill Magazine. VAGARIES OF INSANII7.-A man may for years have made a hobby or pursuit of some particular subject. Its influence is ever with him; he becomes absorbed in his pet idea; and it forces itself upon him, no matter in what occupation he may be engaged. This one object being constantly in mind plays havoc with his brain; and, should the nature of the object admit, he finally comes to regard it with extravagant imagination. For example, take the case of George 111., who found him- self BO often repeating that it was he who won the battle of Waterloo that he at length appealed to the Duke of Wellington dsmanding if it was not so. On Somewhat similar lines were the vasetries of a citizen of London who imagined himself Sir Walter Raleigh. The individual in question lived in an attic somewhere in the neighbour- hood of Westminster Bridge-road, and regularly every night (during the daytime he was sane enough) he shut binsself in his room to go through the principal events in the life of the courtier. He strutted about the room in a dignified manner, spread his coat for the Queen, ordered people here and there, and sat on a three-legged stool smoking a clay pipe. But he was cured at last- by a remedy that is supposed to cool the exalted ideas of most people and bring them down to the commonplace. A doctor who resided in the same neighbour- hood, and who had an extensive practice among the poor of Westminster, learned of the young man's ailment. One evening, when the latter Was smoking his pipe as usual, the doctor borrowed a small hose, turned the water full on, and kept it in play for about ten minutes, at the end of which time he had had enough of the ex- periences of Sir Walter Raleigh to last him for some considerable time to come. No more melancholy story could be related than that of Charles and Mary Lam& Charles himself was in confinement in a madhouse for sist weeks. 6' In your absence," he wrote to Coleridge, "the tide of melancholy rushed in and did its worst mis- chief by overwhelming my reason." And later he says, "Dream not, Coleridge, of haying tasted all the grandeur and wildness of fancy till you have gone mad." Mary's case baffled the skill of every physician. In a fit of frenzy she Stabbed her mother. Her attacks were rarely of great length, seldom exceeding six weeks; And, strange to say, they varied considerably in violence. ' Whenever the two had a holiday together it was followed by a seizure, and Maly Lamb never set out on a pleasure without packing a straight waistcoat with her own hands. Feeling the dread symptoms coming on, she would as gently as possible prepare her brother for the duty he must perform, and he would take her to the asylum. On one occasion it is related that a friend met them slowly pacing together a little footpath in Hoxton Fields, both weeping bitterly, and found on joining them that they were taking their solemn way to the ac- s customed asylum. A DAY IN YORKSHIRE.
BY T. H. KNONW.ES.

We were being whirled rapidly along, one beautiful August day, towards that Paradise of ,Lancashire fly- fishers—Yorkshire. Coming from a busy manufacturing), town, with the clatter, rattle, and rush of thousands of looms and spindles echoing in one's ear, the beauty and. calm of the country act upon our troubled nerves in a" manner which no physician's tonics or prescriptions could attempt to rivaL Our errand is the capture of the wary trout. Trnut! How the very name causes a thrill to run through the body of a fly-fisherman! How the sight of one, though it be only a poor specimen on a' fishmonger's slab, conjures up to the mind's eye of an angler visions of days gone by, of rivers' banks, favourite streams, pet rods and flies, and former con- quests. But here we are.. "'Go! 'Go!" calls a porter; which being interpreted, means Langho, a small village in Lancashire, close to the Yorkshire border.

But we—my brother and I—have not arrived yet the scene of ourformer, and, we hope, future triumphs: A long tramp of four miles is before us ere we reach the banks of that pearl of streams—the Ribble. By Ribble's streams I'll pass my days, If wishes aught avail; For all that anglers want or praise Is found in Ribblesdale.

Our walk Tieii-;r-O-u-gih--a-beaiitiful and interesting country. Pasture lands, meadows, woods, and dairy farms are on every side of us. In front stretch the mountains and fells of Yorkshire, purple withiheather, and echoing with the guns of the grouse shooters. On the right is Pendle Hill, I,Booft. high, the highest moun- , tain in Lancashire, like a couchant lion, guarding Clitheroe Castle, an ancient keep, at its base. [Coniston Old Man, 2,632 feet high, is the highest mountain in Lancashire.— Ed.] This castle is said to have been bombarded and left in ruinsby Cromwell. Like theclub which killed Captain Cook, and which is possessed by every museum in America, all other castles in England have been bombarded by Croniwell—according to tradition. On the left we catch a glimpse between the trees of a molten streak, flashing like silver in the sun—the Irish Sea. But here ,we are. The water is s:mewhat low, but we do not I despair, as the trout in these streams are numerous, small, and voracious, and do not pause to examine too closely into the nature of the lure presented to them. Notwithstanding, it is not every tyro who can make a good basket. A fine casting line, small flies, hackles for preference, and a light hand are necessary; for if the line do not fall like gossamer upon the clear as crystal waters which prevail in summer time, farewell to sport. • The Ribble here receives one of its largest tributaries, the Hddder, and where the two streams mingle is a favourite haunt of salmon. I remember, the last time we visited this spot, seeing a beauty of 241bs. hooked and grassed by a fishing-tackle maker and enthusiastic sportsman, from a neighbouring town. We quickly put together our 121 t. rods, and, for a beginning, I try a Hawthorn Black, Snipe Hackle, and Orange Dun. My brother puts up a similar cast, sad we proceed to arrange our plan of campaign before parting. He is to fish up the Hodder as far as the bridge, about a mile. lamto do likewise with the Ribble. Then, taking the road which joins the two bridges,:we pass each other and change streams, ultimately meeting where we now stand. Taking off his boots and socks, Charlie is quickly at the other side. and I notice that he draws first blood with his initial effort, for, throwing into the slack water where the two streams join, and gently coaxing his flies into the current, he secures a beauty of half a pound. I go on a few yards, to where a miniature Niagara of two feet in depth crosses the stream, and, letting the flies drift over the same—a favourite trick of mine, but not to he recommended,, as it frequently ends in getting hung up in the moss which grows on the edge—l am rewarded with a gentle tug. Out he comes. Confound it! it's a smelt, or, as it would be called in other parts of the country, a fingerling, pink, or parr. In he goes again, and next cast I are more fortunate, bringing to grass a crimson spotted beauty of six or eight ounces. I pick up two more in the ripple beyond, and then pro- ceed to a more rocky stretch, where the water goes seething and foaming between high banks. The stream here is interspersed with boulders, and a ledge of rock runs down the centre, beyond which is a very fishy. looking pool. In fact, as I approach, keeping well behind the trees, I see a tremendous fellow for these streams, fully 2.1b5., poised in mid-water. Before casting I change my stretcher for a Hawthorn Black, as I notice that all the fish I have already taken have given this the preference. At the third cast he is hooked, but a long way from being landed, for I am in the most difficult position that I ever, remember. Standing a con- siderable distance above the water, on a perpendicular rock, which submerges itself for some 61t. or more, •I can scarcely prevent myself from going in head first. There is a tree in front of me, behind which I have screened myself, and whose branches interfere sadly of the free play of the rod, and to crown all my difficulties, a length of rock between me and the fish projects some two feet into the air, against which rock my line is sawing. There's no help for it. I can't move, so the fish must, and selecting the flattest portion of the projecting rock I endeavoured to haul him bodily over it. Of course, I only succeed in tearing away the hook. I swallow my disappointment as well as I cm, and round the bend in the river, and by keeping well back and going down on my knees -when the bank is low and free from timber, I pick up ten more before reaching the bridge, none exceeding half a pound. In addition, I hooked about twenty smelts, which are here qui. nuisance to the trout fisher, specially during the months of April and May, and again in August and September. The change from the beautiful river's bank, with its carpet of green and pattern of every tint of the spec- trum, to the dusty highway, is not pleasant, but ten minutes' walk brings me to the Three Fishes, one of those old-fashioned country inns which Izaak Walton describes SO vividly; but as Charlie has not arrived I stroll in the direction of the Hodder. lam just in time to witness one of those unpleasant little contretemps of which every angler must have a lively recollection. On arriving at the bridge I perceive Charlie down below, in the act of springing on to a rock some distance in the stream, for the purpose of reaching a pretty little ripple under the old bridge, which is about fifty yards lower down the stream than the one on which I was standing. This old bridge is a picturesque ruin, moss-grown,and threatening Iwith every flood to come down bodily. Cromwell crossed it on the eve of the battle of Preston. and from it may be seen the celebrated Jeauit college of Stonyhurst, memorable from its connection with the Tichborne trial, and also as being the seminary where Waterton, the celebrated naturalist, and many of our Roman Ratholic clergymen were educated. Mats rerenons a nos moutons. Charlie misses his spring, and, alighting on a sharp rock, retires gracefully back- wards into the water, which is, fortunately, here only a few inches deep. I am , qutcky on the spot, and find him gazing ruefully at his tackle. Where is now the supple wand, pliant as a rush, and as strong as steel, which seemed to obey the wrist of its master in directing the line like a being instinct with life? Alas ! it hangs limp and motionless. "Broken the second joint close by the ferrule," says Charlie. After asking him the time-honoured question on these occasions, "Did you go in to hook them on ?" I secure his hat, which has floated away under the bridge, and then we determined, on account of the accident, to abandon the second part of our programme, so, after a good meal at the Three Fishes, we wend our way in the gloaming to the station, having thoroughly enjoyed our day in Yorkshire. In conclusion, I may. advise anyone wishing for good fishing to try the higher reaches of the Ribble or Hodder. • The trout are not large, but they are plump and well- fed, and a creel full of them is a pretty sight. If the reader be cursed with a hot, dry day, as we were. I can advise him to leave the swift flowing stream and try the slacker water close in by the banks and under the trees. He can scarcely fail to be successful.—From F.shing.

Hatters are the people oftenest caught nipping. Lloyd's agent at Margate telegraphs on Thursday that a vessel laden with timber ha .4 gone to pieces off that port, and that the crew are supposed to have been drowned.
A vessel called the Ebenezer, belonging to the Balti- more Fishery School, Co. Cork, went on the rocks on Wednesday near Kinsale, and afterwards sank. The crew were saved.

In the Camelot series for April Mr. Walter Scott punishes a volume Of "Select Writings of Ralph Waldo Emerson, with an introduction by Percival Chubb."--Rtnerson ass writer• is entitled to be a favourite amongst favourites.; but there are people , who Cannot idmire'him, because they do not always understand him. The di i fficulty they experience s that, while his thoughtq strike them as past, they appear to lack sequence; but the fault is in them— not in him. He travels too fast and thus leaves them behind; but when they get into going his pace they will be evermore delighted. The introduction by Mr. Chubb is an exceedingly interesting memoir. It makes the way easier for the general reader., since it presents the• great American in a true light. Emerson was not a politician as we understand the terni ; but how happily he goes to the root of the matter when be says; "Men are Conservatives' when they are least vigorous, or when they are most luxurious. They are Conservatives after dinner or before taking their rest; when they are sick or aged. In the morning, or when their intellect or their conscience has been troubled, when they hear music, or when they read poetry, they are Radicals." The current issue of the Canterbury Poets is entitled "Border Ballads." The work is carefully edited with a valuable introduction, and a series of no less valuable notes, by, Mr. Graham R. Thompson. These songs are altogether different from the drawing-room ballads of the present day. They are instinct with life; for, as Mr. Thompson observes, "they deal with the strong primal elementa of human nature while it still remained unsoftened, unveiled by the neutral tints, the perhaps more delicate influences of civilisation." The stories en- shrined in some of the ballads are of universal interest, and are founci in the songs, and folk lore of many lands. For instance, the story of Mary Colvin has been traced' in one form or another, ia over' a dozen languages. "Helen of IGrkconnell" has always been a prime favour- ite; it is so simple and so pathetic even as it begins : I wish I were wheje Helen lies! Night and day on me she cries; 0 that I were where Helen lies, t On fair Kirkconnell Lee! This voltunVof "Border Ballads" is like the rest of this series, well bound and well printed, and therefore a won. derfulshilling,'s-worth. The Magazine of Art for April leads off wit a fine etching of "The master brewer of the monastery," fol- lowed by a paper on J. B. Camille Carot; which is ac- companied by illustrations of his niost notable pictures. Mr. W. P. Frith, ILA, contributes an article on "Crazes •in Art," and we have a portrait of Mr. Frith at the 'age of thirty. "A personal view of Japanese Art" by AL% Mortimer Menpas, is alike interesting in text and illus- tration. Irish lace-making receives special attention, and Mr. Alfred Higgins writes in "Old Masters of Sculp- , ture at the Royal Academy"; but the paper of most in- terest to this district is one on the city Art Gallery of Manchester by Mr. J. Forbes-Robertson. Engravings are given (amongst others) of Mr. Herkomer's " Hard times," and Mr. Henry Moore's "Mount's Bay" with both of which visitors to the late Exhibition will be familiar.

The frontispiece to Cassell's Magazine is a powerful piece of engraving illustrating some verses in this month's issue. Mr. Gordon Stables continues "A family of boys and how they were started in life," and the Family Doctor tells us how to face the east wind. Cardiff is pleasantly written about and illustrated as "A Rising Welsh Town"; Mr. F. J. Crowest peers into song-worlds ; and there is the average supply of stories continued and completed, with, as an appropriate conclusion, the odd* and ends of "The Gatherer."

In the " Quiver " the most attractive illustration is that of the girl "in the high-back, old-fashioned pew," in which a she sat on Sundays long ago," though the frontispiece makes perhaps a prettier picture. Mr. Edward Garrett has a third paper on "The Salt of the Earth ;" the Rev. D. Hiles Hitchens discourses on "Bible ' trade's and what they teach;" a correspondent in India deseribes "A: day with the Zenanas ; and a Special Commissioner gives an• account with a portrait, of an interview ;with the Rev. A. M Vairbairn, Principal of Mansfield College, Oxford. There are, beside, other articles, &c., and a striking poem by Mr. George Weather' ey. "Little Folks" has for frontispiece a coloured picture of a jaguar disturbed in its sleep by a monkey which has fallen from a tree. "Daisy's Dilemmas" reaches the eighth,chapter and is "tq be continued." Some very funny.pietures illustrate tile funny story of "The Bad Baron'and the Buns;" and there are further details of "The Mystery of Master Max." Mr. Walter Crane con- tinues " Lancelot's Levities "in outline drawings; and we have the Editor's Pocket-book full, as usual, of in- teresting notes, not to mention the good things in the paper written by little folks themselves. Part 3to hand of Milton's "Paradise Lost," as illus- trated by Gustave Dore, sustains the excellent im- pression of the first issues. Each part contains a portion of the life of Milton by Dr. Vaughan. We have also received from Messrs. Cassell part 23 of the Life and Times of Queen Victoria, which furnishes, among other illustrations, portraits of General Wolseley, General Gor- dan, Sir Stafford Northcote, Professor Darwen, and of Princess Beatrice and Prince Henry of Battenburg. We have also to hand the current number of the Enu'- clopcedic Dictionary; the Illustrated Shakespeare; The Sea—its stirring story of adventure, peril and, heroism; Familiar Wild Flowers; and the Dictionary of English History. The current issue of the Manchester Quarterly is a varied number. Mr. Harry Thornton has a solid paper on The Later Works of George Cruikshank " with nu- nierous illustrations; Mr. W. E. A. Oxon contributes "Barber Folk Tales"; Mr. C. E. Tyrer, " Oxon, May"; and Mr. George Milner does justice to "A neg- lected Poet." There is an "In Memoriam" article with a portrait of the subject of the tribute—Dr. Adolph Samuel- son, while the Library table furnishers the reader with several thoughtful reviews. The Quarterly is published by Mr. John Heywood of Manchester.

WOD MON AW DO Wl' EAWR TUM? ' Wodever i'th' world mon aw do wi' eawr Turn? He's th' wost lad ov onny aw've sin ; For i' o manks o' lumber un mischief, bi gum! He's as certain as deoth to be in. Forth' windos he's brokken aw've paid mony a creawn, Un aw've lickt him, bud still he's just th' same; Un th' bad name ut's gie'n him bi fooak up un deawn, Wey, it's raylee a scandalous shame. He's full ov his gain as a egg's full o' meyt, Un allus good-natured un bowd; He keers nowt wod comes iv he's summat to eyt, Bud aw'm blest iv he does o he's towd. Aw darend tell his fayther for th' world wod he does, For he is Bitch a comical lad; Aw've lafft mony a time when he's spun me a "buzz," Just to wheedle me when aw geet mad. He's as quate as con be when his fayther's abeawt, Then he shapes a bit gradely un reight; Bud when th' husband's ut th' factory, or gooan wokin' eawt, Tura ull wrostle, un marlock, un feight. He's o sooarts o' hobbies, he's rapputs un hens, Un a whelp yon as big as a cawve, 0 th' lot ov a rook into the.pig-coyt he pet's; Thad ut's th' feawest he likes t' best bi th' hawf. He wears a striped jersey as fits tight to t' skin, Un aw'm towd as he plays ut footbo. They say he's a forrud i'th' team as he's in; Well, he's forrud ut hooam, thad aw know. He's one o'th' best beawlers as stept on a green, Boos th' lads reawnd abeawt allus say, Un ut buck off th' stick end, wey, he'd oppen yor een, Iv yo'd nobbia just watch him at play. Hey, wod antics he plays ! mi heart sinks to mi clogs, When aw think heaw eawr Turn carries on; He'll come lorryin' hooarn wi' gret letherin' dogs, Un boils urn hoss beef i' th' best pon. He's as wick as a snlg, un as plump as a bo', Aw wish aw could stop his wild rigs; Yesterday, ther wur fairly a noise med th' row, When Bob Burley fun eawt he'd green pigs! Owd Betty o' th' Speawt, sweears hoo'l wring his young neck For teem' hur door to fat Nan's, Wi' a rooap, across t' Fowd, as kept booath gabs i' check Till 'twur loasened bi Dick o' Daft Dan's. Owd Buttermilk Bill co's him th' imp o' owd Scrat, For this mornin' when he oppen'd th' door, He fun his bay mare wearin' th' tall Sunda' hat, As he'd left into th' barn th' fleet afoor. For o he's so keerless, un brimful o' fun, Ther's nooan better natured than him ; T'other week aw wur ill, un he sect off ut run For th' doctor, wi' eon red un dim. Un when he coom hick he wur quate as a lamb, Un his voice wur so, gentle un low, Then he ceawred bit!,' bedside, un he :sobbed, "Bless yo', rnam." Dud aw cuss him? Ay! clic, him un o! He's a bad un, bud herdly as bad as fooak sez ; He'd a feight t'other day wi a lad, Un he hided him wee!, causehe'd struck poor lame Bess. Neaw, heaw could aw sauce him for thad ! Wod rnon aw do wi' him? He'll happen soon mend, When youth's bed id bit ov a fling; He's my lad after o, un his main's his best friend, Un hoo will be—aeaw, that's a sure thing! JACK 0' ANN'S.

that his hearers were glad to listen to, both as to Wagner himself, and as to the theme he treated. Very interesting it was to hear of that first perfor- mance of this opera twenty years ago in the theatre at Munich—King Louis in the royal box and the composer by his side. When the curtain fell the icing led the musician to the front of the box to re- ceive the applause of a thronged house. With such little bits of personal detail the lecture• waS ren- dered specially attractive. But solidermatter was not left out. Mr. Armbruster had much to tell of the origin of these guilds, who, taking up the study of music and poetry that the nobles somehow had neglected, carried on this task from the fourteenth ' century, at first bravely and conscientiously, till the crust of clique and pedantry settling upon them, led them to absurd regulations, which Wagner satirised, and from which he drew the topics of his comic opera. Mr. Rider Haggard has set sail for Ireland, where be means to spend the London season. He has a new novel in prospect, and, casting about for a locality hitherto untilled by the novelist's hand, he has determined to try Ireland. He was tempted, be- fore deciding on this place, to visit the United States, where the indefatigable Major Pond, who "runs" all notabilities, from Mr. Matthew Arnold to Dr. Parker, invited him to undertake a series of lectures. The negotiation broke down on a question of terms. Mr. Haggard modestly estimated the value of his services at £lOO a night. This staggered Major Pond, who hastily closed the correspondence, and Mr. Rider Haggard was free to embark for Ireland.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THIJRSDA.I"

Lord Randolph Churchill's speech in the House of Commons, yesterday, obscures by its importance all other political events of the week, including the passing of the second reading of the Local Govern- ment Bill. Lord Randolph, with all his wayward- ness and occasional flippancy, has a habit of going straight to the heart of 'a matter, and he did this yesterday with an effect that has shaken a Ministry which, five minutes before he rose, was, throtigh the mouth of the Chief Secretary for 'lreland, exulting in its impregnable position. The whole scene was intensely dramatic. For .nearly two hours Lord Randolph had been sitting in the corner seat behind the Treasury Bench, where he hovers as a kind of Providence watching over poor Jack, represented in this case by Mr. W. 11. Smith and his colleagues. There was a strong whip out on both sides, and at this particu- lar moment every bench was full. The bill before the House was one of the long series drawn up under the immediate supervision of Mr. Parnell, and taken charge of by some one from the rank and file of his party. If it had been simply Mr. Carew bringing in his bill for the reform of Local Government in Ireland, the scene would have been very different. We should have had the usual desultory. Wednesday afternoon, with empty benches and interminable speeches. But behind Mr. Carew stood Mr. Parnell, with Mr. Parnell his compact party, and behind them again Mr. Gladstone and the full muster of the Liberal host.

At four o'clock Mr. Gladstone was speaking, mak- ing the third animated speech delivered in the course of the week. It seemed to little ,purpose that he should recall the pledges of Lord Salisbury's Government given in 1886 on this very question of Local Government in Ireland. Mr. Balfour lolled on the Bench, scornfully smiling. The Conservatives ciied "Oh, oh," and `iNo, no, and the Irish mem- bers kept up a constant fusillade of cheers for their redoubtable champion. It was the old, old story, the beating of the inconstant sea on the everlast- ing rocks. Mr. Balfour rose to reply in jubilant mood. Ile chaffed Mr. Gladstone, snubbed the Irish members, and made great fun out of some of the doings,of an obscure Board of Guardians in Ireland. which he selected as a fair specimen of the kind of local body to which it was proposed to ex- tend the powers of Local Government. As for the Bill, he would have nothing to do with it. It would be time enough to talk about establishing equality of law between Ireland and England at that indefinite period when there should have beeri established in Ireland what Mr. Balfour would re- gard as a state of peace and order—that is to say, a condition of unquestioning obedience to Castle rule.

Here it seemed the debate might end. It was close upon five o'clock; at half-past five the debate ' must necessarily close. Mr. Balfour had disposed of the whole business, and it only remained for Con- , servatives and Dissentient Liberals once more to , unite their forces and triumphantly reject this fresh cry from Ireland. It was then Lord Randolph Churchill rose, his opening sentence fixing the at- tention of the House. He had asplendid audience, prominent among them being Mr. Gladstone, lean- ing forward with hand to ear to catch every word. Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain sat side by side. From the Peers' Gallery Earl Spencer looked down on the memorable scene. Lord Randolph spoke with quite new earnestness, even approach-1 ingto solemnity. Atenetime his voice faltered,and he seemed as if, overcerne with emotion, he Ivo going to break down. But he went straight forward to the end, delivering the' most damaging speech which ever attacked a Government from within its own ranks. He said exactly what Mr. Gladstone had said an hour earlier, only it Was uttered with more authority and with more effect. Lord Ran- dolph was himself the Minister who, in 1886, had given that pledges of general and particular policy towards Ireland which he now declared was the foundation of thelinioniat party. The effect of the speech was indescHbable. The nearest parallel I can think of is a case in a criminal court, where the prisoner, accused of a capital offence, is just on the verge of acquittal when an accomplice comes for- ward. makes a clean break of the whole affair, and details the minutest particulars of the scene and circumstances of the.) crime.

_ Unlike many moving scenes in the House of Com- mons, this one is certain to have practical and im- portant effect upon Ministerial policy. If Lora Randolph stood alone, or in select company, as a Conservative rebel, it might be a difficulty which the Government would presently get over. But Lord Randolph, with his great adroitness and inborn skill in political tactics, took hikstand, not on Cor- aervatism, but on what he calle4 "Unionism," was as the spokesman of the Dissentient Libehas that he menaced the Government, and the know- ledge possessed on the Treasury Bench that earlier in the sitting he bad " been in conoritation with Mr. Chamberlain, lept added force to his position. Mr. Chamberlain backed him up, cautiously it is true, and subsequently voted with the GOvernment against the bill. But he did se specifically, on the ' understanding that the Government would abandon their non posaumus attitude towards the demand of Ireland for a reformed scheme of local governments That must come,and come speedily: or the Govern— ment will go to pieces. "After all" as Mr. Goshen says, Prince Henry of Battenberg accompanied the Queen to Berlin. This mrst undoubtedly be taken as a sign of the Queen triumph in the little battle that has been raging at the Court of Berlin. Of course, if Prince Henry chose to accompany the Queen as the late John Brown used to go about with her, no. objection coda be offered by the high and mighty dignitariet of the German court. But the Queen, who has made him Royal Highness" in this country,in- slated that if her son-in-law went at all he waS to be received as such, and as he is at present in Ber- lin it is presumed that this point has been yielded. It has been an Interesting, and doubtless an exci- ting struggle; the person to be least envied in the matter being the Unfortunate prince himself. The Marquis of Lorne has not found his royalty connec- tions a source of unqualified pleasure. But at least he has been spared this battle overr his body for a recognition which Foreign Courts and princes were aisinclined to give. The Campbells are at least of as ancient lineage as the Battenbergs. But the Marquis of Lorne's royal mother-in-law has never sought to take him about with her on her trips to foreign Courts upon a footing of equality. Both he and Princess Louise are left, very much to them- selves.

The Queen will sleep at Windsor on Saturday night. But her stay in the neighbourhood of Lon- don will not be long, as she leaves for Balmoral on the l&h of May, and will remain in Scotland for five weeks; that is to say, through the very height of the London season. To tradespeople and the upper crust of society chiefly concerned this would seem a serious matter. But it has come to be one of annual occurrence, and so has lost the sharp edge of novelty. As far as the Court is concerned, its intervention has this year been more than usually depressing. The Drawing Room hastily commanded for a couple of day 9 after the Queen left for the Continent was a source of great tribulation. A new cloud has arisen by the fixing of two draw- lug rooms for May the 9th and 16th, subject, it is well known, to anything that may happen at Ber- lin. Dresses will have to be ordered, and till arrangements made, with the dire contingency that death may simultaneously cut short the Emperor Frederick's life and the Queen Victoria's drawing room ceremopieS. . Mr. CarlArmbruster is continuing his lecture on the later works of Wagner. The lectures are given at the Royal Institute, and I attended the last. where I found an appreciative, interested, and aris- tocratic audience. The subject was-Wagner's comic , opera of the Meistersinger, and he had much to tell

div.head: WITWATERSRAND GOLD FIELDS.
div.p: WITWATERSRAND GOLD FIELDS.

The following letter, written by the son of a respected townsman, will be real' with interest as a graphic description of life in Soigh Africa:— . JOHANNESBURG, L.A.R., FEB. 17th, 1888. Sir,—Being a resident of the above wonderful place, some account of ,the journey to the Rand, arid also bf the Rand itself, may te of interest to some of your readers. 'After spending four days in Kimberley, and seeing all 'therewith connected, I took a seat by the mail coach from Kimberley to Johannesburg. There are various lines of conveyances from Kimberley to Johannesburg, the majority of which take from six to eight days with no night travelling. The mail coach takes three days, with fresh relays of ten horses every night and day. The cost of the journey by mail coach is £l2; by other coaches £5. Many people' with whom speed is co object prefer the £5 coaches, for there are excellent hotels all the way. Messrs. Heys & Co. have the mail coach,con- tract, and it is probable that as a service it is unique, for the arrangements are perfect. The average speed is seven miles an hour, which is, wonderful, censidering that in many•places the roads are dreadfullybad, and that rivers and streams are driven through at full speed, there being no such things as bridges. The mail coach carries 14 passengers, and each passenger is allowed about 301bs. weight of luggage, excludingpillows, rugs, &c. It is a very ,trying journeyfor ladies or delicate people, forrdeep is out of the question (on the mail coach), by reason of the oc- casional and sudden terrific jolts. It would be advisable for ladies, &c., to travel by the Jubilee coach, which does not travel at night, and gives passengers a good night's rest in a comfortable wayside hotel. During the whole journey we passed and crossed innumerable ox waggons, mule and transport cars loaded with machinery, &c., also many foot passengers, everything yielding before the mail coach's bugle. The way the coach, with its ten horses, is manipulated by the Boer drivers over danger- ous places and through streams at full speed is marvel- lous. The coaches are of American build, and rest upon combination leather springs of immense strength and elasticity. .

After twelve hours driving we reached the Vaal river, and the coach and ten horses were taken over the river on an immense raft or punt. On crossing the river we were in the Transvaal, and the coach stopped at Christiana whilst the passengers dined at the hotel. The country from Christiana to Rlerksdcrf is very level, and for the next 18 hours we could sleep. At daybreak we observed that we were in a most lovely country. We arrived at Potchefstrom at six pan. Potchefstrom is a pretty vil- lage of 3,000 inhabitants. We stayed at the Royal Hotel.' An excellent dinner was provided, and we were allowed five hours' rest.

At two a.m. we left again in a drizzling rain, and at daybreak noticed that the country was of the same luxuriously fertile nature we observed the day before, but not one inch is cultivated; all is allowed to waste. in passing over these vast tracts of land, one cannot but think bow different it might have been in English hands, opened up to the fields with a railway. At two p.m. we sighted Johannesburg, and at 3-30 drove into the town. The plade was overcrowded, and al- though there are numerous hotels, etc., it was with the, utmost difficulty that I managed to get a floor to sleep on.

In September, 'BB, the Witwatersrand district was de- clared a public gold field. At that time there were pro- bably not 25 people in the plaite i , and to-day Johannes- burg sas big as Cape Town, and rapidly growing, and numbers 12,000 inhabitants. There is probably no par- allel in the history of ancient or modern times to the marvellously rapid growth of this town. Buildings are solid, and not as they were in the diggings of Australia, made of canvas. ' Large squares are laid out, and ini- merous hotels, quite equal to the best in South Africa, are here. Five banks are busy as bee-hives. Seven news- papers are in full daily swing. The Theatre Royal supplies all the most recent plays and operas to theatre goers. Two fashionable cubs .meet the requirements of social life. The Rand Club is a fine building, the dining hall seats 100 men, and reading, coffee, smoking, and billiard rooms are attached. To become a mem- ber, one requires to be proposed, seconped, name up for one month, and balloted' for. The entrance fee £l5. There are Churches of England, Wesleyan, Roman Catholic, and Dutch Reformed chapels. The Stock Ex- change is a magnificient building, and some immense Government buildings are now in courw of erection at the top of Market-square. , The Witwatersrand Fields offer no scope to poor peo- - for the gold is not alluvial, and has to be extracted by most expenSiVe machinery from the ore or " banket." As is usual, there are no end of bogus companies floated here, and let the inexperienced beware 'how they invest their money. The place is overdone with clerks, but strady blacksmiths, joiners, carpenters, miners, trust- worthy men for batteries, are in great demand from 203 to lOs a day, The sanitary arrangements are, of course, not good yet, and there is no light in the streets yet, but in the course of the year thesa defects will be remedied. The climate is cool by reason of the altitude, and In summer it rains almost incessantly. It is to be hoped that immediate steps will be taken to remedy the sani- tary arrangements, otherwise epidemics cannot be escaped. There is not the slightest friction between the Transvaalers and the English. The Boers know too well where the almighty dollar comes from which is filling , their coffers. - ' I

As regards the Witwatersrand financially. The nomi- nal capital is £3,238,500. The subscribed or working capital is £824,560. The return of gold for February will be equal to about 17,000 ounces, worth £3 15s per ounce, equal 4o £63,750. The number of stamps which is returning this amount may be estimated at not more than 800 heads, and this is equal to approximately £BO per stamp per month. There are erected and in course of erection 1,400 heads of stamps, and at least 2,000 heads of stamps will be working before the end of July of the present year. Several of the mines have paid over 50 per cent for six months working, with exceptional difficulties to overcome. Computing the present output of gold and deducting therefrom working expenses, which can be put down at the high figure of '2ss per oz. of gold saved, the Witwatersrand gold fields are return- ing 15 per cent on the notninal capital thus :—Return of gold, £83,750 ; leas 258 per oz. on 17,000 oz. £21,250—; £42,500; nett profit per month, £42,500--£LIO,OOO pet annum, which it will be easily seen represents over 15 per 'cent an the nominal capital.--Now, seeingthat 15 per cent is at present being obtained on the nominal capital with 800 stamps, it must be clear that when the stamp's are in- creased the profits will be infinitely greater, so that the future of the fields is most brilliant, for the reef extends over 40 miles. The cost of mining on these fields is at present computed at 18s 9d a ton, and that is a very high rate as compared with the cost of mining in Australia and America ; however, with the exceptional facilities' there are here, operations will be eventually carried on at a very small cost. Coal can be got in large quantities 25 miles from this centre, and although the price at pre- sent is 50s a ton, it is expected that before long it will be delivered at 30s, the price of coal at the pit being,los a ton. I send you herewith a tabulated statement of the gold mining conipanies of the Witwatersrand goldfields, compiled bMessrs. Frater, Hutton, and• Co., the well- known brokers of Johannesburg.' Mr. William Hutton, of Prater, Hutton, and Co.,- has just left here to establish an office in Lenclun, and should any of your 'readers de- sire to see specimens of gold quartz from here, or see the interesting process of washing and panning, Mr. Hutton, who is the soul of urbanity, will be glad to demonstrate and explain. 'Address, meanwhile, carei of Standard Bank of South Africa, 10, Clements-lane, London, E.C. I intend shortly. visiting Pretoria' Barberton, Malmani, to return by 144dysinith and Natal, and will send yoti some aceount of these fields.—l am, sir, yours truly, WARRING' TONIAN.

div.head: CHAPTER XV.. FOR CONSCIENCE SAKE.
div.p: CHAPTER XV.. FOR CONSCIENCE SAKE.

The dinner in Eaton-square, alter Simon Knight's departure was a very silent one. Both Geoffrey and Irene saw that some subject of a serious nature was engrossing the attention of their father and mother, and as, from what they themselves knew, they believed it to be Ferdinand's delinquencies; they had too much tact to rush with small social babbling on to ground which was evidently, • appro- priated by far graver interests. Old Marks, how- ever, at last took himself off for good, ,to carry con- sternation to the housekeeper's room by informing Mrs. Purvis that "the master looked as black as thunder, and if someone else isn't going to catch it all round, well, he hadn't lived ten years in the Stanhope family.l "Of course the someone was Ferdinand," Mrs.' Purvis decided. She was so accustomed to his being treated as the black sheep that she could not believe anyone else would be likely to come in for a share of the master's anger." • "Though Mr. Geoffrey deserves it quite as much as Ferdinand "purvis has long sincedecided. "She would just go upstairs and listen, she thought; "now the servants had left the room it was pretty sure some word would be let drop.".-• - Tile dessert, however, was well nigh as silent as the dinner had been, and Parvis was beginning to thlik that the dining-rooni mus,t be already vaes.teld: when the door opened so Saddenly that she had only time to: catch up a dish which had- been forgotten, and which it certainly was not her duty to remove, and mutter so/nettling about" them feather-headed Men who never remembered nothing," when Mr. Stanhope t strode out of the dining-room and passed her without seeming to notice that she was there. ' "Law 1" 'she said 'to herself while she made oA down the kitchen stairs as fast as she could. "If the master don't look' as if he'd seen aghost. There'll be a change in this yeie house afore long, and 'preps me and Marks 'ill be cast out to do as best we can in the wide world. There's always a death when folks looks as the master does to-night. He's gdne into that study too andleft her ladyship at the table." Another moment and the slamming of the street. door broughtPurvis' astonishment to a sort of climax, for Mr. Stanhope was not in the habit of going out in the evening, but that he had gone out now she Was very certain. Meantime the trio who had been left in the dining-room seemed in no hurry to leave it. It had ever been One it Lady Fedora's .rules with her children to abstain as much as possible from. secrets, and as, between Geoffrey and Irene, she did not think that any existed, it was not her desire to make one if she could possibly avoid it. Irene gave her an opening to begin the conversa- tion by saying "How' dreadfully ill papa looks this evening. Has anything awful happened ? " Lady Fedora stated briefly and practically as much as she judged it expedient thattheyshould bothlcnow of Ferdinand's shortcomings, and then made a pause as though waiting' for an, answer. But no. answer came ;• Geoffrey sat' with his head down, playing with his waistcoat buttons; Irene, with a mixture of horror andwonder on her face,was watching .Geoffrey; yet neither Prince Sergius nor Simon Knight had been mentioned. Lady Fedora wa,s puzzled; she could not understand that a statement which chewed that some thousands would be required to free the family from the disgrace of Ferdinand's perpetual gambling shortcomings, should be met with so much seeming apathy: It must be her own fault, she decided; she must put the matter a little more forcibly. • "He has given bills to the extent of nearly a thou- sand pounds, she said, "and someone to whom we don't wish to be under an obligation has backed these bills." _ _

" Indeed I Who has been fool enough ?" asked Geoffrey, at last. • "Geoffrey,, pray don't speak in that tone. Remem- ber, notwithstanding his faults, Ferdinand is your brother; he must be helped. The individual who has kindly come forward is Prince Sergius. Irene became as red as a peony, and Geoffrey burst out laughing. "No fitter man," he said, "rich and anxious to please. If he would carry-Ferdinand off to Siberia and remain there to see he did his duty, we should be .killing.twO evilomened birds with one stone."

"Geoffrey ! And both the ladies in different tones uttered his nanu3 together. Nothing daunted, however' by their seeming displeasure, he got up ant began to walk about the room. There was a good deal of decision of character about Geoffrey,notwithstanding his rather effeminate appearance and frequently almost letharg icinsouci- ance. The fact is, he lived to a great extent in a world of his own creating, leaving the practical exigencies of life to be worked out by his father, who had hitherto left him completely outside the pale of his private affairs. Once admitted there, there was little doubt but Geoffrey would act with an amount of worldly acumen, for which perhaps neither of his parents gave him credit. He had a sort of instinctive idea that Lady Fedora had some pur- pose 'in speaking of Ferdinand's shortcomings, a pubject which she had never broached before, and he at once resolved to receive the confidence with care.

"I mean what I say," he replied, in answer to the duet of exclamation, "I hate that philandering Ruindmi, mid Irene knows it full well." Lady Fedora was aghast; this was a fresh complica- tion fox' Which she was not prepared. She fesOlved, however, not to appear as if she were taken aback. "I am sorry, you do not like Prince Sergius' " she replied very quietly," but' ascribe your dislike to mere English prejudice against foreigners, which in these days, when steam and electricity bring us till so closely together, you should, my dear boy, learn to surmount." - -

Geoffrey shrugged his shoulders rather irritably, but this Lady Fedora did not wish to perceive am. went on: "It is not, however, of Prince Sergius that I, would talk to you just now, but of port, Ferdinand. He has got himself, and in fact all of us, into difficulties. Yipur dear father is at his wit's end; for all our sakes he has been struggling more than either of you children can dream of to keep annoyance, indeed dishonour, from our door. He can do no more ; every acre of his estates is mort- gaged; he absolutely (onnot raise this money for Ferdinand unless—" and once more she stopped, as though hoping that an offer would be made which would prevent her from having to ask a favour from her eon. -

Pleading wife and mother, she was doomed to dis• appointment, for Geoffrey interrupted rather eagerly. This is the first time, mother, that my father's affaim have over been discussed with me. I have never, therefore, considered that I had any right to give an opinion about them; now you have given me that right I will do so freely. I have naturally known 'more of what has been going ,on than perhaps you 'even know yourself, and I say now without flinching that it has scarcely met with my approval." "Geoffrey. you have ventured to condemn your father, a father who has had so much care and thought for you all." " Yes, mother, Ido dare-for conscience, sake. For years now we have not had the ready money to live as we have been living. Then why make the effort? Is not doing so a cheat and a fraud? Ought we not to have retrenched, and by boldly shewing the world we were honest, should we not have gained commen- dation rather than blame?" ' _

_ . "My boy, you are severe, especially as it was for your sakes that this struggle was made. Our darling Irene well married; Ferdinand launched in the world —you, yourself, Geoffrey, settled in life with some pretty, heiress, then your father and I hope to retire in the background, and save up the sums b.e had raised to start you all. You, my children awe the last who should blame, for if his hopes of success have proved abortive, you, rather than your father, have created the disappointment. Irene seems the only one of his children likely to carry out his wishes," and Lady Fedora drew her daughter to her and kissed her on the brow. Even, however, as she did so, a shade passed over her own, for she remembered what opposition any allusion to Irene's marriage with the Prince had called forth from Henry Stanhope. "A beastly foreigner l" muttered Geoffrey: Lady Fedora raised her face, still lingering In a caress on her daughter's brow, and said, with a sort of gasp— " A foreigner, Geoffrey, is not so bad as —But no, my son, I will not malign you; that which I have heard is not true, but the mere senseless ramblings of a besotted bfain." Geoffrey looked surprised. "I don't know what You mean," he said. "No, dear boy; just as well, perhaps, that you should not; "for Lady Fedora was diplomat enough n2t to wish to discuss with Geoffrey whether he is or was not in love with Phyllis Knight until that other money point, about which she was so deepry interested, had been settled. Mostuse,—Seeing that it 'was the first time Queen Victoria had get foot on Austrian territory, the meeting of her Majesty and the Emperor Francis Joseph- Was one of momentous interest. The reception was ef a nature so thoroughly unofficial that even the representa- tives of the press—both native and foreign—were kept in the background, whilst, the public •in general was refused admittance to' the platform. There was no military, no band, no civic presentations, and every demonsteative greeting ITSS strictly forbidden. A. the train' glided in the Emperor, in the uniform of an Austrian Field Marshal, followed by Prince Hohenlohe, emerged from the reception-room, and hastened to Resist his Royal guest 'to alight. The Speaskec took the,chair at 3 5 p.m. Petitions were presented against the compensation clauses Of the Local Government Bill by Mr. P. S. Powell from Wigan; Sir H. Roscoe frmn Good Templar lodges in South Lancashire; and Mr. Sully from the same hi 'Carlisle.

The 'Chancellor of the Exchequer was again ques- tioned about the 'horse tax, and raised a laugh by the replythat he certainly should not regard cab and omni- bus 'horses as "pleasure horses," nor would the vehicles that they drew be classed as carriuges. Asked by Mr.ldaple if he had considered the repre- sentations made to him on the subject of the wheel tax, MT. GOSCHEN alimitted that he had in his mind a scheme for modifyingthe tax, but in 'view of the deputation which was •to wait upon him next day he thought his statement upon it had better be delayed.

THE INCREASE OF IRISH SENTENCES ON APPEAL. Several questions were asked in regard to the increase of sentences upon appellants in Ireland, wfto had been convicted under the Crintes Act, and the Home Secre- tary and the Lord Advocate were respectively invited to state their experience Mr. Mar-maws was understood to say that there had been cases of the kind in England; but the 'LORD ADVOCATE, amid Irish cheers, answered that in Scotland such practices were not followed. Sii WU. HARCOURT supplemented an inquiry put by Mr. James Stuart, as to how many cases the Solicitor- Gene/ for Ireland had known of as having occurred in Ireland, in the last ten years, in which a sentence appealed against by the person convicted was increased by the Court of Appeal.—Mr. MADDEN answered that he had not the information at hand.—Sir WIC HAR- COURT, however, asked who was the proper person to apply to.—Mr. MADDEN admitted his responsibility, but- submitted he had already answered the question. —Amid loud cheers from the Irish members Sir Wm. HARCOURT again pressed Mr. Madden for a reply,— Finally the Solicitor-General said that, so far as his personal knowledge went, there had been no such cases as those referred to In the question.

div.head: MR, GLADSTONE ON THE EQUALISATION
div.p: MR, GLADSTONE ON THE EQUALISATION
OF THE DEATH DUES.
The House then went into Committee of 'Ways and Means. On the second reading of the Customs and In- land Revenue Bill,

Mr. Gtans-rost, rising at 4 50, Moved the following amendment :—" That in the opinion of this House, after Parliament shall have made the appropriations it may deem just in relief of local rates, the duties accruing upon deaths should he so fixed as to equalise the charge Upon real and personal- property respectively." Mr. Gladstone claimed tied his resolution would not in- crease the financial diffieulties of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, but ratheptincrease, is accepted, his re- sources, which would give him an opportunity of exer- cising greater freedom in regard to his financial policy.. He entertained a strong omnion that the death duties, upon personalty ought nit to he reduced. The amend-, ment meant an increase or the death duties upon real! property, and eonsequestly an augmentation of the fund, which was at the Chancellor of the Exchequer's disposal. , The augmentation was particularly seaaenable in view of the fact that ti- re were before the 'House a nuniber' of proposals for new taxes with respect to some of which he entertained the gravest doubts. (Opposition cheers.) The first of the propositions he 'wished to day down was that the present enormous disparity under the death duties between the charge 'upon realty and the charge upon the personalty was :only tolerated because of the advantage enjoyed by personal' in. respect to its limited contribution towards the rates. He did not know whether people generally were aware what that disparity was. The total amount of the death duties was £7,519,000. Of this sum personalty paid .4.'6,980.000, and realty £650,000. peisonany pitying at the rate :of :nearly-5 per cent, and realty at. the rate of 13-16,4 per cent. 'Under the present law, therefore, personalty paid almost ex- actly six times what realty did. (Opposition .cheers.el Under these circumstances he contended that this an no other was the occasion when the disparity should be remedied and removed. (Cheers.) It :wairnot'for him to say what was the sum that ought to'be paid over by the Exchequer to the local treasury. All he said was that the sum ought now to be consideredand fixml. It was a question of doing justice between the 'Various kinds of propert9- There was it supposition -that the whole question lay between realty and :personalty, but than that there could not be a MOTO gross mistake. It was necessary t: distinguish between 'rated personalty and unrated personalty. A Parliamentary-return pre- sented when Lord Salisbury's first Government was in office showed that £4,820,000,000 of personalty was sub- ject to rates, and that £4,590.000.000 vrasnot-subject to rates, so that the whole burden of rates and of local taxation was at present laid upon a little more' than one- half the property of the country. Mr. GOSCIIEN said the whole of the ,£.800,000,000 of railway property included in the amount he had taken' was not rated.

Mr. GLAD STONE said the railwar property which was visible had to bear a charge upon the whole. There was, therefore, a very good and a strong case for adjustment, and this tikparity ought to. be removed. He had also to 'submit that under the proposals ot the iGovernment from £4,000 000 to £5,000,000 now leriedimoneferm or other upon personalty would eo in aittof•rates,.and par- ticularly in aid of realty and the landed interests, for while seven-twelfths of subvention wae‘thelandlord's ultimate share, five-twelfths would be 'the ,ultimate share of the occupier. Now he came to a most im- portant proposition, which was that there would remain after the rectifying process .of the Chancellor of the Exchequer it gross disparity between the charge under the death duties upon personalty and the, charge under the death duties upon land. Personalty would: pay to the Exchequer £2,054,000. 'He 'understood the proposal to he that the 1 per cent. succession duty was to be raised to LI. and that the •other rates on the consanguinity scale were to have per cent. added. The result would be that the whole amount .paid • to the Exchequer on the probate, legacy, and succession duties would be £5,046,000, and that amount,citarged on 133. millions, represented 3R per cent. Realty would pay a total amourt of £840,000 as the entire charge upon 570 millions worth of property, which represented I 1-sth per cent.. so that after the Chancellor of•the Exchequer had deliberately proposed the addition of per cent., to be by way-of establishing a sort, of equality between the death duty charge on personalty and that on realty, .he made the comparison of figures, and be ,came to. the conclusion that there still remained a system under which personalty would be charged .3/ per cent., and realer would be charged 1 1-5 i it per cent,—that was to say, personalty would continue to bear three, times the charge of realty (Loud •Opposition cheers.) How was it pesSible to justify such a state of! things as that, and what view would the public take of it? Now he came to his last proposition. immoveable' personalty, which had by far the largest and strongest claim, would still ieinail liable to that gross inequality.' Visible personalty was represented by real property, mines, ironworks, leaseholders and occupiers of mes- suages and tenements, and he wanted to show the griev- ances those people would still suffer. Though the claim: of landed property was a strong one, it was by far the; weakest., because he urgency of that eitina had +mainly. arisen in connection with the fact that there 'had been an; enormous increase in the rates. Between 18'T4 and 1885 • there had been an increase in London of £2,623,000, or 67 per cent., while in the case of all other urban districts outside the Metropolis there had been an increase of £2,729,000, or 59 per cent. In the mixed urban and rural districts the increase was £1,194,000, or 13.8 per cent.; while in the purely agricultural districts the increase dwindled down to £213,000, or 12 per cent. The landlords were going to have the benefit of the whole contrib.,tion. The increase of 60 per cent. its the rates in the Metropolis, and of 59 in. the other urban districts, was an increase nearly the ' whole of which had fallen on the owners of visible per- sonal property. )ther classes had been touched on one ; side only. The owners of real property had been touched by the rates, end not by the death duties. Tne owners of visible ,personal estate had been hit both ways—by the rates and by the worst of rates, the peobate duty and the death duty. It was the case with this enormous mass of property held by occupying tenants, and they were lost and merged in the equalise, Lion scheme.. He had shown their claims to be a maximum, and their gains to•bea minimum. They gained from the income tax, and from the succession duty; but they would pay enormously under the probate duty, and yet the plan was a good plart. They gave 2 millions of the probate duty as compensation to the ratepayers. But the owner of visible propetty paid his full share to the fund out of whieet he was compensated, while the landed proprietor gets his compensation from other parties. (Hear, hear.) The position of the owner of visible pro- perty was this, that the Chancellor of the Exchequer put money into one of his pockets and extracted it from another. Ile will have to pay through the medium of probate ditty. He will be called upon to pay under the death duties three times as much as is levied on the landed proprietor. (Cheers.) Sir M. Heess-Benert, remarking that Mr. Gladstone had not put his principles into practice when he was in uffice, maintained t not ha present suggestions would be unjust and far from a complete settlement.

Mr. Haldane, Sir H. Paet., Mr. O'Doberty, Mr.. Elton, Mr. Sidney G.:Age, and Mr. Shaw-Lefevre continued the debate, the latter contending that the Inequalities and injustice of the death duties could not be for a moment defended.

Mr. SLUM pointed out that agriculture had not been alone of late years in suffering distress and privation. On the contrary, the landed classes had really come off the best. Their losses were inconsiderable in compari- son with the enormous disasters which had hefillen nearly every industry in the country.
