1.0r4 'FlAirrisurox said that whether the Government treated this resolution as a vete of want of confidenceer not, it must have the effect nf setting aside the whole financial proposals of the Government and the Local Government Bilk Consequently, even if be agreed more completely than he did with Mr. Gladstone's argu- ments, he should hesitate to vote for the resolution. ME. CHILDERS failed to SOO that the tat QUOT&C argu- ment of Lord Hartington was an Answer to the resolu- tion, and denied that it would in any way prejudice the Local Government Bill or the local Budget proposals. Contrasting The speech of SirM. Hicks-Beach with re- cent statements by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, be maintained that they did not coincide, and claimed that the Budget .d 1885 and the amendment were identical in principle. The CHANCELLOR of the t XCIUQUER, while accepting Mr. Gladstone's chaVenge, pointed out that a good many of his figures—" piling up the millions," as he described it—were conjectural, and also that no answer had been given to Sir Michael Hicks-Beach's demonstration that local taxation still fell mare heavily on realty than personalty. Sir W. HARCOURT, commenting on Lord Hartington's speech, protested against his disclaimer of responsibility for the Budget of 1885, which, he asserted, was in direct opposition to constitutional usage. The question at issue was whether 'land should continue to enjoy the immunity which it did not enjey in any other country in Europe; and in the present Budget land, he main- tained, NOW very exceptionally treated. The division was then taken, and Mr. Gladstone's resolution was negatived by 310 to 217. Mr. Ptcrow moved the adjournment of the debate, which was resisted by Mr. W. H. SMITH, and, on an appeal from Sir W. Haricot-tar, it was not pressed, and the bill was read a second time, the Committee being fixed for Thursday. The House adjourned at 12 40 a.m. 1101.75 E OF LORDS.—Tinisircr.

The Lord Chancello-r*took his seat at 4 15 p:m. MUSICAL 'COPYRIGHT BILE—The Earl of 'ONSLOW moved the -second reading of a bill to amend the law with reference to the copyright of musicaLcompositions. Persons were now able to recover 40s. and.costs in all cases where an infringement of copyright songs was proved. The costs obtained in these car,es'amounted to so largea-sum as to become a species of blackmail. The bill intended to remedy this by leaving the amount of costs to the discretion of the judge trying the case.— The bill was read a second time. Tarres.—On the motion of Lord Ssusnour, the Tithe Rent Charge Bill was read a second time without dis- cussion.—Lord SALISBURY then moved the second readinrof the Tithe Charge Recovery and Variation Bill. DELAWARR expressed the opinion that the tenant farmers were not beaefited by the bill, whilst the position,of landlords was worse.—The Archbishop of Carrassintr, al behalf of the clergv, thanked the Govern- ment for the pains taken to introduce a bill which would not do injustice to the clergy. The clergy were suffer- ing so much from agricultural distress that a very con- siderable fund had been raised, and was being distri- buted.smongst the clergy. The clergy as a whole ac- cepted the bill, although it caus^d them an immediate loss for the next two years of eight per cent —Lord SAussuar sold the bill sought to get rid of the objec- tionable ani costly process of enforcing a payment of i tithes, but did not n any way do away with the obliga- tion to pay tithes.—The bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at 6 15. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tunsnar.

The Speaker took the chair at, 3 p.m. ?dr:Balfour was questioned as to whether he was pre- parefl to give further explanation to the House of the action of the police and military at Ennis ; but the CHIEF SECRETARY merely replied that he saw no reason for supplementing the statements he had already made. Mr. W. Macdonald came into cDnflict with the Speaker, in -reference to some questions which he had upon the paper. Flia complaint was that his questions had been considerably modified.—The SPEAKER accepted respon- sibility for the altered form of the question, and called upon the hon. member to put it. —Mr. MACDONALD, however, angrily answered that he would not ask the question at all. Mr. tqtaw-I.grityna inquired of the Attorney-General whether there was any practice prevailing in cour.ts of quarter sessins in England to aggravate sentences in Appeals in criminal cases, as was now being done in Ire- land. The 'lrish members cheered loudly.—Sir W. WEnsran said the Quarter Sessions certainly had such power,' but whether it had been exercised, and, if so, how many times, he was unable to say. EXCITED DEBATE.
THE 'IRISH CRIMTNAL APPEALS-MOTIONS FOR

be turned to the Speaker and said I wish to sob you' whetherit is relevant to discuss the action Government in a bill of last session? -1-7 r 137111 r/ The-Sesanatts: The question rose as to whether the right bon, gentleman had observed some promise which ho gave-with reference to appeal, and therefore the allu- sions that have been made seem to me to be certainly relevant to the subject before the House. (Loud Oppo- sition and Parnellite cheers.) Mr. GLADSTONE: Is there the smallest doubt that the power of appeal was given entirely in the interests of the person who received a sentence? Yet it had now been wantonly and cruelly used against him. We claim that that, after what has been promised, is a breach of faith. (Opposition cheers.) The first attempt tolivade and nullity this power of appeal was by accumulated sentences, a ,trick of the meanest order—(bud Irish cheers) the dishonour and discredit' of which I will not attempt to divide between the Govern- ment and the authorities in Ireland. The Government found that by the accumulation of sentences they„evoked public indignation, and that practice has not been repeated. Bat the Government say our resources have not yet been exhausted. We possess ao2ther power, namely, the power of enlarging the seated& in a court 3f appeal, which will make you think twice or thrice before you resort to this power of appeal. Sir William Harcourt complained of the power as one which ought not to be used at all, but which was now for the first time put into action. Is there a case in which Quarter Sessions in this country has increased a criminal sentence On appeal If there is not, I sar there is a case that there is no such power in England— (Cheers)—and if there is no such power in England, it ought not to be exercised in Ireland, unless indeed you wish to exhibit what Mr. Disraeli used to call anPorgan- ised hypocrisy—a pretence that nothing in the nature of equality or right treatment is to be accorded to the people of the Sister Isle. (Cheers.) The ATTORNEINGENERAL said they had just listened to a speech in which insinuation and innuendo had been freely hurled at every one who was responsible for the government of the country and the administration of the law in Ireland. (Mmisterial cheers.) Three or four very serious charges had been made. The tight hon. gentleman had thought fit to characterise the conduct of the Government as organised hypocrisy—(Opposition cheers)—and that .auggestion he was not entitled now to withdraw. (Miniliterial cheers.) He (the speaker)— though without the right hon. gentleman's command of language—would endeavoar to meet these charges, and would venture to throw them back upon him and show there was no foundation for them. (Government cheers.) Among the remainder of the language Mr. Gladstone had thought fit to make use of, with the responsibility of his years, was that in which he spoke of the Government having "evaded and nullified the power of appeal by tricks-of the meanest order." (Loud Home Rule cheers.) The hon. members for Newcastle cheered. (Renewed cheers.) The SPEANER : Order, order. .

_ The ArSORNET-GENRRAT., resuming, said Mr. Gladstone went on to say he would have thought that every honest man would have condemned those tricks. What did Sir George Trevelyan think of that statement in that House some weeks before the Government produced chapter and verse in which. under the. Crimes Act of 1882, and with Sir George 'frevelyan as Chief Secretary in Mr. Gladstone's Government, exactly the same thing was done. (Loud cheers and counter cheers.) Sir Wm Harcourt had also attributed a breach of faith to the Chief Secretary, bnt far that allegation he (the speaker) declared there was not the slightest foundation. (Loud cries of " Oh" from the 'lrish benches.) The accusa- tions, he might-point out, were not established by cries of " Oh." That, 1w,..-ever, was .not the point on which the motion of the night had been raised. Sir Wu. HARCOURT: The Chief Secretary said; " I will give a n appeal to the County Court Judge in every , case," but afterwards that was withdrawn, and no ap- peal was given in sentences of under a month. Sir CHAS. ItUsSRLI, who was cheered by'the Opposi- tion on rising, reminded the House that in the discussion 1 on the Crimes Act the 'lrish Secretary had distinctly said, "We (the Government) propose.to give an appeal ,in every case." That pledge was unmistakable, and it had not been carried out. ,(Opposition cheers.) He urged the House not to permit any additional grievance to be added in Ireland totheexistine•flame of discontent and distrust and hatred Tor a law which was odious in itself, and Um administration of which was in many res- pects disreputable. Mr. GLADSTONE: May 1 make an .explanation with reference to the answer made to me by the Attorney- General. Be said with great truth that I had on a former occasion stigmatised as a very mean trick a par- ticular proceeding of EL,COuTt of justice in Ireland. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL remarked that the right hon. gentleman had made that statement that evening. Mr. GLADsTONEI And that I had referred to the charge again to-night. It is quite true I listened to the answer of the Chancellor .on that occasion, and it then an-, neared to me not St all to touch the point. (Hear, hear.) On looking at his speech its reported, it appears to me that the report had been considerably enlarged--(Oppo- sition cheers)—and made-much clearer than it was as I heard it That may have been rhy fault. All I wish to say is that I cannot change my opinion of the Act, whether done coder our Government or any other. (Irish cheers.) 1 entirely agree that if there was a similar act done -under our Government, I personally am completely put .out•of 'court, and have no right to make any charge against the present Government in regard to this particular action. (Cheers.) Sir Geo. TR/MST:MN: It is, I think, unfortunate, in dealing with this .judioialmatter, to say anything about abuse in England or Irchied. (Ooposi t ion cheers.) The right hon. gentleman then went on to refer to the case of Mr. Blanc. That hon. meniber hal, he said, last year brought a charge against a resident magistrate, and, he believed, moved to reduce his salary. It was by this very magistrate that the 'hon. member was sent to gaol, and was sent to be treated as a common misdemeanant. (Irish cheers.) Mr. W. H. Sulam protested against the course taken by the right hen. gentlemen opposite. They desired to discredit by every possible means the judges In the dis- charge of their ifuties—(Ministerial cheers)—and even to intimidate them in the discharge of those duties. (Irish cries of • "Order") 'lt warthe first time that right hon. gentlemen who had held office had rebuked the Executive Government and their nominees on the Bench for impropriety, partialit-,-, and incapacity, and he confidently naked the House to reject such unworthy suggestions. (Ministerial cheers.) The House then divided, loud cheers being elicited from the Irish benches upon the announcement of the Opposition whips as tellers for the motion. There ap- peared For the adjournment lB5 Against .
The. result was greeted with loud Opposition cheers and counter cheers.

HOUSE OF COMMONS—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at half-past twelve o'clock. COUNTY GOVERNMENT .IN IRELAND. Mr. CARSOV moved the second reading of the County Government (Ireland) Bill, asserting that the desirability of dealing with and reforming local government was ad- mitted by all parties in Ireland and that the force of pub- lic opinion was behind his bill—Mr. Smint-Banar said the measure seemed to go a great deal further than the English bill, and it would sweep away the loyal minority on every board in Ireland.—After remarks from Mr. Clancy, Colonel Waring, Mr. J. O'Connor, and Sir C. Lewis, Mr. GL.t.DSTONE said that in 1881 local government was promised to Ireland in the Queen's Speech, and at that time the amount of agrarian crime was four times what it was now. That promise was repeated from time to time, and the party which was returned to power after the election of 1888 indignantly repudiated as a cruel and unworthy imputation that they intended to with- hold local government, and yet the Government had not thought to do anything to redeem the pledge on which its majority was elected. They bad withdrawn their promise' and declared that till Ireland had foregone its national aspirations and withdrawn its claim to a central government for Irish affairs in Dublin, no local govern- ment bill would be 'extended to it. Every man who on this occasion refused to say " Aye " to the second reading of the bill be- came by implication a party to that declaration. Mr. BALFOUR said he would never be a party to refusing Ireland any reform of local institutions because the people keld one or the other of two political convictions, but it was not possible for the Government to bring in a Local Government Bill for Ireland at present, because the time was inopportune, and because it would be used as an instrument to carry out a political and a social revo- lution.—Lord R. Csuakintt attacked the Government for breaking their pledges with•respect to local govern- ment for Ireland. He did not hesitate to state that the pledges to produce a Local Government Reform Bill were the foundation of the Unionist party, and he believed that it was the only platform on which they could resist repeal.—Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Morley, and Mr. W. H. Smith having spoken the House divided, with the result that the second reading was negatived by a majority of 87. The House adjourned at 10 minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THITIASDAY. . .

The Lord a312.e110r took his se-ai—JrTii;; Woolsack at half-past four o'clock. There was a large attendance of peers, and several peereqqes were present in the side galleries. REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS. The House discussed, on the motion for its second read- ing, Lord Dunraven's bill for the reform of the House of Lords. According to the noble earl's explanatory state- ment, the reformed House would contain 180 hereditary peers, representing the hereditary peerage of the country, about 120 lords of Parliament sent up by the new county councils, ten colonial representatives, two Nonconformist, and two Roman Catholic representatives, two representatives of learning and science, and ten representatives of our great colonial interests; besides the peers of thq blood Royal, the law lords, and the bishops and the representatives of the counties—an array of consultative and deliberative power amounting to about 400 in number. Lord DEN- mix moved that the bill be read a second time that day six months. After speeches by the Earl of Pembroke, the Earl of Camperdown, and Earl Cowper,

the MARQUIS of SALISBURY criticised adversely the/ of the measure, and intimated Oat w ible the Government could con- den tdreading, but promised that the Goverbment would make a beginning in the direction of reform by plachig before the House a measure for facili- tating the entry of life peers.—The Earl of DUNRAVEN: on the suggestion of the Earl of HARROWBY, with- drew the bill, explaining that his great object had been to get the Governmenb to take up the question. The Electric Lighting Act (1882) Amendment Bill was read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at eight o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair shortly after three o'clock. Tan POST OPFICE. SAVINGS liont.—ln reply to Mr. Wodehouse, the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said it was not the fact that the cost to the country of the Post Office Savings Banks was more than £3 per cent. He- had no intention at present of introducing a bill to re- duce the rate of interest paid to depositors in these banks. "SWEATING DENS" IN LIVERPOOL .—The Hoax SEC- RETARY, in reply to Mr. William C,orbet, stated that the attention of the Chief Inspector of Factories hkd been called to the statements which had appeared in the "Lancet," in regard to the "sweating dens" of Liver- pool, Manchester, and other places. The migration of the sweaters from one street to another made it very difficult for the inspectors to discover their whereabouts, and secure the enforcement of the law. Tan WHEEL Tax.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER intimated that on Monday'he would substitute the re- solution with regard to the Van and Wheel Tax by a new one wider which there would be no tax on wheels under 10 cwt., and under which two wheels would be charged 10s. and four wheels £l, making a difference in the yield of the tax of £lOO,OOO. PENSIONS.—Mr. SMITH was questioned as to whether the recipients of Ministerial pensions had n3t to make a, solemn declaration that their means were otherwise in- sufficient to maintain their position. The right hon. gentleman replied in the affirmative.—Mr. Guaisroxa caused amusement by stating that in two cases he had obtained from receivers of pensions engagements that on addition to their fortunes they would surrender the pen- sions—but the engagements had been forgotten. THE BUDGET.

The House went into committee on the Budget Bill, Mr. Pic-rox moving tho omission of the clause re-impo- sing the duty !'on tea, which, he urged, operated as a great hardship upon the poor. The clause was never- theless carried on a division by 259 to 98.—Mr. GLAD- STONE, speaking against the duty on bottled wines, showed that it was objectionable because the lower- priced wines would chiefly feel the blow, and also be- cause the proposal contained the protective element, and was likely to bring into prejudice and danger the French treaty arrangements. Such a duty, he contended, was likely to check Free Trade, and the imposition of the tax was all the more to be regretted in- asmuch as protective ideas had recently made Freat progress in France, as he was aston- ished to find, they had in this country; such he added, amid laughter, was.the unfortunate faculty of human nature to relapse into barbarous conditions after basking in the sunlight of civilization. The prospect was so dark and dangerous, and the perils so enor- mously out of proportion to the frivilous and insignifi- cant benefit to be derived, that he could not do other- wise than raise his voice against this proposal to tax bottled wines.—Mr. GOSCREN denied that the proposal was a Protectionist one, and regretted that Mr. Glad- stone had increased the difficulties in his path.—Mr. Mundella, Mr. SPigg, and other hen, members spoke against the duty.—The Committee divided, and the votes were—for the new tax, 248; against, 121 ; majority 125.
STRANDING OF A CHANNEL STEAMER.

Considerable anxiety was occasioned in London on Monday by the non-arrival of the South-Eastern Railway Co.'s boat Express, which was due at Charing Cross at 720 p.m. The fears for her safety were increased by the fact that the Baroness Burdett Courts was one of the passengers qm board the company's steamship Invicta, which left Calais Ilarbour at 3 15 p.m. for Dover, where the vessel is met. by the Express. It was not until the evening that the railway authorities at Charing Crass received an intimation that the Invicta had stranded off the French coast. It appears that the vessel left Calais harbour safely, but soon niter stranded on one of the many sandbanks which skirt the harbour. Signals were sent up, and several tugs proceeded to her assistance, but all efforts to move the Invicta proved futile. , When the Invicta grounded she heeled over, and water rushed through the cabin ports, drenching-many passen- gers, but no panic or even alarm was manifested. One of the small boats was sent with a tow rope to the steamer Wave, hut the iymt was swamped, and one of the men was drowned. The Wave tried to tow the Invicta off. but 'failed, and broke her paddle in the at- tempt. When the tide receded, a dray came along the sands and took off the baggage, and the passengers descended on to the sande and had to walk ashore, amongst the number being the Baroness Burdett-Coutts. The mail picket Prince arrived at. Dover, on Tuesday, at 7 30 a.m, with the passengers of the Invicta. When the Prince left, the Invicta was firmly fixed on the bar.

The "Sons of Temperance," numbering 4,000 members, have passed a resolution condemning the licensing clauses of this Local Government fill. Two soldiers, named Sherrard and Lifson, were com- mitted for trial, on Monday, for forcibly entering An Saints' Church, Colchester, and stealing various articles
John Coleman, a lodging-house keeper atStockport. died, on Monday, from the effects of a blow. on the liead with a poker, said to have been inflicted by his wife.
At Pontefract, on Saturday, two photografthers, were each fined 5. for following the ocenpattorknt itemsworth on Sunday. Two labotzrera, for unloadttg coal on Slnday, were mulcted in cost& _

A coroner's jury. on Monday, returned a verdict of wilt ul murder against Sarah Helen Proctor. who is charged with killing a fellow lodger, named Whale, by beating her over the head with a jug at lsleworth. At fligh,ate Police Court, London. on Monday, Edwin Crane, 19, milk carrier, was further remanded on a rharge of setting fire to a number of haystacks in the neighbourhood. and doing damage to the amount of nearly £5OO. The Treasury prosecuted. Samuel Broughton, and Caroline, his wife, were com- mit ted for trial at Grantham, on Monday, chamed with the murder of Wm. Lee, a labourer, who had accom- panied she female prisoner home, and who was after- wards found outside with his skull fractured.

A Wevbridge gentleman named Castle took his two eons ana their schoolmate, John Curteis, out for a sail ,a 1 the Thames. on Saturday. While turning Dock Point the boat was capsized, and Colin H. Castle and Curteis, who were rood swimmers, but did not get dear of the boat, were drowned. DAMAGES FOR FAI.sR IMPRISONMENT.—In the Queen's fteneh Division on Monday, a Mr. W. G. Deli recovered £5O Damages from the Southwark and Deptford Tram- way Company for false imprisonment and preferring an* unfounded charge against him, to the effect that he had travelled without paying his fare.

SAW MILLS DEST-11101.:XD By FIER—MeSSM Wilhiat Denny Brothers' saw mills at Leven shipyard, Dumbar- ton, we.re destmyed by fire on Monday afternoon. Three In rge frame SAWS were destroyed, and the damage ie esti- mated at £4,000. The fire is supposed to bave been caused by the overheatinir of a shaft..

M LATIOUCHERT, M.P., ON MINING ROTAISIES. Writing to Mr. C. M. Percy, Wigan. author of "Mine Rents and Mineral Royshies," Mr. Labouchere, M.P., says : "I have read your pamphlet with very much t,leasure. I quite agree with ynur Views. We must insist upon legislation on the matter as soon as we have a Radical Parliament."

On Monday, William Talbot, 54, a collier, of Fern- will)), Bolton, hanged Itimselr in an outbuilding attached to his house. Ile WAS in rood health, and had shown no signs whatever of a suicidal tendency. Although he had lieen out of work for four weeks, he did not seem to be much troubled about it. and his wife is at a loss to con- jecture what was her husband's motive Mr destroying his life.

At Bow-street Police-court, on Monday. Lord de Lisle appeared to a summons. elif ng him with publishing an alleged libel on Mr. A. nly,he, of Craven-street, Strand. Lord de Lisle applied for t month's adjournment. The magistrate adjourned the case for a week. The plain- tiff's counsel stated that the alleged libels were on post- cards. All his client desired WKS to put an end to the nuisance which he had been subjected to. On Monday, at Rochdale, Patrick Deacon. of Man- chester, and George Wade, of Bradford, were sentenced to two months' imprisonment for using gaming boards at the Rochdale steeple hunt on Saturday. The boards consisted of the "spinning jennie's steeplechase," and underneath one was concealed a spring. and under the second a string, with which the prisoners could stop the hands at any part they liked, and thus make it impossible to lose money themselves.

M -TIMER OF A 'N'FFTTIRART Al, BIRMINGHAM.— An inquest was held at Birmingham, on Monday, on the body of Emma Flastings, daughter of a Birmingham publican, who w.s shot by her sweetheart, Geo. Daniels. and died on Friday last Evidence was forthcoming that Daniels was perfecUy sober when he shot the girl, that there had been no quarrel 1 ,wen them, and that he had been heard to threaten injury to her. A verdict of "Wilful murder" was returned.

At the Bristol Police Court, on Saturday, Wm. Henry Phillips, a member of a well-kncevn firm of auctioneers, and secretary of the Atlas Building Society, was charged with obtaining by false pretences divers sums of money, amounting to £3,000, belonging to the said society. There were also charges of embezzlement, and counsel for the prosecution intimated that charges of falsification and perjury would also be preferred. The accused was re- manded, the bench offering to accept substantial bail.

SUICIDE IN A POLICE STATlON.—Frederick Evrens, who carried on business as a fine art publisher and dealer at Cheltenham, was charged before the mAgistrates of that town, on Monday, with wilfully setting fire to his pre- misa on Sunday morning. After the firemen had extinguished the fire they found signs of arson. The accused was remanded, and when at the police station retired to the closet and hung himself with his pocket handkerchief. A Sprints SENTENCE.—Two girls, aged 15 years, named Annie Gill and Emma Turner, sad described as daughters of respectable parents, were brought up at the County Police Court, Manchester, on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly. The Stipendiary said it was outrageous that children like those should be served with drink, and he regretted he had not the parties before him who sold it. The girls were sentenced to a month's imprisonment, a sentence which caused much sensation.

ALLEGED MURDER 'BY A FATHER.—After sitting five times, the coroner and ;ury concluded their inquiry on Saturday into the death of an infant named Longman, three months and a half old, whose body was discoyercd, tied in a sack, on the Thames foreshore, near Battersea. The coroner commented strongly on the fact that the child's father, who could have given important evidence, had absented himselt from every one of their sittings. In their verdict the jury found that the deceased had been wilfully murdered by 'is father, for whose arrest a warrant was issued.

According to news from the West Coast of Atrial., there have been some hutnin sacrifices in consequence of the death of a son of the King of Grand Jack. Selected victims were obliged to drink "sass water," a poisonous liquor. and were then pitched into the surf on the sea shore. When the rollers dashed them ashore, men, women and children cut at them with knives until they were dead. The chief of the tribe flies the British flag, and the captain of a trading vessel remonstrated with him in vain.

AntrtransrioN fl Baxso.--in a Divisional Court of Queen's Bench, an important point was decided under the Food and Drugs Act. A baker was prosecuted by the local authority of Nottingham for selling bread adulterated with alum. The baker pleaded that he had not put alum into the bread, that if it were there it might have been in the !Jour when be bought it, and that it was not in the flour to his knowledge. The jus- tices had dismissed the case, holding that the defendant was not liable, as he did not khow of the presence ot the alum. Their lordships now reversed the judgment of the justices, holding that knowledge of the adulterati6n on the part of the seller is not necessary. A ltomatertc Etormincr.—A romantic elopement has come to light at Cubbington village, near Leamington. A short time ago Mr. Ferdinand Capel Hamburg Wil- liams, an extensive landowner at Abergavenny, dis- covered that love passages had occurred between his daughter, aged 25, an heirrAs in her own right, and her groom, James Alfred Levey, aged 19. The amorous groom was discharged, and the lady placed with friends. She immediately communicated with her lover, who came to the house as her cousin, and partook of hospi- tality. At night the lady threw her portmanteau from the bedroom window, and jumped into the arms of her lover, who was waiting below. They fled to Levey's parents' cottage at Cubbington, and on Saturday were married at the Registrar's office.

Tiss FORTHCONfING GLASGOW EIRIBITION.—On Satur- day, Glasgow submitted its exhibition to a first general inspection an the part of the Press of the United Kingdom. It is to be opened on the Bth of May, and, of course, touch remains to he done, but a view of the building, grounds, and exhibits, already shows that the exhibition will be worthy of the city and country. It bas been organised under a guarantee fund of £300,000, and the buildings cover 14 acres. It is situated in Kelvingrove Park, under the hill tapped by the Univer- sity. This magnificent situation shows off effectively the lofty minarets and towers of the,edifice, which 1, Moorish in architecture, and internally decorated in the style of the Alhambra. A lofty dome is one great fea- ture. The exhibition will be specially noteworthy for its displays of sculpture, pictures, machinery, architec- tural ironwork, shipbuilding, textile manufactures, and women s industries.

BUFFALO BILL AS AN ACTOR.—COIOneI Cody was present at the Manchester Press Club on Friday even- ing, when the members entertained Major John Burke, the general manager of the IVild West Show. Joining in the eulogium of Major Burke, Buffalo Bill said, "John's been annoying me now for about fourteen years. I remember meeting him one day when I was studying to become an actor. r wa.s gojeg on the stage, and they had given me a part. to read 141 I struggled very hard with it, but I couldn't learn a line. I tried to be conscientious, hut I didn't seem to catch on no how. It wasn't very clear to me, so I asked John here, What are these?" OW said John, 'those are the cues; the other chap speaks those.' (Laughter.) I'd never heard of anything tr:t a billiard cue before. Well, I studied it hard, but when we got on the stage I did not know a cussed line of it. (Renewed laughter.), General Sheridan was in one of the boxes. When I' came on the people expected me to act, but I couldn't do that, so I told them some Indian stories through three acts. NVe had about twenty people in the company, and they wanted to have a show themselves; but the audi- ence would have me. When it came to the fourth act Sheridan came behind and complimented me. I calcu- lated I'd done enough, so i began to dress. They wanted me to go on again, but I said I'd fixed three acts, and if the company, couldn't run one hy itself it was no good." (much laughter.)

div.head: ADJOURNMENT OF THE HOUSE.
div.p: THE ADJOURNMENT OF THE HOUSE.

Mr. JUSTIN MC.CARTHY then asked leave to move the adjournment of thedlouse on a matter of urgent public importance, viz., the recent departure from the long. established practice of Irish County Court judges by increasing sentences in criminal meet on appeal. The whole of the Nationalist members, as well as the unoffi- cial Liberals, rose in support of the motion to grant leave. Mr. Justin Mc.Carthy, after describing the various cases, said the innovation might lead to ill-feeling of the most serious character, and he trusted the House would mark its sense of a• proceeding which would both -close the gates of mercy and open those of a despotic coercion. (Opposition cheers.) 'Mr. MADDEN. Solicitor-General for Ireland, explained that the appeals were not such in the exact sense under- stood by the hon. gentleman, but entire rehearsals of the case, and that it was the duty of the County Court judge to exercise his discretion, apart from the decision Come to in the court below.

'Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE challenged the legal authorities of the Government to show a case in which a court of criminal appeal at Quarter Sessions in England had in- I creased a sentence. (Opposition cheers.) That being ; the case they ought to scrutinise very carefully the new ' departure which had been taken in Ireland within the last few days. especially as it had somewhat singularly been taken by three County Court judges almost at the same moment. (Opposition cheers.) The sudden spring- ng of the practice was indeed open to the suspicion of a,suggestion from head quarters (Opposition cheers.) Mr. BRADLAUGH contended that 4if the legislature had- intended sentences to be increased on appeal special words would have been added giving express authority tooageravate the sentences, just as express authority was given to modify, reverse, or confirm them. (Opposition cheers.)

Sir Was, Haltom:7er said it was not necessary to deter- mine whether the proceedings were legal or not. There were a number of unused powers in fhe law of England —rusty weapons of brutal tyranny,—which, if they were brought into operation, the English people would not tolerate for one moment. (Opposition cheers.) The employment of exceptional powers for the purpose of turning the criminal law into an engine of brutal oppression, however legal• it might • be, was unconstitu- tional. To say that in administering the law they could introduce a novel practice of that sort without violating all the principles which ought to regulate the adminis- tration of justice, was a position which could not he sustained. (Opposition cheers.) Mr. BALFOUR said he had watched, with considerable regret, Sir Wm. Harcourt's decline and fall, ever since the unhappy day when, without a moment's notice, be changed the opinions of a lifetime. He rejected as a foul libel and aspersion to their character, the ,insinua- tions thal had been roads. The statutes under which the power used was given, was in no sense antiquated. and dated no further back than 1879, and the language used was so precise, that it was possible to suppose thnt the legislature was not conscious of what it was doing when it gave the power to County Court judges. Me. GLADSTONE, who VMS greeted with loud cheers, agreed that they ought to do anything rather than desire that the time of the House should 'be occupied in con- sidering the proceedings of a coltrt oflustice in an ad- verse or critical sense. But the greater evil was when the proceedings of the courts called.,by law, Courts of Justice, were conducted, not in a bpirit of justiCe, bet in a spirit such as to require the exerCise of the high functions of that House as a Grand Court of Inquisition. (Opposition cheers). When no instance could be produced by the united ingenuity and knowledge of the whole party. opposite, and the law officers of•the crown, of the enlargement of criminal cases ni appeal were they pre- pared ,to say 'that they would talk of equality of righteand administration between England and Ireland? In the face of your plea that the proper method to governlreland would not he by givinwher a Legislature of herovrn for the management, of her own internal-con- ceens,tut to govern her from Westminster in a manner so mild, -so equal, so generous, that she shall have no reason to,complain, you introduce this odious inequality. The Solicitor-General ,says there may have .been new evidence. Was there evklenee ? (Irish cheers.) If there had been new evidence lie would have known it. He did not know it; and it is an idle and an empty pretext. The provision which rives the power of appeal, gives it exclusively tb the party on whom the sentence hasteen passed, &early showing ti,at it was a nower.of appeal intended -to be exercised in favour of that party, If justice has miscarried, and not to be exercised in the aggravation of the sentence. Mr. Balfour has been criticising the moragity of my right hon. friend,eir Wm. Harcourt. Morality is the text of most. of the sermons delivered by the .§scretary for Ireland. He has taken upon himself, almost since. his official infancy, the busi- ness of teaching morality to those who were here long before him. fLoud Onponition and Parnellite elseers.) I ask myself what kind of inorality is that which treats the maintenance or breach of pledges as a matter of such indifferenc• that it requires no notice from the House? -
_ Mr. Bet.rorrn : It was not unimportant ,but irrelevant. I said the right hon. gentleman was out of order in intro- ducing it.

Mr. GLADOWNE I know he accused my friend of irrelevance in some part of his speech. It cannot be doubted that we have a rTeht to look to the history of the power of ;appeal. My lion. friend charged the Irish Secretary, and has repeatedly charged him, pith breach of faith.
Mr. BALFOUR, amidst considerable excitement, rose to a point of order. Liaving read the words of the motion,,

div.head: TECHNIcAL ED UVATION.
div.p: TECHNIcAL ED UVATION.

We have received a copy of the Bill now before Parlia- ment to provide for Technical Education in England and Wales. After the passing of this Act any school board may make provision for giving technical education in any school under their management, and either by day or evening classes, or both, as may seem fit, having regard to the daily occupations of the persons to be benefited thereby. If no inch provision is made, or if it is insufficient, and if the local. authority by special reso- lusion determine that prevision or further provision ought to be made, they may themselves make such provision. Where technical education is given in any school, not being a public elementary school (including for the purposes of this section any college), which is not under the management of a school board or local authority, and is either within their district or accessible to the inhabitants thereof, the school board or local authority may contribute or they may join together with other school boards or local authorities in contri- buting from their respective funds towards—(a.) the maintenance or improvement of that school, or of its provisions for technical education; or (b.) the payment Of the fees at that school of deserving students who before proceeding to-such school may have been resident in the district of the contributing board or authority; (e.) the establishment of scholarships fordeserving students. The mode in which and the terms upon which contributory school boards and local authorities shall be represented upon the-governing bodies receiving such contributions, so far as technical instruction is ccomerned, shall be such as may be agreed upon between the school boards, local au- tl torities and governing bodieerepectively in each case, and in default of agreement by the Science and Art Depart- ment, provision is made for the needful Parliamentary grants to schools for the purposes of technical ipstruc- tion. The'provishms of the Elementary Education Acts as to accommodation fees and in forth, are to apply to schools benefiting under this measure. For the purposes of this Act the expression 'technical edueation means instruction in—(i.) Any of the science subjects for the time being specified in the directory of the Science and Art Department upon which that Department under- takes to examine; and (ii.) in any or all of the following subjects, that is to say :—(”) The use of ordinary tools, (b) commercial arithmetic, (e) commercial geozraplrY, (d) bookkeeping, (e) shorthand, (f) French, German, and other modern languages. (q) freehand and machine drawing, (h) any other subject which the Education Department and the Science and Art. Department jointly may from time to time prescribe as being a proper sub- ject of technical education for the purposes of com- merce, agriculture, or any trade or handicraft. The bill is backed by Sir Henry lingerie. Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth, Sir Bernard Samuelson. Mr. G. Dixon, and Mr. Arthur Acland.

Tint Dntvvirr.n MURDER.—The supposed murderer of the little girl whose hi-4:ly ,was found in the Driffield Canal on Good Friday by two men when fishing, was brought up sp remand at Driffield Co Sat.tuday. The prisoner is the Mother of the girl, and it was alleged in the course of the evidence that the bottom portion of a woman's gray jacket, being clearly the-half of the one found in the canal, was discorere at the house in which she resided. The woman was col. mit•cel for trial at the Assizes. ANOTHER TUFArlts DFS rROYED BY FIRE. The Grantham Theatre was totally destroyed by fire on Sun- terday morning. The alarm was given by a policeman on duty in the neighbourhood, and the volunteer fire brigade was soon in attendance. Within a quarter of an hour of the outbreak the roof fell in. The greater part of the building internally being of wood the place burnt rapidly, and it was soon evident that nothing could be done to save it. The efforts of the firemen dwere accordingly directed to saving the adjoining property. Half an hour after the outbreak, which was first reported at 250 a.m., a steam fire engine from the agricultural implement works of Messrs. flornaby arrived, manned by the employes of the firm, and its influence was soon manifest on the burning mass. The fire originated near the stage of the theatre, which on Saturday evening was being prepared for a meeting of Salvationists on the following day. A remarkable circumstance is that only a few weeks ago the same theatre sustained a good deal of damage by fire. This also occurred on a Sunday morning, and the building was then being got ready for a Salvation Army gather- ing. The damage is estimated, at £5,000.

The bill to authorise the Corporation of Preston to borrow £510,000 to complete the Ribble Navigation works came before a Select Committee of the House of Lords on Thursday. . The Baptist Union on Thursday passed resolutions in favour of the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, and in opposi- sition to the "compensation" clauses of the Local Government Bill (licenses.) Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's, which for strength is unequalled.—Advt.

div.head: COLLIERY EXPLOSION AT WORKINGTON.
div.p: THE COLLIERY EXPLOSION AT WORKINGTON.

The work of flooding the pit in width the diaastrousi explosion took place on Thursday night has been °Gni- Dieted ; but no attempt has yet been made to recope;r the bodies known to be in the pit. Seven of the thirteen bodies brought to the surface were buried on Sunday, one of them, Sergeant Smith, with military linoiirs, he having been a member of the local Artillery Volunteers. Several more funerals took place on Monday afternoon. Some horses were stilt alive in the pit on Saturday. and on that ,day a man yen. tured down to feed them; but on Monday the condition of the pit as deemed too dangerous for the operation to be repeated. The arrangements for organising the fund for the relief of those bereaved by the accident is making good prngag.e.s. Dr. Orrnrnd, Workington. who was one of the eiplorine natty, states that although he had had experience o& many colliery explosions, he had never known one in which the violence of the explosion seemed to have betel so great. Ills experience led him to the conclusion thee #tbe explosion exceeded in Aeverity and in the violeiace done to the miners many accidents in which a gresteg number of lives had been lost.
An inquest was opened on Saturday on the bodies of; the men Hodgson and Robinson, who died at the In- firmary, and was adjourned after evidence of identifica- tion until May 18th. . .

The two injured men in the Infirmary were, on Monday' afternoon, reported to be not doing so well, and little hope of their recovery is entertained. A meeting of the Workington Local Board. of Health! was held on Friday, to consider the best means of rais- ing a fund for the relief of the distress caused by the catastrophe at the William Pit. Mr. George John Smithl presided, and on his motion, it was resolved to call tv, public meeting, and it is anticicipated that through this' means at least £4,000 will be raised. The feeling or sympathy is very general, and all'aopear to be anxious 4 to do what they can to alleviate the sorrow of the, bereaved.

div.head: TWO MORE DEATES.
div.p: TWO MORE DEATES.

Hobert Hodgson, aged 39, a hewer, of Flimby, married,- one of the men who were injured, and taken to the infirmary, died late on Friday. On Saturday, about ten o'clock, Joseph Robinson, another of the men injured in the explosion, died in the• Workington Infirmary. This brings the number of- killed up to 30. The company have now got a good supply of water, and the la-Kling operations are proceed- t ing very satisfactorily.

div.head: PRESENTATION AT WALTON HALL.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT WALTON HALL.

A deputation from the Warrington Conservative Club on Tuesday afternoon went to Walton Hall, the residence of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., to present an address of congratulation to Mr. (iilbert Greenall on his coming of age. The deputation consisted of Councillor R. W. Francomb, J.P. (chair- man), Mr. John Roberts (treasurer), Mr. H. Collin and Mr. Thomas Mason (joint hon. secs.), Mr. James Smethurst, Mr. Alfred Jolley, Mr. George Jolley, Mr. C. McDowell. and Mr. John Hampson (registra- tion agent). The party left the Conservative Club in Sankey-st. at 3-30, and arrived at Walton Hall about four o'clock, when they were received in the library by Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, and , the Misses Greenall. The address, which was signed on behalf of the members by Messrs. R. W. Francomb, John Roberts, Henry Collin, and Thomas Mason, was worded as follows: "To Gilbert Greenall, Esq., of Walton Hall, Cheshire, on attaining his majority. Sir,—We, the members of the Warrington Conservative Club, beg most respectfully to offer you our hearty congratulations on your attaining your 21st birthday. Our affection and respect for your honoured and revered father lie deep in our hearts; and it is a source of the greatest gratification to us that hiee has been spared to see this happy and eventful day in your history. It is also our earnest prayer that he may long live to give you counsel and advice, and so prepare you for the high position which eventually you must be called upon to occupy. We trust that you will long live amongst us, and that you may continue to enjoy the richest blessings which a merciful Providence can vouchsafe to you." It has a very handsome appearance, and is illuminated in the sixteenth century style. In the initial letter the armorial bearings of the Greenall family have been in- troduced, the shield being surmounted by an esquire's helmet, from which depends the lambrequin or mantle. The crest, a winged orb, rests upon the helmet. Under- neath the shield, upon a scroll, is the motto of the family, "Alta Pete." In the left hand corner is a tinted "photo' of Mr. Greenall, taken by Mr. Birtles, of Sankey- at. The corners of the panel containing the "phcto" are filled in with a design composed of the horse shoe and the fox's mask and brush, and a pair of crossed hunting crops. In the lower border an ornamental shield bears Mr. Greenall's monogram. The frame, by Mr. Booth- royd, of Sankey-street, is of English gold, with a raised pattern of ivyleaves running the whole way round the frame. Inside this is a wide gold flat, and then a thick bevelled cardboard mount of a greenish shade with gold bevel. The presentation was made by Mr. R. W. FRAN- costs, who, in a few prefatory remarks, expressed the pleasure of the deputation at knowing that Sir Gilbert Greenall had so far recovered from his recent accident as to be able to receive them. In congratulating Mr. Gil- bert Greenall on his attainment of his majority, Mr. Francomb assured him that there was no class of persons in Warrington who took a more lively interest in his wel- fare than the members of the Conservative Club. They therefore desired to present him with the address as a small token of the esteem in which they held both him and his parents. Ile then referred at some length to the MICTPCS that had attended the Conservative club, which he thought was one of the best in Lancashire, and to the interest that had been taken in its formation and carry- ing on by Sir Gilbert and Mr. Gilbert Greenall. Mr. JOHN ROBERTS also referred to the presentation in a short speech, and wished Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, and their family, every happiness and pros- perity. Mr., T. MASON re-echoed the senti- ments expressed by the previous speakers, and sincerely hoped that Mr. Gilbert Greenall would live long to enjoy the inheritance which ultimately would be his. He trusted that Mr. Gilbert would continue the good work done by his father for the Conservative party in Warrington, and spoke of the respect that was felt for Sir Gilbert as a gentleman, not only by the Conserva- tives of the borough, but by a great portion of the Liberal party. A few remarks having been also made by Mr. J. SMETHURST, Mr. GILBERT GREENALL briefly, but appropriately, thanked the deputation. Afterwards Sir GILBERT GREENALL remarked that he thought the Conservative Club had become an excellent and valu- able institution. They must maintain it in an efficient manner, enlarge its operations, and make it a place to which they tould at all times resort, and at which they' would.be able to get the best political intelligence and advice. He sincerely thanked the deputation for their visit and its object, and said he hoped it might please God to grant his son long life and to make him a useful man, and that in all things his son would " go straight." The deputation then returned to the Conservative Club; where the toasts of the "Chairman of the Presentation Committee" (Mr. Francomb), the "Committee," and the "Press" were duly honeured.
It is announced as prabable that the Whitsuntide re- cess will extend from Thursday, the 17th of May, till Thursday, the 31st.

MR. C. M. PERCY has issued in panarlet forra the paper on Mine Rezits and Mineral ,oyalties which he read before the Manchester ological Society. It is a valuable contribution° taz mv

portant question, and will pave the wy io that ftuther inquiry on the subject which i s much needed. There can be no doubt tht gnglish trade is suffering in part from the wa7i which our manufacturers are handicapped by tj exces- sive sums Paid for .mine rents and ro..lties se compared with what is paid in other entries. Tile mining industry of this country hamen de- pressed for at least ten years; profits he in the majority of cases vanished; arld yetas Mr.. PERCY puts it, "royalty owners have reived, up- on coal and ironstone, and limestone, mainly not less, and probably more, than 260,000)0, out of a very considerable portion of which thing has gone for local rates, whilst the other 'o parties, colliery proprietors and colliery wolien, have had to pay all local calls." This, eatte of the. total sum is admittedly a low one, am:l4 it means six millions a year to landowners for tDermission

to obtain minerals from the bowels the earth. Other people must take all the trole and the risk, and the risk is always great, wh they sit at home at ease and enjoy this uneied wealth. Colliery proprietors must struggle ofith little or no return, and workmen must toiard for low
wages, in order that the great orof the earth may grow rich in idleness. TH are some

Speaking at' Newcastle the other week, ' jouw MORLEY said :- "There is a very great place in the county of Bur- nam where I ani told that within 20 years the wners of minerals which, if our forefathers had 'Known of them as well as some of their sons do, Would never have accrued to the owner of the sur- face at all, but would have been reserved for, the nation and the state—(hear, hear,)—that the owners have drawn within 20 years .£6,000,000 in the shape of raining royalties, and they have not contributed La Penny piece to the schools, the parks, the wash- uousea, and the other instruments of civilised exis- tence. That will n.t go on for ever, gentlemen. Another point —and I think I made a mistake—l think this is what affects Jarrow. Will they en- ure for ever that a man who draws revenue from ground-rent is to contribute nothing locally to the , etPenditure which every day adds new value to his Property? Be quite sure that there is a great open- -1"g still for the application of Liberal principles to national finance when it falls into the hands of Liberal men. (Cheers.)" The time is approaching when there will be a aearching investigation into matters of this kind. 'The reference which Mr. lionLEv makes to the Possible right of the State to the minerals below the surface is especially interesting. It raises a question which is certain to be brought to the ,fccult before long; and that is—whether the State uen parted with its 'original right to the minerals of the kingdom; and, if so, whether it has parted With it in such a wily as to preclude the possibility Of resumption ? Mr. PERCY makes it clear that he Is not in favour of confiscation; but if it can be Proved that there has been something like confis- cation on the part of the landowners, what then? /le himself makes reference to an act applying to Scotland, which provides that the right of all nlines, metals, and minerals belongs undeniably to the Crown. That act has been quoted within the 18st few years as a regulating statute; and there can scarcely be a question that what held good of Scotland would hold good of d; not, of course, by the same statute, tirli*ln:ly another statute, or by inalienable title. Whatever may have been filched from us, that the Crown rthould have a right is in harmony with equity and common sense that is, taking the

, .°rolvn as holding the title on behalf of the nation. Tlie holder of the surface land might reasonably claim that he was entitled to the crops, because, by the labour of cultivation, he had made the surface valuable. But this plea is not one that could be put in as to the mineral wealth below the
'urface. No landowner can claim that he has 44ded a shilling to the value of the minerals under- gr°tlnd. These may be looked upon as "the gift c!f God" to the nations of the earth; and they

should -therefore be treated as national and not as iadiyidual property. In France, Belgium, Ger- illanY, and Spain, the whole or greater part of the alinerals are the recognised property of the State; .4110:1 the State takes care not to oppress those who have to use these minerals by such heavy royalties '4B are imposed in England. It thus happens that °av continental competitors secure a double advant- age; minerals cost thorn less in the first instance; au(' in the second place the reduced sum which is Paid for rent and royalty goes—not in the pockets Of private individuals, but to the relief of general taxation. It is suggested that royalty in this a(nintry should be paid on a sliding scale, so that the impost would be low when profits were low; alnl not as it is in igany cases to-day—exceedingly Iligh when profits are nil. That this would bb an jelprovement upon the present state of affairs is

'let to be denied; but the proposed remedy does not go to the root of the difficulty. What thoughtful 41411 lyisb to know is how it happens that the State thjs country does not exercise its original right the minerals below the earth's surface. If the has been bought out fairly and honestly, so tleh the better for landowners; if. not, it may be rlie the duty of the State to resume its right, 44(1 Put England on a level with other countries.

.211 E Tories slipped into office in 188:5 by pro- to remove every remnant of coercion in eland; but they will go out of office, so far as the sent Government are concerned, with the evil seNtation of having administered in the worst taY the worst Coercion Act of modern times. With ARTHUR BALFOUR as Irish Secretary, there ;eerils no limit to the meanness and tyranny of the „ti3b authorities; like master, like man; they take air cue from him, and find a coarse pleasure ap- Rarently in doing the dirtiest of work. Under the uoercion Act, power of appeal is given as to Ben- exceeding one month's imprisonment; but, ttfter a certain speech made by the CHIEF SECRE- -I'44F, in which a good deal was to be read between the lines, the resident magistrates in Ireland pro- eeeded to rob some of the Irish prisoners of their tight of appeal by passing two sentences of one 410rith each! The meanness of the thing was so that when the practice became known it tW,as universally condemned. The result was that ne word was given, in some form or another, that this ino<le of administering injustice in Ireland rhust be dropped, and it has been dropped. But th e resources of tyranny were by no means ex- natisted ; and the next move was, when sentences wtre appealed against, to increase the sentence 111)011 appeal—a thing unheard of in the criminal u.law of either England or Ireland. Mr. JUSTIN CsOARTHY raised the question in the House of 'Ominous, on Tuesday, and an exciting debate en- iii which the foul tactics of the Government 1,...ere exposed, and their majority diminished. Mr. leeArrrify mentioned no less than six cases of appeals in which the sentences had either doubled or largely increased! The Tann 4:ettETARY and the law officers were challenged to , _trle a precedent for such an extraordinary pro- and they were unable to cite a single "e• Mr. BRADLAUGH pointedly observed that, if the intention of the Legislature that in Ca of appeal the County Court judges should he authority to increase sentences, that would t,ve been declared in specific terms as it was by 07 law of France. Sir WILLIAM HARCOLTRT at ee took the bull by the horns, and said that to ilaZiease sentences on appeal was to turn the criini- „ 'aw into an engine of brutal and ferocious op- F. e 88i0l ; however legal, it was unconstitutional. his minded the IRISH SECRETARY that he began fai°licY with regard to appeals by an act of bad he to the House; for he made a promise, I'vhich 1A;:413 broken, to give an appeal in every case. eee3/4 brought Mr. BALFOUR to his feet, who pro- to sneer at Sir Wm. HAncoriar's morality, bri'llat he sought to get rid of the reference to his aeceaell of faith by impudently affirming that the thislisation had been a thousand times refuted. At 1141,8tag° Mr. GLADSTONE intervened, and gave Mr. de 61:713, the castigation which he so richly ofBel'ved• Morality," he said, "was the text u almost every sermon delivered in the 0:11'11111° by the CHIEF SECRETARY. He had taken the t Iself, almost since his official infancy began, the t 1( of teaching morality to those who were in "Ise long before he was. But he (Mr. that sTONE) asked himself what kind of a morality hreacitv4B which treated the maintenance or the that 1 (If Pledges as a matter of such indifference it . tio equired no notice to be taken of it in the 118°2' eyhien, s sharp thrust pierced the hide of the *". Secretary; 111 winced under the rebuke,

and appealed to the SPEAKER for protection ; but the SPEAKER told him that, as a question had arisen as to whether the ham SECRETARY had observed some promise he had given with regard to appeals, the allusions which had been made were perfectly relevant to the subject before the House. Mr. GLADSTONE, proceeding with his argument, said "he would ask whether there wasthe smallest doubt that, at any rate in that house, the power of appeal was given entirely in the interest of the person who should receive sentence? It was asked for in his behalf, it was given as a concession to him, and it was stamped on it that Parliament intended it to be a gift to him; whereas it is now being wantonly and cruelly used against him:, Concluding what was throughout a fine example of close reasoning and sustained eloquence, Mr. GLAD- STONE said "the practice was that there was no power of enlargement exercised in England, and it ought not to be exercised in Ireland—unless, in- deed, they wished to show that it was, to use Mr. DISRAELI'S phrase, an organised hypocrisy' to pretend that anything in the nature of equality of right or treatment was to be accorded to Ireland.' The Axxourisx-GENERsi, showed himself angry at Mr. GLADSTONE'S attack; but, as Sir CHARLES RUSSELL afterwards said, he did not devote one single minute to the consideration of the matter ' before the House. The debate was altogether a merciless exposure of the iniquity of " Castle Government." It was pointed out that the Act gave the power of appeal exclusively to the pri- soner, thus implying that it was to be exercised on his behalf and in his interest in case he had reason to believe he was being hardly used. The law as to appeal is right; it is the administration of the law which is wrong;' and every day this is being forced on the mind of the people not only of Ire- land, but of the rest of the United Kingdom.
Pity is the virtue of the law, And none but tyrants use it cruelly.
, The tyrants in this case are conspicuous; and if they do not cease to do evil, they will go lown be- fore the righteous wrath of an indignant nation.

MR. GILBERT GREE/fAI,L is not. yet a " much- married " man; . but from all that has been said and done in connection with his coming of age it would not be inaccurate to vary Mr. Artemus Ward's phrase by describing him as a much. addressed young man. He has, within the last few weeks supped full of flattery, and we dare say he is by this time well nigh sick of the over-dose. When he is a few years older, he will have realised that the effusive display of affectionate re- gard which he has witnessed, was not in every case so disinterested as it seemed to be. When he has taken stock of his hangers-on, he will perceive that anew reacting may be given to the text—" There is a lad here which hath five barley loaves and two small fishes, but what are they amongst so many"; and he will discount accordingly some of the com- ing-of-age speeches and addresses. If he is at all anxious at the present time to profit by the re- marks good, bad, and indifferent to which he has had to listen, he will be not a little puzzled to know what course to steer. For instance, he must have had a misgiving either as to himself or as to his sire, when he heard one of the tenants express the hope that he would prove a better man than his father—a misgiving which would scarcely be set aside, on Tuesday, when M. Smzruunsr told him he trusted that now he was a man he would put' away childish things. What more natural than that he should wander about, after this, won- dering if he was really childish, and what other things he should put away, seeing that he has long since disposed of his tops and marbles? It seems, somehow, as if all the speakers on Tuesday had pecu- liar ways of expressing themsellies. (Can they have called at Wilderspool Brewery on their way to Walton Hall?) Mr. Joust ROBERTS, to give

another instance, speaking out of the fulness; of his heart, embraced the whole family in his bles- sing (?), for he hoped that "when all their toils on earth were over, they might rest from their labours in that land where the wicked cease from troubling, and the weary are at rest.'" "That land" can scarcely be the heavenly land, for the wicked would seem to be there, although•they have ceased from troubling. Mr. JOHN ROBERTS should explain; it is a point upon which a miscon- ception is of moment. Mr. FRANCON; the chief spokesman, was as all-embracing in another direc- tion; for he did not hesitate to say that the name of Sir GILBERT GREENALL was "revered by all classes of people, whether Liberal or Tory." As to this Sir GILBERT might be tempted to exclaim with "Hamlet,"—" They fool me to the top of my bent." We must plainly; the name of Sir GILBERT am'—pe'a`k GREENALL is not revered amongst all classes. After what we have had occasion from time to time to say of him, it would be hypocrisy to assent to such a state- ment. Let Mr. FRANCOMB be content to speak for himself and his party; he will be going far enough. As to young Mr. GILBERT. we will not affor him any advice of our own; but will commend to his attention thevise words—not of Job, but of our great national poet This above all—to thine own self be true; And it must follow as the night the day, Thou eanst not then be false to any man.

A W.AtruiNGToN ABSENTEE. James Ross, a young man, was charged at St. Helens, on Tues- day, with absenting himself from the South Lan- cashire Regiment, stationed at Warrington. Pri- soner said he was due at headquarters on Sunday night, but missed his train, and thought he would wait until-Monday night. He was committed to Walton Gaol to await an escort.

• DRAT OF A RAINHILL MTNISTEIL—The Rev. Robert Lewis, who has bean a supernumerary mini- ster for about ten years, and who for the last four or five years has been stationed at the Itainhill Wesleyan Chapel, died on Sunday at the age of 74 years, and his remains were itlterred on Thursday, in the burial ground of St. Anne's Church, Rainhili. The funeral service was conducted by the Revs. G. G. Brown, J. Kent, and J. Barton (vicar of Rainhill). THE WARRINGTON FEVER IlosPlTAL.—We'under- , stand that the negotiations which have been en- tered into between the Newton Improvement Com- missioners and the Warrington Corporation, with a view to the former being at liberty to send cases of infectious disease to the Warrington Fever Hospital, have resulted in a satisfactory arrangement being made. The Newton authorities will in future make use of the Warrington hospital, the terms being ..£2 per week towards the permanent expenses of the hospital, and lOs for each case that may be sent. It will be remembered that Mr. Henley, on his recent visit to the Warrington Board of Guardians, sug- gested that it would be better for small authorities to have arrangements with a central hospital ; and now that the Newton Authority has moved in that direction it is to be hoped that the Rural Authority will follow the example. THE Pauraosn DAY FABLE—The general supposition is, says the Liverpool Post London correspondent, that the primrose was Mr. Disraeli's favourite flower—a fable which arose from a curious incident, Among the wreaths vnt to the funeral of the great Conservative statesman was one from the Queen, composed solely of primroses, on which was written the inscription—" His favourite flower." This was naturally regarded as a reference to the preferences of the dead ex-Premier. but I have been assured by a gentleman in a position to know the facts that " " referred to in the inscription was not Lord Beaconsfield, but the Prince Consort. The Prince Consort was really fond of primroses, and to the Queen the use of the personal pronoun seemed quite sufficient. , As for Lard Beaconsfield and the primrose, Mr. Escott I use. to relate an incident which directly bears on the IqueStion. Strolling through the grounds of Hughenden with Lord Beaconsfield,- he saw one of the peacocks pealing away at a root of primroses, and made some I remark upon it. "Yes," said Lord Beaconsfield, "it is sad, but to tell the truth, I prefer peacocks to prim- roses."
TOUCH AND GO."

Mr. Robert Davies is not at the Swiss Rivieral as we stated last week, but at the Riviera di Genoa, on the coast of the Mediterranean. Even this is divided into Riviera di Levante, and Riviera di Poente. They are all pleasant places, and " what's.the odds, so long," Btc.

The Comte de Paris has given the world to understand that all would go well with Franco if the people would fiend for him and restore the monarchy. But Frenchmen do noesee the matter in that het. They have paid too high a price to get rid of kings to wish now to " give themselves away."

It is stated that Mr. Waddington, the French Ambassador to the English Court, has been in- structed to say that if the duty on bottled French wines is maintained, there must be reprisals on English goods imported into France. This will be one of the many unpleasant 'results of Mr. Gos- chen's meddle-and-muddle Budget.

A rough-looking fellow named Edwards was brought up at the Liverpool Police Court on Wednesday morning, and charged with stealing several bottles of sweets from a confectioner's shop. His explanation was that he took them "for fun." It was not a case, however, of "sweets to the sweet," so he was sent Po gaol for a month. As he has a way of his own in larking, he will per- haps do the hard labour for the fun of the thing.

There is further delay iri the proposed presenta- tion of an address, on the part-of the Warrington Corp Oration, to Mr. Gilbert Greenall. It is ques- tioned whether additional excitement of this kind would not be injurious to Sir Gilbert Greenall, who would be expected to take part in. the pro- ceedings. All things considered, and seeing that the young gentleman Who, has just come of age has•received as many addresses as would paper a room, no harm would result if this particular document was taken as read.

+Mr. Goldwin Smith used to pose in this country as a Radical. In New York his utterances are of tho Tory typo. Ho has been making a speech "to prevent Englishmen being trampled upon by those who are angling for the Irish vote." It is note- worthy that an important speaker who followed him expressed his unqualified dissent from every opinion he uttered. How things have changed with Mr. Goldwin Smith sinee Mr. Disraeli stung him to the quick by hitting off his weaknesses in a novel t ,

• There can be no doubt that in German Court circles there is a feeling against the German Empress and 'against everything English. But the feeling does not extend to the people of Ger- many. This was revealed when Sir Morrell Mackenzie drove out amongst them; and t'here is further evidence of the good-will of the masses in the enthusiastic reception which has been accorded to Queen Victoria, as the mother of the German Empress. Good feeling and good sense are happily not confined to Courts.

Mr. Goschen cut a tolerable figure as a financier so lone as he was not called upon to measure him- self with Mr. Gladstone; but he looked small on Monday evening besides the great master. Mr. Gladstone dealt with the complicated question of the death duties with the old grip and freshness. He made figures dance till they looked as interest- ing as the figures of a quadrille; and at the same time drove his arguments home in the most con- vincing manner. His exposure of this part of the Budget as a sop to landowners at the expense of the rest of the nation will form the starting point of a new campaign. •

Lord Hartington was cornered for once by the statement that he was committed to the policy Mr. Gladstone advocated as a member of Mr. Glad- stone's Cabinet in 1885. There was no easy way out, but it was shabby of his lordship—and he is not usually shabby—to force a way, pleading that he was so occupied, at that time, with affairs in the Soudan, that he had to commit his financial conscience to Mr. Gladstone's keeping without really knowing much about the Budget of 1885. Lord Hartingtoia has been in too many Cabinets not to know that Cabinet responsibility_ is collec- tive—not individual. His plea was a bad plea, and—we repeat—his conduct was shabby. '

Lord Randolph Churchill is still a tactor in politics. His exposure of the "organised hypo- crisy" of the present Government has caused weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth in the Tory-Unionist camp. Lord Haztington, in par- ticular, is said to be annoyed ; but Lord Randolph has no cause to love the member for Rossendale, for did he not give the Tories Goschen to take Randolph's place? The Prince of Wales had Lord Randolph to dine with him on Thursday evening; His Royal Highness likes a lively time; and he likes the plucky fellow who helps to make the time lively.

The latest rumour as to Lord R. Churchill is that ho wants to take the place of Mr. Balfour as Irish Secretary, while Mr. Smith is to .be pitch- forked into the House of Lords. Mr. Balfour talks a deal about what he is doing; but the Irish landlords say that with all his talk they do not get their rents. But what will Lord Salisbury have to say? It is stated that last time he was approached by Lord Randolph's frionds, he grimly remarked that when a man has had a carbuncle on his neck, and has got rid of it, he doesn't want it back again. The story is good enough to be true; it is like Lord Salisbury to compare the Irish to Hottentots, and Lord Randolph to a carbuncle.

This much is now clear as to Lord Hartington and the Liberal Unionists, namely, that, as a body, there is no inconsistency which they tire not prepared to face, if by that means they cah main- tain the present Government in office. They are so "deeply sworn," and have such a dread of meet- ing their constituents, that, right or wrong, they mean to keep the present Parliament alive as the last they may see. There is a good deal of human nature in this; but it is the worst side of human nature. The Liberal party must be content to ad- vance without them; ' Liberal Unionists are for the most part Whigs, and it has always been found necessary to leave the Whigs behind when any great reform was to be accomplished.

" Truth " says:—" The Primrose League is not working smoothly, in spite of the elaborate sound- ing of brasses and tinkling of cymbals last week. The ladies of rank and position,' who ostensibly head the League, will have nothing to say to the aspiring 'Dames' who joined it in the hope of making social play by drudging and spending money. The grandees of the movement meet the less im- portant ladies with condescending affability on offi- cial occasions, and greet thorn with a frozen stare elsewhere."

The Primrose Club cannot be in a very flourish- ing condition, or it would not resort to indiscri- minate touting for members. A Warrington gentle- man has handed us a circular he received by post. It is supposed to be very tempting, for it holds out such attractions as dancing, boating, lawn tennis, and smoking concerts ; in other words, it is what Shakespeare calls "the primrose way to the everlasting bonfire." There is an en- closure which sweet innocents are expected to sign, and which runs as follows :—" I desire to be- come an original member of the Primrose Club, at an annual subscription of £1 is., without entrance fee, and swill forward the amount upon receiving notification of my election." In the case in ques- tion the bait was not taken; it was laughed at.

"In the House of Commons, on Monday, Mr. Bradlaugh asked if the Home Secretary was aware that the Conservative journal of Church boasted on Saturday that, in spite of his question in the House, the lottery of the local Conservative Asso- ciation had taken place. Mr. Matthews said he was not aware of it. Mr. Bradlaugh said he would , supply the right hon gentleman with information , on the subject, and hoped he would make a strict inquiry. Mr. Matthews nodded his assent." We are not in a position to say what proceedings are being taken as to the breach of the law by a local journal ; but some statement will be made, it is understood, at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday next.
