LOCAL NEWS.

*** A MOLY AND A CHALLENOE.=OII Saturday April 14th the Warrington Guardian said as to its circulation that it was "many times greater than that of all our local contemporaries com Vined." As we have good reason to doubt 60 extraordinary a statement, we are willing to put this trumpet- blowing to a practical test. We, theretoie, offer to submit our books to any firm of accountants agreed upon, on the understanding that the pro- prietors of the. Warrington Guardian do the same ; and we undertake to subscribe £lO to the War- rington Infirmary if, as the result of the investiga- tion, it is not shown that the Warrington and Old- Cheshire Examiner has a Lanoitn. SALE in the borough of Warrington than ourboastful contem- porary. We mention the borough of Warrington • because it is a distinct and definite area, the cen- tre of local population and the head quarters of both newspapers. The further condition stipula- ted is that the proprietors of the Warrington Guardian shall engage to subscribe £lO to the Infirmary if they, on their side, fail to make good similar claim. By SALE, we mean the total , number of papers for which payment can be shown to have been received; the time covered , to be the first three months of the present year. As ..the Warrington Guardian is a ' bi-weekly journal, either the Wednesday's or the Saturday's issue can be taken for comparison. It is time the public ascertained, beyond cavil, what there is . behind this bounce on the part of our local 'con- , temporary, and whether it will be able to boast when it has been brought to book. We have only to add .that this challenge will be open for ac- ceptance for four weeks. THE REV. THOMAS CHAMPNESS AT WIDNES.—The REV. Thomas Champneas, editor of "Joyful News," preached two sermons in Victoria-road Chapel on Wednesday. There were good congregations, and collections were made in aid of the Moss Bank Chapel Trust Fund. PROPERTY Sate AT Winges.—Missrs. J. B. and B. Leach, auctioneers, on Thursday evening, at Widnes Central Hotel, offered six lots of property in Egypt-st. and Moor-lane, Widnes, but in neither instance was the reserve reached, and the property was withdrawn Tom VICARAGE OF FARNWORTH.—The Bishop of Liver- pool has appointed the Rev. W. Edmondson, curate in charge of the parish of Farnworth, vacant 'owing to the sospension of the Rev. George Bond for three years. Mr. ' Edmondson has been curate of Parr, St. Ilelehs; since 1883, and he has the reputation of being a diligent visitor and a fair preacher. He has worked most amic- ably with the Rev. A. Nunn, his vicar. He will commence upon his duties at Farnworth three months hence. , MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHORCH, WIDNES. The annual tea meeting and conceit in connection with this place of worship were held on Thursday evening. There was a good attendance at tea, and at the concert after- wards the room was comfortably filled. Mr B. Brown presided. The vocalists were Miss Poole (Sandbach), soprano; Miss Linaker (Runcorn), contralto; Messrs R. H. Williams (Runcorn), tenor; G. Lacey (Runcorn), tenor; and Francis Mason (Winsford), bass. There also contributed to the programme Miss Tyril (Runcorn), reciter; and Mr G. Coupe, violin. Mr J. Jones was the accompanist. HARRY SPEAKMAN IN AITSTRALIA.—The vessel bearing the British football team arrived at Dunedin New Zealand, about a week ago. Intelligence has been re- ceived of some sports which Were held on board en St. Patrick's Day in honour of Sir Thomas Brady, an Irish Knight, who is taking out a few hundred thousand salmon spawn to stock the rivers of Tasmania. Our townsman. Harry Speakman, distinguished himself greatly in the contests, carrying away the first prize in 'the three-legged race. tl-e obstacle race, and the sack race, while he came in second in the potatoe race, the wheelbarrow .ace, and skipping. WESTON POINT WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—The last meeting of the season in connection with the Weston Point Wesleyan Band of Hope took place in the school- room on Tuesday evening. A tea meeting, provided free for members, was held, to which about 60 sat down. Miss Whitby, Miss Dunbavand, Ms..; Herrington, and Miss Okell presided at the tables. At the subsequent meeting, Mr. W. Leathwood, of Runcorn, occupied the chair. and there was a crowded audience. The Chair- man delivered a brief address, after which a miscel- laneous programme of songs, recitations, and dialogues was gone through in a very creditable manner by vari- ous members of the society. AN INeacinors RUNCORN DESIGNER.—There is on view In the window of Mr. Carr, jeweller, Regent-st., a coro- nation pendant, which has been engraved from the de- sign of Mr. Sam Boyers, of Runcorn. The pendant, which takes the form of a Maltese cross, has on one side the Queen's head "of 1838" engraved as a centre piece, and the arms of England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales are displayed on the corners of the cross. On the reverse side is a representation of a jubilee 3d piece, whilst the rose, the thistle, the shamrock, and the leek are en- graved on the bars. The workmanship of the pendant, which is of silver, is of the highest class. The jubilee of Her Majesty's coronation will be celebrated on the 28th June next, and this pendant will form an interesting memento. RUNCORN TONIC Sot-F.'. Cnoin.—The third grand con- cert of the season will be given in the Public Hall on Monday evening, when the public will have an opportu- nity of hearing Pattison's new" May Day" cantata, and, judging by the previous performances of the choir, we should say that they may rely opon hearing a good inter- pretation of the work. The programme also includes a specimen of the old madrigal in vogue three hundred, years ago; three of Mendelssohn's exquisite part-songs, , and in memoriam of the lately deceased composer, Pin- suti, a rendering of his part-song, "The Watchword," will be given. On this occasion the choir will ha+e the assistance of Miss Emilie Wiwi', Eistedfodd prize winner, and Mr. George Butterworth, honours Royal Academy and Trinity College, London. Rtnedonie PUBLIC HALL.—The magistrates held a special session on Monday to hear an application from Mr. A. Salkeld for a license to perform stage plays at the Public Hall. There were on the bench Major Hazleliumt, Mr. James Reynolds, Mr. James Handley, Mr. A. Thomas, and Mr. G. L. Davies.—Superintendent Hollingworth said he had no objection to raise against the granting of the license. He believed there were some alterations be- ing made to the hall.—Mr. Salkeld said there were some alterations to be made in connection with the stage.— The Chairman: They have nothing to do with the exits. —Mr. Salkeld : No sir. The license has been granted for about nine years.—The Bench then granted the ap- plication, and Messrs. IV. Whittaker and Thomas Brewer becgme sureties for the proper carrying out of the terms of the license. HALTON Buniza, BOVRD.—The dsual monthly meeting was held on Tuesday evening, in the girls' school. There were present—Rev. .1. Lockwood (elected chairman for the year), Messrs J. Barrow, J. W. lituidock, G. Leath- wood, J. Looker, H:Rowe, J. Rutter, and J. S. Jeacock (secretary). The chairman reported that the auditor's statement of accounts for the past year had been pre- sented to the ratepayers at a meeting held for that pur- pose, which was duly passed. It was resolved to pro- vide seven seats for the cemetery, six feet long, to lay out flower beds, and to set flowers, and, in the autumn, to plant suitable trees, as the exposed site and noxious vapours had blighted the shrubs which were placed in last year. It was decided, too, that a board of regula- tions should be fixed atthe cemetery showing the various fees and charges. LECTURE AT HALTON.—A lecture in aid of the funds of the Halton Mutual Improvement Society was given on Tuesday evening, in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, by Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn. Subject, "Ireland—its Natural Beauties, Past History, and Present Misery." The lecture, which was illustrated 131170 oxy-hydrogen photographic views (shown by Mr. Horace Handley), was listened to throughout with the greatest attention'' by a large audi- ence, who showed their appreciation by frequently ap- plauding the lecturer. The Rev. R. F. Hornabrook, in proposing a vote of thahks to Mr.. Handley, said that whatever the political opinions of those present might be, he felt sure that after listening to the lecture they would all wish for Ireland in the future a better govern-, ment than she had had in the past. Mr. W. H. Bradbury seconded the proposition, which was carried unani- mously. The meeting was presided over by Mr. J. H. Gamon. RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. A well-attended special meeting of the members of this society was held on Tuesday, under the presidency, of Mr. D. Worthing- ton. Mr. Watson proposed, and Mr. Whinyates secon- ded, a proposition that in future the accounts should be audited by a firm of public accountants, but the meet- ing almost unanimously decided to retain the present system. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Whin- yates, seconded by Mr. W. Cropper, that a clause be ad- ded to the building rules, empowering the committee to relieve a borrower from making repayments if the com- mittee think the mortgage a good and safe investment, and the society does not need the money repaid. The committee, however, may at any time when necessary enforce the repayments. It was further decided to add a cottage building clause on the principle of one member one cottage repayment and interest to be charged as ren- tal worked upon a lssis of 7i per cent per annum-5 per cent interest, and 2.k per cent repayments—on the first account, A premium of 2i per cent to be charged in each case instead of the usual one-fifth.—Mr. Clarke proposed, and Mr. J. Betney seconded, a proposition that permission be given to build a ceutral store for gro- ceries, drapery, and boots and shoes in the Market- square, Widnes, but it was resolved that the subject be adjourned until the half-yearly meeting, the committee in the meanwhile to obtain plans and estimates of the probable cost. Permission was however given to pur- chase a shop at Simm's Cross, Widnes, for the butchering business.
TOOM

NET/ Rens FOR Rc.ini Uwzow. The Runcorn magistrates have this week sanctioned the following poor ra.tes :—Aston-by-Sutton, Is id in the £, to realise £338 Os 3d; Aston Grange, is Iltd in the £, to realise £BO 7s id; and Sutton, is Id in £, to realise £398 4s 2d. _

FOOTBALL MATCH AT WIDNES.—A football match be- tween teams representing the works of Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele, Runcorn, and the Widnes Alkali Company,etook place at Widnes on Thursday qyening. The Runcorn team were victorious by one try and three minors to four minors. Colictirr AT WIDNES.—In aid o St. Mary's Roman, Catholic Young Men's Society brass band, a successful concert was given in the Drill Hall on Monday night. The vocalists were Miss R. O'Keeffe, Miss K. O'Keeffe, Miss M. Dwyer, and Miss Jameson; Messrs. Lester Bar- rett, Henry Holland, and C. Finn. Miss Cullen and Mr. F. Morris were the accompanists. • THE ASSAULT BY A 'WOMAN AT WIDNES.—On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Catherine Lawrenson, of 11, Marsh-st., was charged on remand with having grievously wounded George Jackson by biting his finger on Saturday, the 14th inst.—Dr. Hutchinson said blood poisoning had set in the finger, and possibly the man would lose the ihnb.—The prisoner was again remanded for a week. , PRESENTATION AT WIDNES —As a token of the esteen land regard in which they held the Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson, curate the members of St. Paul's Church Bible , Class on Tuesday evening presented that gentleman with a 'handsome travelling bag. Mr. F. H. Pankhurst made the presentation on behalf of the class, and Mr. Wilson suitably replied. Mr. Wilson has accepted an appointment at Glossop, Derbyshire. A PAWNBROKER'S CASE AT RUNCORN.—At the Runcorn Police Court, en Wednesday, before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. G. L. Davies, Martha Wakefield was charged with stealing a shawl, worth 4s. the property of Henry Dodd, pawnbroker, Princes-st. The shawl • was Missed on the 17th March,-1887, and a few days ago Mr. Dodd saw the article, exposed for sale at the shop of Mi. Davies, pawnbroker, High-st. It was then ascertained that it had been pawned by the prisoner over 12 months ago, and she was apprehended by P. S. Woolley.—The prisoner said she was taking a bundle of her own to the pawnshop when a woman asked her to pledge the shawl and she did so.—ln consequence of the lapse of time since the theft, the Bench discharged the prisoner. ROBBERY FROM 'A'SCHOONBR AT HUNCORN.—On Wednes- day, at Runcorn Police Court, John Bute Haldane, was charged with stealing £6 belonging to Edwin Noel. Noel is the mate of the schooner Velocity, and on Saturday ' night about half past ten he was on his Way to the vessel at the Docks, when he met the prisoner, Wlio. was: in a state of intoxication. With commendable kindness Noel gave the prisoner a night's lodging. Next morning the prisoner appeared anxious to depart, but, his entertainer said he would not permit him to ao until he had had some breakfast, but whilst Noel was away ordering the repast the prisonertook his departure. Shortly after- wards Noel discovered that £6 in gold had been taken from a box in the cupboard. The money was safe on Saturday morning. The prisoner when apprehended had 5s in his possession.—lnspector Millington said he hai ascertained that the prisoner was a sailor and was paid off from a vessel that arrived at Runcorn a few days ago. At that time the prisoner deposited £.5 with a publican in the town, and he received back the last 10s on Saturday morning.—The prisoner said he was quite innocent of the charge, and he was discharged as the Bench did not consider the evidence sufficient.

DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS. BARCLAY.-011 SlMlday last Mrs. Barclay, widow of the late Canon Barclay, for over 40 years Vicar of Runcorn, died at her residence, Liverpool-road, Chester, after an illness extending over several months. She had attained to the advanced age of 74 years. On Thursday her mortal remains were de- posited beside those of her much-lamented hus- band, in the burial ground attached to Run- corn Parish Church. The funeral arrangements were I entrusted to Mr W. H. Rogerson. of Runcorn, and Messrs Yarwood and Son supplied the mourning coaches. The body was caiveyed from Chester to Runcorn by road, and as the mournful procession wended its way to the church there were many instances of the respect and esteem in which the deceased lady was held. In front was the Doctor's ca.riage, containing the Rev. Canon 131encowe (canon in residence, Chester), the Rev. W. C. Safford, and Dr. MacDougall • Ist mourning coach, Mr. Rougier, Mr. J. Brundrit, J.F., Rev. J. J. Bryant. and the Rev. Thomas Douglas (Irleth Vicarage) • 2nd mourning coach, Mr. J. Douglas (Nottingham); and five grand-children of the deceased. At the church gates, the body, which was enclosed in a coffin of polished oak, with brass furni- ture, was met at the church gate by the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, M.A. (vicar of Runcorn), and the Rev. -W. Bryant, M.A., who were accompanied by the stir- piiced choir, who chanted the first portion of the office for the dead. The service was conducted by the Rev. Canon Blencowe and the Rev. W. C. Safford. The coffin was hidden beneath floral tributes to the memory of the deceased. There was a large assemblage of the parish- ioners to witness the interment. Tint ALLEGED "PRIZE FIGHT " AT WIDNES. —Before Mr. John Brock and Mr. H. Gaskell, jwir., at Widnes , Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Joseph Harrison, described as of Widnes, and George Hardman, of Lugsdale-road, were charged with creating a breach of the peace by "shouting, assaulting, striking, and fighting with each other, making a great noise and disturbance" on the 4th April.—Superintendent Johnston said having read a report of a prize fight on the Old Marsh, he sent PC. Thompson to make inquiries, and he found that a fight, had taken 'place in Peelbouse-lane.—William Byrne, of ' 9, Eleanor-st., employed as a labourer at the works of ' Messrs. Hall Bros. and Shaw, said the defendants were having a "bit of a lark " with one another in the Alex- andra Hotel, when one of them got vexed and they went out on the waste ground near the Cheshire Lines Rail- way. They fought one or two rounds together and then returned to the hotel. In answer to Mr. J. 0. Swift, who appeared for the defendants, the witness said the men were quite friendly, and neither of them were hurt Hardman admitted that Harrison was a better man, and they had afterwards had a drink together at the Alexan- dra. He (witness) was the only spectator, and there was no noise.—Mr. Laws, reporter, having given evi- dence, Mr. Swift contended that these proceedings'had arisen through a paragraph written by an imaginative reporter. So long as they acted in a private and friendly manner, with no intention of hurting one another, they were entitled to decide which was the best man either with gloves or fists. There was no crowd or disturb- ance.—Mr. Brock said these men were unquestionably fighting in a public place, and they would each be bound over to keep the peace for three months, in two sureties of £5 each. RUNCORN WESLEYAN TEMPERANCE SOCIETY AND COM- PENSATION TO PUBLICANS.—A meeting of the committee of the Runcorn Circuit Wesleyan Temperance Society which is composed of representatives from each Wasleyan Chapel in qie Runuorn circuit, was held in Brunswick ,School, Runcorn, on Wednesday, to consider the licen- sing clauses in the Local Government Bill, The Rev. G. Wood presided, and there was a good attendance. The following resolution was passed with only two dissen- tients :—That in the opinion of the meeting the proposal to compensate publicans to whom—for the public good —licenses may be again granted, is unjust and contrary to precedent, and would, if adopted, be such an intoler- able burden to the ratepayers as to prevent the exercise of the principle of local option which the bill proposes to establish; and this meeting earnestly appeals to the Government to at once withdraw the proposal, and Should they decline to do so, calls upon all fauminded citizens to use every effort to prevent the adoption of such a proposal by the House of Commons." It was , further resolved— That this meeting welcomes the aTe eeptance by the Government of the principle that the ratepayers should control the liquor traffic, but considers that no legislation for dealing with it can be at all ade- quate which does not confer upon the ratepayers the power of preventing by direct vote the issue and re- newal of licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquors in their respective localities." Mr. J. D. Jones, the secre- tary, was instructed to forward these resolutions to Mr. J. T. ,Brunner, M.P., and to the President of the Local Government Board. In reply to a private letter from Mr. Jones, Mr. Brunner wrote as follows :—" House of Commons, 24th April, 1888.—Dear Jones,-1 feel sure you need no assurance from me that I view the compensation clauses of the Local'Government Bill with regret and alarm and detestation. I will lose no oppor- tunity of voting against them.—Yours faithfully, JOHN T. BRUNNER." ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE AT WIDNES. —At Widnes Police Cond on Monday, Richard Rawlinson, a youth, whose home is in Sutton's-lane, was charged with hav- ing been drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Worsfold. Another youth named John Heyes, of 18, Eleanor-st., was charged with assaulting P.C. Houghton, and also with attempting to rescue Rawlin- son. About a quarter past ten on Sunday night P.C. Worsfold was 'on duty in Waterloo-road, when the Prisoners and another youth came along. Rawlinson was drunk, and the prisoner ran at him and struck him, and would have done so again but his companions held him back. At length he released himself from his com- panions and struck the officer a second time. After a brief struggle P.C. Houghton arrested the prisoner, and was on the way to the police station when Reyes at- tempted to rescue; him. A great crowd assembled. It was stated that P.C. Worsfold some months ago brought a charge of felony against the prisoners, who were each sentenced to three months' imprisonment.— For being drunk, Rawlinson was fined 5s and costs, and was sentenced to a month's hard labour for the assault. Hayes was also sentenced t 6 a similar term of imprison- ment.—Joseph Smith, a rough-looking young man, of no settled residence, was ,charged with sleeping out, and with having assaulted P.C. Houghton. It appeared that about a quarter to one on Saturday morning the con- stable found the prisoner lying without coat and vest in the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. The officer told him to get up and dress himself, when he rushed at him unawares and threw him to the ground, struck him on the head several times, and kicked him on the legs. The prisoner also bit the constable on the wrist, and the latter had to use his staff .—The prisoner was sentenced to seven days for sleeping out, and to fourteen days hard labour for the assault.—Wm. Dermott, labourer, of Net- son-st., was fined 5s and'costs for being drunk and dis- orderly on the 17th inst., and 5s and costs for assaulting P.c. Houghton whilst in the execution of his duty.

LICENSING MATTERS AT WIDNES.—The Widnes magis- trates on Thursday granted the transfer of the following licenses :—A beerhouse at Farnworth, from Mary Lea- ther to Susannah Leather; the Market Gate Hotel, Wid- nes, from Sarah Price to Peter Price; the Queen's Hotel' ' Moor-lane, from Mary Doyle to Philip Blessington ; the Cuerdley Arms Inn, Widnes, from Philip Blessmgton to James Howard; the Railway Inn, Ditton, from William Lea to Joseph Lea; the West Bank Hotel, Church-st., from Frank McGovern to Paul Caldwell • and the license held by William Henry Whelan, at R;inhill, to Joseph Copple. , "Housa BREAKING AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Robert Wilson, a young man, whose home is at 51, Wellington-st., was charged with breaking into the house of James Lloyd, labourer, 12, Wellington-st., and stealing two coats and a pair of trousers, worth altogether 10s. The evidence showed.that on Saturday night about half-past seven Lloyd locked up his house and went away. Shortly afterwards his son Edward, aged 12 years who had ob- tained the key, entered through the front door and went and set at liberty the dog,which was barking in the par- lour. Ile then saw two men, one of whom was the pri- soner, standing in the kitchen. He "set "the dog upon them and they ran away through the wash-house. Hear- big of this the father returned home about ten o'clock, and observing that the house was in confusion he searched the house, and under a bed in an upper room he discovered the prisoner. The prisoner attempted to make his escape, but Lloyd closed with him and a long struggle ensued. P.C. Maitland coming upon the scene, took the prisoner into custody.—The prisoner, who said he was under the influence of drink at the Ulu% was committed to the assizes for trial.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOAIID.-At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mr. G. 11. Danby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following pare'nts for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of 5s was imposed in each instance :-John Handley, 12, Parson- age-road • Alfred Rushton, 108, Tee-st. •' Charles Yuc- hanan, 21, Peel-st. ; Annie Abrams, 31,Davies-st. ; 'Mar- tin Weir, 6, Nelson-st. ; James Harrison, 31, Beamont- st. ; Alice Williamson, 83, John-st. Owen Lewis, 17, Ellison-st. ; Edward Ryan, 37, Victoria-st. ; Charles McKenna, 14, Elizabeth-st. ; William Wright, 101, Travis-st. ; Thomas ' Mannion, 10, Arthur-st.; John Byrn, 52, Wahnsley-st. ; John Cunliffe, 18Major Cross- st. ; Peter McCarthy, 14, Oxford-st. ; Charles McKenna, 14, Elizabeth-st. ; Edward Price, 74, Walmsley-st. ; Peter Stewart, 53, Victoria-st. ; James Mason, Barrow's-row; ISamuel Cartwright, 93, Midwood-st. ; William Jones, 11, Chatham-st. : Henry Whitefield, 8, Cross-st. • William lEdwardson, Farrant-st. ; John Sparkes, 72, iiraterlob- road ; Denis Malone, 38, Pear-st. •' William Carter, 19, : John Eurery, 20, Bank-st. ; James Ffynan, 63, Nelson-st. ; Patrick Fitzsimons, 80, Bridge-st.; Michael iMaher, Cromwell-st. ; John Heyes, 52, Beamont-st.; William Carter, ; William Melton, 37, Elizabeth- st. ; Matthew Burnes, 19, Sutton's-lane: Patrick Callon, 58, Timperley-st. ; Mary Donogha.n, 2, Poole-st. ; Timothy Kilmartin, 44, Davies-st. •, Peter McLochlin, 18, Catherine-st. ; Patrick Daley, 47, Moss Bank-road ; Catherine Kennedy, Lunt's Heath,: George Grice, 17, Church-st., Faniworth.-The son of William Fallon, of 8, Bedford-st.' was committed to an industrial school. SUDDEN DEATFI AT DARESBURY.-Albert Edward .Tohnson (14j, an errand boy, died suddenly at Daresbtiry on Monday night. Yesterday ,week he complained of being unwell, and, after apparently improving, he was taken suddenly worse on Mon- day, and died. The coroner was communicated with, but as deceased had been under medical at- tendance for a rheumatic affection it was not thought necessary to holdall inquest. • SOLDIERING.-The total number of men who en- listed in the Army last year in Lancashire was 2,476, a decrease of neatiy 1.300 as compared with 1886. In Cheshire the number of men who joined the ranks was only 223, a decrease of 352 on the previous year. At Warrington 469 were accepted. against 410, an increase of 59. As regards the re- cruiting in connection with the army localisation scheme, 131 enlisted at Warrington for King's Liverpool Regiment, and 158 for the South Lanca- shire Regiment. THE VICARAGE OF FARNWORTH.-The Bishop of Liverpool has appointed the Rev. William Edmond- son as curate-in-charge of the parish of Farnworth, now vacsnt owing to the suspension of the Rev. George Bond for three years. The Rev. William Edmondson has been curate of Parr, St. Helens, since 1883. He has the reputation of being a most diligent and helptul house-to-house visitor, a fair preacher, and a man likely to bring peace and pro- gress to his difficult and arduous sphere. He has worked most amicably with the Rev. A. A. Nunn, the vicar of Parr Church. Mr. Edmondson will enter upon his new duties about three months hence.

CLERICAL CHANGES AT RAINFOILIX—IS is stated that the Rev. 0. A. Jones will vacate the curacy of Rainford parish in the course of a tew weeks. Mr. Jones has laboured zealously during the three years he has resided there, and his duties have been heavy owing to the illhealth of the former vicar. On medical advice he intends to spend some weeks on the South coast, with the view of recruiting his health. The Rev. J. W. Williams, of Widnes, the vicar-elect of Rainford, will commence his new ministerial duties next month. The vicinage is being altered and renovated, and Mr. Williams will be assisted by his present curate, the Rev. J. R. Jones. CHESHIRE LINES PROVIDENT SOCIETY.-- The thirtieth annual meeting of the Cheshire Lines Platelayers' and Workmen's Provident Sick and Burial Society, which consists of the workmen em- ployed in the engineers' department of the Cheshire Lines Railway, was held at the works, Battersby- ' lane, Warrington, on Wednesday. Mr. W. G. Scott, C.E., the chief engineer of the company, presided, and the meeting was largely attended by officials and delegates from various parts of Lancashire and Cheshire. The secretary submitted the annual re- port, which stated that the number of members was 942. A large amount of benefit money had been ex- pended during the financial year, 165 sick members having received assistance from the funds, while 15 death claims had been paid. The report and state- ment of accounts having been passed, Mr. Thomai I Pratt was eleeted secretary for the ensuing year, and the auditors, Messrs I). S. Duncan and S. Dale, were re-elected. The proceedings terminated with , a vote of thanks to the chairman. Loc.tr. Divoucn Surr.—ln the Divorce Division, on Saturday, the president, Sir James Hannen, had before him the divorce suit of Pickmere v. Pick- mere and Walters, which was the petition of the husband, Mr. William Travers Pickmere, for a dis- solution of marriage on the ground of his wife's adultery with the co-respondent, Walters. The co- respondent filed an answer denying the adultery, but he was not represented.' Mr. Inderwick, Q.C., and Mr. 'Jean appeared for the petitioner; and Mr. Barnard for the wife. The parties were married at St. Nicholas' Church, Nantwich, on the 13th Sept., 1881, the husband being a wine and spirit merchant in that town. There were no children of the marriage. In April, 1886, Mrs Pickmere's father died, and she came into an income of £7OO or £BOO a year, as well as a reversionary interest of £2OO a year on the death of her mother. Alter that quar- rels arose between husband and wife, and the respondent left the petitioner in January, 1887. Subsequently a deal of correspondence passed between them as to a possible separation, but the husband later on ascertained that the res- pondent and the co-respondent had been living as man and wife at the Colston Hotel, Bristol, and also at Beech House, Weston-super-Mare, and filed a petition.—llis Lordship granted a decree nisi. Sin A. B. WALKER'S BREWERIES.—It was recently announced that the brewing businesses of Sir Andrew B. Walker, at Warrington, were about to be formed into a limited liability com- pany. It is expected that in a few days the prospectus will be issued by Messrs. Baring Brothers and Co., who so successfully floated Messrs. Guin- ness's company. The capital will be .£3,000,000, divided in equal parts into debenture stock at 4 per cent., cumulative preference at 6 per cent., and ordinary shares of £lO each. The profits of the busi- ness, it is said, have recently been at the rate of .£185,060 per annum. The following letter on the matter is taken from a Liverpool contemporary := "Messrs. Peter Walker and Co. Sir,—With refer- ence to the announcements which have lately ap- peared in the public Press, and in answer to the Inquiries of customers and other friends, will you be good enough to allow me to state through the 'medium of your columns that there is no intention of transferring to a limited liability company the business of the trustees of the latent.. Peter Walker, of Burton-on-Trent and Wrexham, nor that of Messrs. Pet& Walker and Co., of Liverpool 7—Yours, &c., Wu. A. HlLL.—April 26, 1888."—The businsss to be transferred is that of Messrs. A. B. Walker and Co. Sir A. B. Walker and his sons are, we understand, to retain one-third of the whole busi- ness; and Messrs. Baring have taken over two- thirds, which they will offer to the public in ordi- nary shares, preference shares, and debentures. Sir A. B. Walker and two of his sons will be among the directors. Two or three other gentlemen connected with Liverpool will be on the directorate.

div.head: lIR&LTH OF THE DISTRICT : OUTBREAK OF FEVER. _
div.p: lIR&LTH OF THE DISTRICT : OUTBREAK OF FEVER. _

The Medical Officer of Health reported that during the quarter ending March 31st, 1888, the registrar's return recorded 151 births and 86 deaths in the four registra- tion sub-districts of Runcorn Union. Of the births 87 were males and 64 females; birthrate 7-5 per 1,000 per quarter, or 30-0 per 1,000 per annum; compared with a birth rate of 6-3 per 1,000 per quarter, or 25.2 per 1,000 per annum in the corresponding quarter of 1887. ,Of the deaths 47 were males, and 39 females; death rate 41. per 1,000 per quarter, or 16.4 per 1,000 per annum; compared with a death rate of 4.3 per 1,000 per quarter, or 17-2 per 1,000 per annum in the corresponding quarter of 1887. Of the deaths 25 oc- curred amongst persons under one year of age, eight between the ages of one and five years, 25 between five and 60 years, and 28 between 60 years of age and up- wards. Typhoid fever accounted for two deaths (both in Dutton Workhouse), croup five deaths, diptheria two (both at Helsby), while bronchitis and pneumonia ac- counted for 26 deaths, or nearly one-third of the total deaths. Only three cases formed the subject of coroner's inquiries. The death rate was one of the lowest he had been able to record, and even this should be corrected and made lower by subtracting from it those deaths occurring in the Union Workhouse, which really belonged to the Ramon. urban district. The Medical Officer also presented a special report, stating that three cases of scarlet fever had occurred at Halton. All the cases were convalescent when brought under his notice. All precautions, however, had been taken and be trusted there would be no further extension.

THE MEDICAL OFFICER AND THE ERIE CANAL. Mr. Hadfield said he noticed from the newspapers that Dr. Adams, the medical officer to the Authority, had , been appointed a medical officer to the Ship Canal. Per- haps some dispute might arise between the Authority and the Ship Canal Company with regard to sanitary matters; would the duties of Dr. Adams, as an officer of the Ship Canal, clash with his duty to the Union ?—Mr. Wallington stated that Dr. Adams had been merely ap- pointed as doctor in ease of accidents, and not with regard to sanitary matters.—The Clerk saidin his opinion Dr. Adams was merely like the medical man of a club.— Mr. Aaron explained that the whole length of the Ship Canal from Eastham to Manthester was divided into sections, and each section had its sick and accident club. Dr. Adams was simply appointed club doctor for his dis- trict.—The discussion then ceased.

NAVVIES AND ovsacnownrma. The Inspector applied for certificates of occupation to be granted to six wooden houses erected on the Weaver wharf at Weston Point for the use of the workmen em- ployed in the construction of the Ship Canal. The houses were supplied with water from the Runcorn Waterworks Co.'s mains.—Mr. Aaron said he had been through the houses many a time. They were a credit to Mr. Walker, and to the builder. Mr. T. Kirkham. There were scores of houses at Weston and hundreds at Runcorn that were much -worse.—Mr. Thomas Hewitt: I can quite en- dorse that.—Mr. Aaron moved that the certifi- cates be granted. The motion was carried. The Inspector reported that there was a tendency to overcrowding of .houses in the townships of Appleton, Stockton Heath, Walton Inferior, and Halton. Some of the houses ought to come under the term common lod- ging houses, and he suggested that the Authority should adopt the Common Lodging Houses Act. He must say that the tenants of the houses he had visited were all very civil, and the bedrooms and bedding he had seen were very clean indeed, "though they be navvies." Still there was the tendency to over crowding‘and there was no doubt that there would be a greater influx of men in to the district, and there would be overcrowding. There was a house in Halton that had been occupied by a gen- tleman was now convertedinto a common iodging-house to accommodate 40 persons. The houses that were being built for the labourers on the Ship Canal were really common lodgiug-houses.—Mr. Wallington moved, and Mr. Aaron seconded, that the Authority adopt the Com- mon Lodging Houses Act.—Mr. Stokes inquired whether a cottager who took in two or three lodgerswould have to register.—The Inspector replied no. A common lodging- house was one where rooms were set apart for men to live and to sleep. The motion was carried.
DANOBR 'TO LONDON BRIDGE.

The Inspector said the agent to the Ship Canal Works had applied to drain a w.c. at London Bridge into the sewer. The Inspector stated that the sewer was 18 feet deep, and if the ground was opened up to make the con- nectien there WILA a possibility that the bridge would fall in. He had authorised the connection to be made with the man-hole at a depth of about five feet. The Authority approved of this course. This concluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The annual meeting was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday. Present—The Rev. .1. W. N. Tanner, Rev. J. Lockwood, Colonel Ashton, Messrs. P. Speakman. J. Knowles, J. Stokes, S. Taylor, E. Aaron, John Weir, H. J. Once, T. Lewis, J. Picker- ing, Warburton, E A. Wallington, T. Hewitt, P. Ilan, Joseph Hall, W. Hewitt, IV. Whitlow, E. Jack- son, D. H. Jones, Smith, and Campkin, with Mr. Dansey (inspector ot the Local Government Board), and Mr. H. Linaker (clerk). RE-APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.—The 'Rev. J. W. N. Tanner moved that Colonel Ashton be re-appointed chairman of the Board. The urbanity he had displayed, and the quickness with which he had despatched busi- ness, entitled him to preside over the members for the ensuing year. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Speakman seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously—Colonel Ashton then took the chair, and expressed his pleasure at this mark of their renewed confidence.—On the pro- position of the Rev. J. Lockwood, seconded by Mr. Had- field, Mr. John Mclntyre was appointed senior vice- chairman.—Mr. Joseph Knowles was appointed junior vice-chairman on the motion of Mr.Speakman,seconded by Mr. W. Whitlow. AN Ixeinnv.—Mr. Whitlow asked why it was that while the assessment of the Union was raised annually the rates should be raised at the same time. There was a heavier rate now. Where he asked did the money go? He had that question to answer to the parishioners that sent him to the Board and he should be pleased if the clerk or chairman could instruct him. The Chairman suggested that the expenditure had been greatly in- creased by sanitary work. The Clerk said there had not been any sanitary rate during the past year. There had however been a great expense in connection with the House last year. ComurrxEs.—The following committees were ap- pointed : Assessment Committee : Edward Wright, Charles Reynolds, Alfred Thomas and Henry Neild (ex- officio Guardians), Edward Aaron, Peter Hall, John Mc- Intyre, Joseph Knowles, Philip Speakman, William Whit- low, Thomas Lewis, and John Weir.—Finance Com- ntittee:—Messrs. John Ashton, John Mclntyre, Joseph Knowles, Samuel Taylor, H. .1. Grice, William Hewitt, John Weir, W. Whitlhow, Joseph Hall, James Bran- dreth, Joseph Stokes, and the Rev. J. Lockwood.— Relief Supervision Committee.—Rev. J. W. Tanner, Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. John Ashton, John Mclntyre, Joseiih Knowles, C. Mounfield, John Campkin, Joseph Smith, J. W. Lightburn, Davies, P. Hall, J. Hall, James Parr Joseph Stokes, Samuel Taylor Thomas Lewis, W. Hewitt, J. Bmndreth, P. Speakman:E. Aaron, William Pickering, 11. J. Grice, J. W. Kirkham, and John Weir.—School Attendance Committee.-Messrs. C. Reynolds, Major VV. V. Fox, Henry Neild, G. L. Davies (ex-officio Guardians) ; Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Lockwood, Mes.vs. John Ashton, E. Aaron' Wm. Pickering, Joseph Stgikes, Joseph Knowles, and John Weir. THE RESIGNATION OF THE DEPITFY CLERIC—The Chair- man said, as unanimously requested, he had written to Mr. W. H. Linaker asking him to reconsider his deci- sion to resign his post as deputy clerk. On the previous day be saw Mr. Linaker, who desired him to thank the members of the Board for their expressions of sympathy. and he authorised him to state that he would withdraw his resignation for three months to see how his health continued. (Hear, hear.) A Comstirmit von 'I2IINCORN.—On the proposition of Mr. Grim, seconded by Mr. Taylor, the committee for the remission of school fees at Runcorn, consisting of the five Guardians returned from that place, were re- appointed. There was no other business'of public interest.

- THE BIRMINGHAM LOVE TRAGEDY.—Miss Hastings, daughter of the tenant of the Golden Elephant, Castle- st., Birmingham, died in the General Hospital on Friday morning from bullet wounds in the head and breast, in- flicted by her sweetheart, a man named Daniels, on Saturday night last. During the ,interval she has re- mained unconscious, except fOr _a-few moments, when she declined to say anything against her assailant. Daniels, whose mind is suppieed to have been upset by pecuniary troubles, is in a rr sst depressed and wretched state.

Croft, of Hatton. DRUNMENNESS.—James Povey was charged with hav- ing been drunk at Hatton, on the 24th March ; the case was dismissed.--Samuel Buckley, drunk at Hatton, was fined 5s and costs. A SLBEPY Curran.—Robert Sheave, a driver, em- ployed by Messrs. Fairclough, of Warrington, was charged with having been asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart, at Stretton, on the 10th March, and was fined 5s and costs. CHARGE AGAINST A Puatic.ix.—John Kirkham, of the Hatton Arms Inn, Hatton, was charged with having un- lawfully supplied liquor to a drunken man named James Povey, and Pevey was charged with having been drunk on the licensed premises in question.—Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, of Warrington, appeared on behalf of the defendants. P.C. 106, who is stationed at Hatton, spoke to having visited the Hatton Arms at 9-35 p.m. on the 7th April, and findino. Povey in a drunken condition leaning against a door. 'Povey afterwards reeled round and sat down at a table from which he picked up a glass of beer, out of which he drank. When asked to stand up in the room Povey staggered about a good deal, and afterwards—about a quarter past 10 o'clOck—the officer found him lying helpless by the road side. In defence it was contended that Povey had not been drunk. The bench, however, considEred the charges proved and liirkham was fined lOs and costs, and Povey, 5s and costs. SWINR FRVER.—Thomas Kirkham, of Comberbach, was charged with having had in possession at Hatton, four pies suffering from swine fever, of which fact he had failed to give notice. It was stated in evidence that defendant, who is a pig dealer, had sold four pigs to Mr. Dodds, a small farmer at Hatton' which turned out to be suffering from swine fever. Defendant pleaded that he had been unaware of the fact that the pigs were suffering from the disease.--Colonel Hamersley, the Chief Constable of the County, who had a seat on the bench, commented on the serious effects of swine fever, and mentioned that last year no less than £7OO had been paid in compensation in the county in connection with swine fever. In 31 cases of the disease which he had inquired into he found that 26 were of pigs that had been bought from dealers, so that he thought it rested to a very great extent in the hands of dealers to bring the fever to an end. He thought that Mr. Kirkham, being a pig dealer, must have known that the pigs in question were suffering from the disease, and as that was not his first offence he (Col. Hamersley) hoped the bench would endeavour to make an impression on the defendant's mind.—The Chairman said that was a very bad case, and the defendant would be fined £5 and costs in each c. ALLEGATIONS AGAINST A CONSTiBLE.—Joha Berry, a farm manager, Appleton, and Richard Fendlebury, , labourer employed on the Ship Canal, andliving at Grap- penhall, were charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly at Grappenhall on the 25th March.—Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for the defence.—P.C. Bennett said ' that at 12-15 a.m. on Sunday, the 25th March, he heard' the two defendants making a good deal of noise on Stanny Lunt Bridge, Grappenhall. He went up to them and they both assumed a fighting attitude, and said they would knock his head off. Berry aimed a blow at the officer, but the latter stepped aside, the result being that Berry fell to the ground. Both the defendants were drunk. When cross-examined witness denied having struck Pendlebury on the head with a stick.—P.S. Booth, and P.C. Dutton corroborated Bennett's statement.—The former, in cross-examination, said he did not see a wound on the top of Pendlebury's head, and his face was not covered with blood, neither was Berry's cravat torn. It was not a fact that Bennett had Berry on the ground, and that witness told the constable to let him go.—Mr. Browne, in addressing the Bench for the defence, said that the case would never have been brought there had it not been that P.C. Bennett committed a very serious assault upon one of the defendants.- Pendlebury received a wound exactly on the top of his head, which did not heal up for a fortnight; it was just such a wound as 'would be caused by a stick or baton. He denied that thq two clek.Zlanrs werA drank. tie further al_l:,ged that P.C. Bennett threw Berry on the grow!!., and then struck Pendlebury a violent blow on the head with his stick, knocking the trian down, and causing a serious wound on the drown of his head. Bennett then caught Berry by the throat, and was holding him on the ground when P.S. Booth came up and told him to let the man get up. The defendants asked what it was all for, and Booth replied, "We are very sorry, we have made a mistake." Pendlebury's head was covered with blood, and his coat was saturated.—Evidence for the defence was called, and the magistrates, after retiring for con- sultation, dismissed the case.

Dimelow, Gilchrist, Egerton, and Forster. ST. HELENS Rms. A TEAM V. WARRINGTON ST:PAUL'S. —This match was played on the Boundary-road ground .on Saturday. The Recs. winning the toss, St. Paul's kicked off against the wind. From a scrummage close to the goal line the Saints scored, the kick failing. From the drop-out the Recs. took the ball to the St. Paul's goal line, and after a grand dribble W. Matthews scored. Grainger proved successful at the place. Kicking off again, the game became very exciting, each goal line having its share of danger. Nothing further was scored, however, up to half-time. Starting again, the game was very even for a while, when a good run by St. Paul's the second try was scored, the place kick being a failure. From the drop-out the Recs. made St. Paul's 'goat line look dangerous, Peachey from a scrummage eventually getting over, the kick failing. The whistle blew at the. close of a very exciting game with the score as follows —Recs., 1 goal, 1 try, and 2 minors, to St. Paul's 2 tries and 4 minors. RUNCORN V. Me, BAINBRIDGE'S MANCHESTER TEAM.— Mr. H. H. Bainbridge, of Manchester, brought a team to , Runcorn on Saturday, to meet the home Club. A strong 1 team had been arranged for, but at the last moment it I was found that several of the players would be unable to fulfil the engagement, and substitutes had to be pro- vided. A fairly good team was placed on the field, but Runcorn had matters all their own way, and the game was rather one-sided. The ground was in good con- dition. Rain fell just before time for the match, but it afterwards cleared off and fine weather was experienced, and a large " gate " assembled. The latter team journeyed from Kendal on Saturday to bring off a match which had been arranged with the Warringtonians. Owing to the match in the afternoon elate start was effected, and it being five o'clock before the visitors arrived, it was after six o'clock before Frank Turner kicked off against a strong wind. Davies was awarded a free kick from Wilson's reply, and punted to the quarter-flag. The visitors repulsed an effort of the home team, and after Barnes and Wilson had been applauded for some pretty exchanges, Bandies came through the pack, and placed the visitors on their de- fence. Holmes saved his side from disaster, and, aided by the strong wind, kicked into touch close to the War- rington line. Armer missed a grand opportunity, and his drop at goal being charged down, Jolley kicked dead. Frank Turner dropped out, and after some exchanges between Jolley and Bell, W. Dillon headed the Warring- ton van to Kendal territory. Antrobus, Speakman, and Barnes now showed up with splendid passes, and a rush by Bandies, E. Dillon, and Ashton compelled Holmes to touch down. The drop-out found play at neutral ground, and Massey and Barnes made tracks for their opponents' line. This effort was neutralised by Holmes, and after Frank Turner had executed a pretty dribble, Bandies seconded his efforts by similar work and tackled Armer with the oval in his possession. Sea- son now retained a kick of Armer's, and directly after- wards, from a pack close to the Warrington goal, the home team showed the finest exhibition during the game. Antrobus passed sharply to Speakman, who in turn handed to Readies, the lattertransferring to Barnes, who gave Massey a chance, Bell checking him on the line. This piece of play was received with loud cheers, and after Massey had made another effort near the line, Antrobus passed smartly to Frank Turner, who got over near the post. No goal resulted from this place-kick. This success was quickly followed by pretty passing on the part of Donohue, Antrobus. and Speakman, the lat- ter handing his charge over to Jolley, who got in at the corner-flag. A capital attempt was made for the .goal •by Frank Turner. Barnes put in some grand work from the drop-out, and Bandies spoiled Holmes returning a kick. After the Warnington skipper and Massey had treated the spectators to a fine display, the last-named got over, but to his dismay he was ruled to have been in touch, although he was a few yards in play. Massey haci a futile drop at goal, and ends were changed, with the score—Warrington, 2 tries, 2 minors; Kendal, one minor. With the assistance of the wind it was thought the visitors were in for a severe beating, but they played with renewed vigour. Armstrong re-started, Barnes and Antrobus placing the visitors on their defence. A tall kick by Jolley forced a minor, and directly after Holmes kicked dead in the nick of time. Speakman next made off and ran to the line, and passing unselfishly to Jolley, enabled the latter to score an easy try. No goal re- suited. It was now the visitors' turn, and after Wil- son, Bell, and Winskill had carried the oval from the Warrington quarter-flag to the line Bell got over, but no goal resulted. Povey and the Brothers Dillon became conspicu6us by a pretty dribble to the Kendal quarter- flag soon after re-starting, and although this movement was baulked by Wilson, Massey again forced the visitors to concede a minor, after an attempt to drop a goal. Frank Turner broke away from a line-out, and Jolley again pressed the Kendal men with a huge kick. Barnes collared Armer before he could get away, and Holmes again conceded a minor. Barnes passed grandly to Massey, the latter being hold on the line. Season saved a dangerous rush here, and after Speakman had given his captain a splendid chance, Barnes dropped at goal, the ball going wide. The Kendal men now looked like scoring again, but Season was safe, and by a huge kick placed the gome at his opponents' quarter flag. Little- weed showed up with a sterling run, racing over near the posts. Barnes registered the premier point. Ex- change kicks by the opposing backs was now. witnessed, and Massey and Littlewood had both hard lines in not adding to the score: Massey, however, had his revenge shortly afterWardsl for after the Wanington halves had passed to each other, Antrobus transferred to Barnes, who gave Massey the leather, thelatter gaining the cove- ted point. No goal resulted, Mt from now to the call of time the home team had inatters all their own way, finally winning by 1 goal, 4 tries, 9 minors, to ltry and 2 minors. The play all round was splendid, the passing grand, kicking excellent, whilst the dribbling and tackling of the home team was a treat to witness. Season was given a trial at full back. Saturday was a poor day to test a rising player's Merits, butdudging from his display,what little he had to do was well done, and with a little more practice will develop into a first-class player, and ably fill a position which has been noted as Warrington's weakest point. All three-quarters playecrgmndly ; the way Barnes passed to his wing men was something out of the common. Both Jolley and Massey did all that was asked of them. The half backs were in splendid trim, and of all this season there has not been such a display as that shown by Speakman and Antrobus. Their passing was well timed, and it would be a hard task to find two others to work in the same uniform style as they did on Saturday. Of a grand team of forwards Frank Turner, Dillon, Bandies, and Littlewood deserve commen- dation.

WARRINGTON v. MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT. This match, which had been arranged for the benefit of J. Rigby, was brought to an issue on Monday evening at Warrington. The District team, which was under the superintendence of Mr. T. R. Sutton, was a strong one, and the home team having mustered their "best possi- ble" a grand game was anticipated. To show the esteem in which the old Warrington forward was held a large crowd assembled, although the weather was some- what cold. A strong wind prevailed, and it having been decided to play an hour, four quarters were weed on. Barnes took advantage of the wind, and A&ton (thd visiting captain) commenced hostilities with a huge kick to the Warrington quarter flag, Davies replying. Smith got away, but Fair Turner compelled the district team to save. Antrobus made his mark from the drop out, Dillon preventing Royle replying. The home team had for the first few minutes been playing without Speakman, but on the latter making his appearance he secured from a pack, and scored the first try for Warrington. No goal resulted from Fair Turner's place kick. Give-and-take play followed from the drop out, and after Antrobus and Speakman had passed to each other, Barnes compelled the visitors to defend their lines. Boyle now temporarily relieved to half-way, and after W. Dillon and Littlewood had ably dribbled to the twenty-five flag, Povey joined the issue and scored a brilliant try, Tamer kicking a goal. A drop at goal by Massey ended in a minor being added to the score, and similar points were conceded after use- ful dribbles by the Warrington forwards. Eagland now showed up with splendid kicks for his side, and Speak- man and Randles both ma.de efforts to cross the line, but the first quarter was ended with the score: Warrington one goal, one try, four minors to nil. Turner restarted the second quarter, and after Smith, had replied Sanson placed the game at half-way. The visitors removed operations to the home quarters, but Speakman passed to Barnes, who in turn handed over , to Massey, this player making a grand run to the line and passing to Davies. The latter transferred to Ashton; and finally E. Dillon got over, but unfortunately theball was ruled dead. having touched the umpire in its transit, and only a minor was awarded. A pleasure boat was driven ashore near Torquay on Thursday, and two ladies were drowned. SHAVING ON SUNDAY.—James Billington, of Fern- worth, Bolton, the hangsman for Yorkshire, on Thursday morning requested the county justices of Bolton to grant a summons against Sohn Jackson, barber, of Farn- , worth, for shaving on the Lord's Day.. The magistrates considered the application trivial, saying that men had more right to be clean on Sunday than any other day. FIRE IN _SHEFFIELD. Early on Thursday morning a serious tire broke out at Sheffield, in a restaurant kept by Mr. John Webster. The fire was discovered by a pas- sing police-constable, who aroused the inmates, who found that means of escape were cut off by the stair- case. The policeman thereupon ran for the fire escape. In his absence another constable arrived upon the scene with a ladder, by means of which he rescued Mrs. Web- ster and three girls from one of the bedroom windows in their night dresses.

Snocinio Sulam;lN BIILME.—About eight o'clock on Thursday mdrning. Mr. Thomas Chapmans, draper, of Great Jackson-st., Hulme, committed suicide in a most determined manner. Hearing the report of firearms In one of the bedrooms, Charles Clarke, an assistant in Mr. Chapman's employ, ran to ascertain the cause, and on entering the room found the deceased lying dead on his back on the floor in the midst of a pool of blood and a discharged rifle across his legs. The back part of his head was completely blown away. The deceased has been very strange in his manner since the death of his father, four years ago. APPROACHING MARRIAGE OF MR. CHAMEERLAIN.—The "Daily Chronicle" of Thursday morning announces the approaching marriage of the Right Hon. Joseph Cham- berlain, M.P., with Miss Endacott, an American lady whose acquaintance he made during his recent visit to the United States. Miss Endacott, the lady tO whom Mr. Chamberlain is shortly 'to be married, is the daugh- ter of the United States Minister for War. Mr. cham- berlain made her acquaintance in Washington during his recent stay there. Mr. Endacott will succeed Mr. Phelps as United States minister in London, and is ex- pected to arrive here in a few weeks. This will be Mr. Chamberlain's third wife.

NO. 15.-I\lOOllE AND ACTON GRANGE,

In the preceding articles of this series, we have traced the course of the Ship Canal from Lower Walton to Lymm, and have anticipated and ex- plained the numerous changes which the making of the canal will bring about in this section of its route from Eastham to Manchester. We now propose to re- turn to the neighbourhood of Lower Walton, and thence to follow tke line of canal westwards through Moore, Norton, and Runcorn, and onwards, forecasting as we go the various alterations that are to be made in the districts through which we pass.

AMONG THE NAVVIES. A contemporary says :—The other day we were in Peel-green-lane, Barton, during the dinner hour from 12 to 1 o'clock. Not many short of a hundred navvies made their way to the Old Rock House, the only public-house in the locality, to eat their mid- day meal. What a run of luck the landlord of this quiet public is in for. His fortune is assured. Three or four rooms were packed by men who stick to the long-fostered belief that there is much virtue , and strength in malt liquor. It is certain that the landlord, judging from what the writer experienced, would rather sell his ale than "victual a traveller, at any rate at a time when the thirst of the navvy has to be appeased. But large numbers of the navvies have a liking for warm coffee or tea, and this is supplied by private enterprise, one man at stated periods each day bringing a pony and cart on the scene, selling either beverage at the rate of a half- penny a gill, and he has some competitors. One of the tea and coffee sellers, by way of a bait, lately put spirits in his urns, but it did not pay, and it has been dropped. That all navvies do not swear by beer is testified to by Mr. Barrett. "Many of them," he says, "tell me they can work much better on oatmeal water than beer. Oatmeal was extensively used on the Kettering and Menton line, and I never heard a man regret it yet." We heard in a short sojourn amongst the spectators at Salt Eye of navvies who had been abstainers for years. Here is a story which illustrates that, as the rev. gentleman says, "In old days, and not very remote either, the drinking customs were abominable. A ganger, when the London and North-Western line was being made from London to Birmingham, actu- ally proposed to raffle the dead body of a mate. Nearly 300 men joined the scheme at sixpence a head, the raffle going towards a drinking bout. The raffle took place, so did the revel, but the funeral, after a fortnight's delay, was performed by the parish. I thahk God, from my very heart, those days are happily past." In the weeks which have elapsed we learn that the police haven't had one single complaint from the public. While the navvies are not teetotallers, and, as a rule, do not like "blow- ing the froth off less than a pint" of ale, not one of those employed under Mr. Walker hereabouts has yet been reported for drunkenness, and the police ver- dict is,that they are infinitely superior in steadiness, intelligence, and good manners to the cornermen of Eccles and Patricroft. Hitherto very little of the surpluslabour at home has been afforded employment on the works To be quite candid, the physique of the average. Lancashire man. compares very Un- favourably with the stalwartness of Mr. Walker's navvies. Then the majority of these men are prac- tically permanent employes. That is to say, they move from place to place with the celebrated con- tractor. They know their work, and being experi- enced hands ire assured of employment. Many of the Ship Canal navvies were, for instance, engaged on the great Severn tunnel works at Bristol.

The townships immediately westward of Lower Walton are those of Acton Grange and Moore, and, as most people know, the work of excavation is al- ready being very actively carried on in both of these townships. According to the quaint, but vigorous and expressive language of an old writer, the name Moore or More signifies "a more barren ground than marshes be; a miry and moorish soil, yet serveth not to get turf thereon " ; and what gives some support to the theory that Moore de- rives its name from the original infertility of its soil, is that even so late as 1816 an Act of Parliament was obtained for enclosing a common called Halton or Moore moss within the township. Aud so with regard to Acton Grange, it is supposed by compe- tent authorities that it was a mere unpopulated and uncultivated waste at a time when some other places in the locality had a recorded existence. But, whatever may have been the former state of things, at the. time the Ship Canal project was taking a practical shape the land stretching away between the village of Moore and the Mersey, and on both sides of the Runcorn and Latchford canal, which here runs parallel with the Mersey, was care- fully cultivated, and well tijnbered. INTERSECTION OF ROADS. This land between Moore and the river's traversed by three bye-roads, all of which branch off from the road leading from Warrington to Runcorn. One of theseroads—the first from Warrington—leads down past Bellhouse farm buildings to the Runcorn canal, over which it is carried on a turn-bridge; the next, which branches off just before we enter Moore vil- lage, takes us down to what is known as Moore turn-bridge, over the Runcorn canal; while the third, running from about the centre of the village, by a circuitous course takes a pedestrian to Bob's turn- bridge. All of these roads are cut through by the canal, but they will be differently provided for. With regard to the first-named, there seems to be no provision for its continuance, and it will conse- quently come to an end on the south bank of the canal. The road leading to Moore turn-bridge is we gather from the sections of the Ship Canal Act relating to the Daresbury Highway Board—to be carried across the canal by means of an opening or swing bridge, and the present turn-bridge over the Runcorn and Latchford canal is either to be pre- served or, it this canal should be filled up, there is to be as a substitute a new road, not less than twenty feet in width, which is to be for ever after- wards maintained by the Canal Company to the reasonable satisfaction of the Highway Board. Respecting the third road—that leading to Bob's turn-bridge—the Canal Company are to "provide in the position of the present turn-bridge, and in ac- cordance with plans previously submitted to the Highway Board, and for ever maintain in good order and condition, a ferry across the canal suitable for the conveyance of vehicles, horses, and cattle." The Canal Company are also under the necessity of at all times hereafter providing the necessary labour to work, free of all charge, this ferry, either by night or by day whenever requisite for the use of the public. The working of the ferry, however, is to be subject to the company's bye-laws. The company, on acquiring the Runcorn and Latchford canal, were to undertake all the obligations of the Bridgewater Company with respect to Bob's turnbridge, and in th e event of this latter canal being filled up, they will, in lieu of the turn-bridge, have to provide and main- tain a roadway over the site of the canal. It should, in addition, be mentioned that the approaches to the ferry on both sides of the Ship Canal are to be "pro- per and convenient," with gradients not steeper than one in thirty.

div.head: SALFORD AND THE DOCKS.
div.p: SALFORD AND THE DOCKS.

The ordinary meeting of the "ie;;;:liWtOa District Highway, &c., Committee of theSalford Corporation was held in the Town Hall, Pendleton, on Monday night, Mr. Alderman J. B. M`Kerrow in the chair. Mr. Alderman Bailey moved: "That as soon as con- venient the exact route of the Manchester Ship Canal in the Pendleton district be placed on the 25in. map of the district." A new street was being talked of. They would find that ultimately some portion of Pendleton would get into Stretford, while portions of Stretford would come into Pendleton.—The Chairman: Would it not be better to wait until the question of the docks is finally settled ?—Mr. Alderman Bailey said the Pendle- ton people should have some control over the Ship Canal in regard to the access to the wharfage, which would be very valuable.—Mr. Alderman Bowes said it was pro- posed to have locks at Mode Wheel,and to leave the canal 3ft. high.—Mr. H. Roper seconded the resolution, which was carried.—Mr. Alderman Keevney said he should like to know whether, supposing a ship loading in America, and having one-half the cargo for Salford, and the other for Manchester, could come through with one bill of lad- mg.—Mr. Alderman Bailey: Yes, the harbour master will have complete control over the docks, and will send a boat to the place most convenient for it. The docks will be called the Manchester and Salford docks, and vessels of 2,000 tons will not be able to get into the Man- chester docks. All the very large vessels will go to Sal- ford.—Mr. Alderman Bowes: We should swallow up all the big ships.—Mr. Alderman Bailey : Whether goods are consigned to Manchester or Salford the harbour mas- ter will have absolute control as to where that vessel is to go. Of course, a potato merchant of Guernsey or Jersey could havo a private dock. Only small boats will be able to get into the Manchester docks, and I want the Salford people to be thoroughly well satisfied that the most magnificent docks are being placed in Salford. It is quite a mistake to think that Manchester is getting a pull out of it. It is all one port for practical purposes. —Mr. S. Johnson: Will Manchester get all the dock dues? —Mr. Alderman Bailey: The dock dues belong to the company; nothing will go to the city of Manchester ex- cept the general rates.

div.head: FIND.
div.p: A FIND.

In the excavation of the Ship Canal, opposite Sir Humphrey de Trafford's Park, near Barton-upon-Irwell, some pieces of tombstones were found laid face down- wards as a support for a cartway over a ditch. It would appear as if the pieces of tombstones had been removed from Eccles churchyard at some time or other. The in- scriptions, so far as they could be deciphered, are as fol- lows :—" Here lyeth interred the body of John Smith, Bachelor in Arts, schoolmaster, register, and parish clarke of Eccls, deceased the 16th day of November, ano dom 1656; here lyeth intered the body of Thomas Smith, schoolmaster and parish clarke of Eccles, deceas—." In the latter case the stone is broken off at this point, and the date is lost. EASTFIAM AND ELLESMERE PORT.

The number of men working on the Eastham section has recently been increased by 100, and another steam navvy and locomotive have been got to work, making a total of eight steam navvies and fourteen locomotives. There has been a striking alteration in that part of East- ham bordering on the river since the first sod was cut five months ago. What was then a green field is now a contractor's yard, which is crossed by no fewer than six lines of rails. The total length of rails on this section is upwards of fourteen miles. A connection has been made with the railway at Ellesmere Fort Station, so that trticks can be brought from the railway right on the works. A line of rails has also been laid connecting the works with the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Co.'s docks at Ellesmere Port. Dr. Bredin, of Little Sutton, has been appointed doctor for this section. At Ellesmere Port the building of storerooms, offices, smiths' shops, and stables is being pushed on with all speed, and within a week they will be ready for use.

div.head: INCE:
div.p: INCE:

On this section there are two steam navvies, six loco- motives, and 650 men at work, but four more navvies are being erected. The canal will cut through the marshes between Ellesmere Port and Ince, and Stanlow Point will also be cut through close to its joining with the mainland. The material used in the canal has all to be brought by the river to Inceyier.___.

div.head: "STORAGE OF EXI'LOSIVES.
div.p: THE "STORAGE OF EXI'LOSIVES.

At the Baresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Mr. 11. E. Taylor, of Chester, applied, on behalf of Mr. Walker, the Ship Canal contractor, for the anction of the Bench to the erection of a store for mixed explosives near the canal works. According to the section of the Explosives Act under which the application was made, Mr. Walker would have power upon the sanction of the Bench being given, to store either 2,000 lbs. of gunpowder or 1,000 lbs. of other explosives. It was mentioned that the in- tended site of the store was the distance required by the act from all protected places, 'such as railways, canals, &c. Sanction was granted on condition that the store was properly erected. PROVISION FOR ACCIDENTS. It is stated that the contractor, in order to make ample provision for any accidents that may occur, has decided to erect cottage hospitals at various points on the route. They will be in charge of resident house sur- geons, and competent nurses are to be engaged.
A barque, the Margaret, of Hayle, was run down off the Goodwin Sands on Tuesday night. The crew were saved, and landed at Dover. . _

Captain William Richard, underground manager of the Mount Morgan Gold Mines, Merionethshire, was, on Wednesday, at Penrhyndeudraeth, committed for trial on a charge of stealing a large quantity of gold quartz. LIBERAL MEETING AT ROCEIDAI.E.—A great meeting of Liberals was held at the Rochdale Town Hall on Wed- nesday evening, and addressed by Mr. T. B. Potter, the member for the Borough. Mr. T. D. Mr. Potter, in addressing the meeting, expressed confidence in the principle of Home Rule, and his intention to hold the seat even against so influential an opponent as the son of Mr. Bright.
