div.head: WHARF.
div.p: A WHARF.

Near to the ferry which is a substitute for the road leading to Bob's turnbridge, there will be a wharf for the convenience of Sir Richard Brooke and his tenants. This wharf, which will have suit- able and convenient approaches, willte used free of all dues and charges for the purpose of landing ma- terial for the cultivation of the Norton Priory estate, but at the same time its use will be regulated by any reasonable bye-laws that may be made by the Canal Company, and approved by the Board of Trade. .

div.head: agnAT VIADUCT.
div.p: agnAT VIADUCT.

When the Ship Canal and itsincidental works have been completed by far the most noticeable thing to a person, who, we will suppose, has passed down the road past Bellhouse Farm, and stands on the south bank of the canal, will be the great rail- way viaduct crossing the canal to the eastward'. This will be the great bridge, 200 yards in length , and 78 or 79 feet above the level of the canalwaters, which carries the main line of the London and North-Western Railway and the Birkenhead, Lan- cashire, and Cheshire Junction Railway over the canal. These two lines at present, after passing the Mersey and the Runcorn and Latchford Canal at Walton Arches, gradually diverge, and one of them runs through Moore and the other through Dares- bury Stations. In the future the main line will cross the Mersey on an entirely new bridge to the west of Walton Arches, and thence rise to the height of the yiaduct over the canal. On the other hand the Birkenhead, Lancashire, and Cheshire Junction Railway will then, as now, run over Wal- ton Arches, but on the south side of the arches it will deviate to the west from its present course, and by a somewhat steep gradient rise to the height of the Ship Canal viaduct, over which it will pass. Once over the viaduct both railways will again diverge and, by a gradual descent will regain the present lines of metals at a short distance on the near side of Daresbury and Moore Stations, neither of which stations, it would seem, are to Co inter- fered with.

div.head: ROADS TO BE ALTERED.
div.p: ROADS TO BE ALTERED.

In its descent from -the—ca-n-al--;ii-JdUct to Moore Station the London and North-Western main line will, as at present, Ncross the course of three roadways, namely, the one leading past Bellhouse Farm, the road to Moore turn- bridge, and the road to Bob's turnbridge, while the Birkenhead, Lancashire, and Cheshire Junction Railway will come in contact with the two first-named of these roads. At present in each instance the roadways are carried over the railway on bridges, but as in future the levels of the rail- ways will in some places be considerably altered it is evident that changes of some sort will have to be made. We find, consequently, that as regards the road leading past Bellhouse Farm, though, its own /evel remains unaltered it will, instead of passing aver the two railways run under them, the railway embankments at these points being pierced for bridges with an arch of 25 feet span and a height of 15 feet. The next road—that leading to Moore turn- bridge—will in the future, as at present, be carried over the railways, but in order that this may be done the levels in each case will have to be raised 25 feet one inch. The road to Bob's turnbridge is not affected by the Birkenhead Railway, but is crossed by the London and North-Western main line. As, however, this latter line will, before reaching this roadway. have regained its present line and level, there will be no necessity to alter the road in any way. PROTECTION OF SIR RICHARD BROOKE.

It has already been shown that in many cases the landowners whose land is to be cut through and divided or otherwise molested by the Canal Com- pany, have sought Parliamentary protection of their rights and claims. Moore and Acton Grange offer no exception to this general rule, for we find that Sir Richard Brooke, a large landowner in the locality, is hedged round with rather elaborate pro- visions. We find, for instance, that "if any part or parts of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal which is, or are, bounded on both sides by land of Sir Richard Brooke, shall be acquired by the Canal Company, and shall not be used for the purposes of naviga- tion or for docks, and shall not be required by the Company for the purposes of the canal or, its inci- dental works, &c., the company shall, if required by Sir Richard Brooke, sell and convey the same to him at a price to be settled in case of dispute by arbitra- tion in the manner provided by the Lands Clauses Acts; provided, however, that the Company, before so selling the same or any pat thereot, shall, if re- quired by Sir Richard Brooke, and may, if they so desire, fill up the bed of the same and the adjoining tow-path level with the adjoining lands and fit for ,
LORD It. CHURCHILL AND TORY

PLEDGES. A WARNING TO THE MINISTRY. In his" warning" to the Ministry, in the House of Commons. on Wednesday, on the subject of their pledges on Irish local government, Lord Randolph Churchill said :—Now, it has been supposed, and I never thought right till now to notice the supposi- tion, though it has been unduly alluded to in the newspapers, that in tho declaration which I made to the House in August, 1886, I spoke much more my own opinion than that of the Government. I think it right to say that was not so—(Opposition cheers)—in any degree whatever. The declaration which I made at that table was, as far as it related to Ireland, a written declaration. Every sentence of it represented the opinion of the Government, and had been submitted to and assented to by the Prime Minister and the Chief Secretary for Ireland (prolonged cheers.) More than that, the declaration I made with regard to Ireland was made without one dissentient voice or murmur raised among the hon. members belonging to the Tory party (hear, hear.) More than that, I was given to understand that the declaration thus made had received the full and entire approval of not only the leaders but the bulk of the Liberal Unionist party (cheers.) My recollection of these matters, which will raise' some differences of opinion before long, is that the idea of local government in Ireland—a just exten- sion within reasonable limits—was to be looked upon as a remedy (loud cheers) for all those great evils which have been alluded to by the Chief Secretary. I venture to say, if the House will carry back its mind to theterrible struggle we were engagedin in 1886, in which, I think, without undue arrogance, I may claim to have borne no inconsiderable a part—(hear, hear)—there is not a member of the Liberal Unionist party who then stood on platforms assumed to be Unionist who did not adopt that view. (Loud cheers.) I feel certain there are none. (" Yes," and "No.") Well, there are very few. (Hear, hear.) It fell to my lot to watch very closely the course of that election and the attitude taken up by the members of the Tory party at that time, and I recollect that the pledges then given by the Unionist party were large, liberal, distinct, and full, and that there was no reservation in the pledges given by them to give self-government to Ireland. Nothing of the kind. (Cheers.) We pledged ourselves at the very earlest op- portunity—(renewed cheers)—to extend to Ireland the same amount of local liberty we were willing to give to England. I do not care how much I may be contradicted.' That was the foundation of the Unionist party. I ven- ture to say more. It is the only platform on which you can refuse repeal. (Cheers.) If you are going to the English electorate, relying upon your special executive power, and contending that the Irish must be looked upon as an inferior race, and are in every respect unfit for local self-government such as the English people themselves enjoy, then you may maintain that position for a time, but that time will probably be a short one. (Opposition cheers.) Ido not know whether I am jus- tified in asserting that the Chief Secretary, in represent- ing the policy of the Government, wishes the House and the public to understand that the question of self- government for Ireland is only to be delayed until, in the opinion of the Government, the state of the country may be so orderly as to justify it—(Ministerial cheers)— yes, that may be your position now, but it was not your position then—(Opposition cheers)—or whether are we to understand that, in the event of Parliament settling the great principle of self-government for England, then you will be pleased, as far as circum- stances will allow, •to extend similar liberties to Ireland. That is the point. (Hear, hear.) For the words which I used at that table, as the pledges of the Government, hon. gentlemen on this side must not blame me. They must blame the Govern- ment. I used the words with deliberation. I used the words "similarity, equality, and simultaneity' so far as regard to the circumstances of the two countries would admit. (Cheers.) The time has one by when I would consent altogether to bear the sole responsibility for these words. They represented the policy of the Government, and I considered there would be a bona fide carrying out of that policy—(cheers)—and no waiting until law and order were restored in Ireland. We who pride ourselves on being progressive must take care that we do not expose ourselves to the well-sustained charge of reaction. Whenever I go to address popular audiences, I never lose an opportunity of tell- ing the people to the best of my ability that it is within the power of the Tory party and of the Unionist party to legislate equally for Englishmen and Irishmen. I place a specific interpretation upon those words. (Cheers.) At any rate I decline to be quiet un- der what I believe to be not only a departure from the original policy of the Government, but also a ruinous' line of policy. (Opposition cheers.) If you give to the Irish the same liberties as you give to the English, I be- lieve you will do much to mitigate the ill-feeling which has arisen in recent years, and you will also do much to detach from the ranks of the right hon. gentleman the member for Midlothian many who are now following him in despair—(" Oh, oh," and \ cheers)—and not only so, but in despair, it may be said, of get- ting from the Government on the other side of the House the legislation they require. (Opposition cheers.) It is all very well to refuse to legislate now that you are strong, and a general election appears to be far off, but you will have to argue this question again before the English people at the next election. (Cheers and counter cheers.) Then you will have to point to the fact that the promises you made with regard to local government for Ireland have not been redeemed. (Mini- sterial cries of "No, no," and Opposition cheers.) No- body can tell when that election may come. ('Oh. oh," and cheers.) At the last election you defeated the policy of repeal introduced by the right hon. gentleman oppo- site. I thank heaven you did defeat that policy of re- peal. (Cheers and laughter.) But you defeated it only because the nation believed the promises you made that you were prepared to enter upon a policy of making Ire- land contented with granting to her people every privi- lege and every liberty which we claim for our own peo- ple in England. (Loud Opposition cheers.)

The Scotch Crofter 6trimissioners, in a batch of cases from the Black Isle and the neighbourhood of Dingwall, have made an average reduction of 57 per cent on the rentals and 83 per cent. on the arrears. . . . . _

An interesting discussion took place in the Lower House of Canterbury Convocation on Thursday on the position of the clergy underthe Local Government Bill, and it was decided to request the Upper House to take steps to prevdnt clergymen being excluded from the county councils. _ _

ALLEGED MIIRDER.—Mary Ellen Coleman, 26, was charged at Stockport Borough Police Court, on Wednes- day, with the murder of her husband, John Coleman, lodging-house keeper in Hillgate. A formal remand was granted. At the inquest, held subsequently, a verdict of manslaughter was returned. _

TITHE Wen IN WALES.—An extraordinary scene ot- curred near Ruthin on Thursday evening. As Mr. Ste- vens was collecting tithes for the Ecclesiastical Commis- sioners, he was proceeding with his armed force towards a farmhouse, when the road was found blocked by a great quantity of combustibles. As the force approached the stuff was fired, and an effigy of the vicarilung upon the names. The force was only able to proceed when the fire burnt itself out, Great excitement prevailed.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The annual meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Greening, J. Houghton, Kilshall, Blackhurst, Jolley, Owen, Moores, Darbyshire, Isherwood, Harrison. Penning- ton, Humphries, Clarke, Eckersley, Wright, Eat- cliffe, W. Houghton, Swinton ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and C. H. Ward (work- house master). •

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMEN..
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMEN..

The CLERK having taken the chair, read a letter from Mr. Balharry, in which that gentleman explained that he was unable to attend the meeting that morning, other- wise he should have been very glad to propose the re- appointment of the Rev. G. F. Roberts as chairman. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. RATCLIFFE then proposed that the Rev. G. F. Roberts be reeelected chairman of the Board fol. the coming year.—This proposal was seconded by Mr. GREENING, and supported by Messrs. Blackhurst, Harrison, Jolley, and W. Houghton, and agreed to.—Mr. RATCLIFFE proposed, Mr. JOLLEY seconded, and Mr. WRIGHT supported a proposal that Mr. Balharry be re- elected senior vice-chairman, and this was also agreed to unanimously.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE proposed that Mr. Jolley be the junior vice-chairman of the Board, and remarked that though they might not always agree, it was quite evident that Mr. Jolley acted conscientiously in all he did on the Board. (Hear, hear. ,—Mr. IILACKHURST seconded, and Messrs. Greening. Harrison, and Ratcliffe supported the proposal, the last-named gentleman saying that he did so "on the ground that Mr. Jolley took such an in- terest in Newton business."—The proposal was amed to unanimously, and Mr. Jolley suitably responded.

.. - REPRESENTATIVES OF THE BOARD AT THS NORTH- WESTERN Poon-Law CONFERENCE.' The Chairman, senior and junior vice-chairmen, and the clerk:
APPOINTMENT OF VALUER.

Mr. W. Owen, architect, Warrington, was re-appointed to assist the AssPssment Committee in the valuation of the several rateable hereditaments in the Union for a peribd of one year at a salary of £2OO each year, and such remuneration to cover all office, travelling, and other expenses out of pocket. 11017 SE COMMITTEE. The House Committee reported that the two children who were in the Workhouse suffering from scarlatina were improving. The Master had also reported to the committee that a lunatic named Kelly had suddenly overpowered the man in attendance, and thrown himself through the window and injured himself. (Particulars as to this affair were given in "The Examiner" a few weeks ago).-2--In answer to a question, Mr. IsnEnwoon said the man had injured hiehead and shoulder.—The minutes were passed.
PADGATE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.

_ The minutes of this committee stated that the doctor had reported the general health of the children to be very good. It was also mentioned that Miss Kate McEvoy thad resigned her post as schoolmistress.—The minutes were confirmed.

SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE. The School Fees Committee reported that they had al- lowed fees in 96 cases, 74 of which were old and 22 new eases.—On the motion of Mr. BLACKHURST, the /minutes were confirmed.

div.head: DOCTOR AND THE PATIENT.
div.p: THE DOCTOR AND THE PATIENT.

'Mr Isuenwoon called attention to the case of a man named Kimberley, living at 17, Dial-st., who had been under the care of Dr.Peacocke, oneof the district medical officers of the Board. The case had come before him .when dealing with the chronic relief cases on the previous Board day, and the man's wife told him that the doctor had not seen her husband between the 24th March and the Bth April, although she had been to the doctor's house three times on the previous Tuesday.—Dr. PEACPCRE said he was called in to this case in February, and he visited the man, who was suffering from erysipelas, four or five times in a week, but as the man got better the visits were less frequent. When the man was poorly he attended him regularly. The man's wife saw him (DT. Peacocke) on Easter Monday, and wanted him to I renew the order for milk, but as he thought the man was .then sufficiently recovered he declined to do so. He again saw Kimberley on the last Board meeting day, and told him he was fit for work.—ln answer to a ques- tion Dr. PEACOCIEE said the hmoanhadwabcu was all craiflleidt last t Bo oathrde • room, made ata rsKismßEteßnifeYn' w t corroborative of what Mr. Isher- wood had said, excepting that she had sent for the doctor three times between the 24th March and the 6th April, land not 'on one day.—After some conversation the CHAIRMAN pointed out that entries should be made in his ,1 book by Dr. Peacocke as to the condition of his patients, II so as to be a guide to the Guardians, who hadthe admin- istering of relief. In this case he thought the offence had been more aglinst the poor-law regulations than against the patients. Dr. Peacocke's error was in not having reported as to the case for so long a period.—Mr. DARBYSRIRE could not see that there had been any error committed by the doctor.—Mr. JoLLEv It is an error of omission only.—The CHAIRMAN said that if a poor person came for the doctor to see a patient it was advisable for him to go and satisfy himself as to how the ease was go- ing on. If he did not he would find people constantly troubling him with representations of that sort.—Mr. HARRISON said he had no doubt, after the explanations that had been given, that a similar case would not occur again.—The matter then dropped. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

' FRODSHAM. HP.SBY CHURCH READING-1100M.—On Saturday even- ing a church reading-room, promoted by the Rev. W. T. Vale, vicar, was opened by Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., of Fox Hill, patron of the living. There was a large gathering of friends and contributors. The Vicar oc- cupied the chair. Excellent speeches were delivered by the Rev. E. Rawson, vicar of Ince, and Messrs. Slater Lewis and Pickles. Mr. Reynolds, in opening the room, referred to the flourishing state of Helsby, and the great improvements that had taken place in church matters, while he gave all credit to the Dissenters for their good work in days gone by before the church was erected. He spoke of the utility of the room for library, classes, and evening reading, and entertainments. An excellent musical programme was gone through, and greatly ap- preciated, Mrs. Rarff, Mrs. Callender, and the Misses Thornley, Messrs. Wood, Harris, and Smith taking part. Mr. Warren gave two recitations in splendid style. A vote of thanks to those who kindly assisted in contribu- ting to such a pleasant evening was proposed by Mr. James Taylor, and seconded by Mr. Romaine Callender.

div.head: ATTEMIIED MURDER BY A JEALOUS SOLDIER
div.p: ATTEMIIED MURDER BY A JEALOUS SOLDIER
AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police—olniii-0/1. Monday, before Mr. John Brock, Daniel Gilmour, a respectable looking middle-aged man, of 24 Barn-st., was brought up on remand charged with having on the 25th March caused grievous bodily harm to a man named Joseph Donovan, "with intent to kill and murder him." Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the prisoner. The prosecutor said he was a labourer and lodged at the house of Patrick Ryan in Barn-st. He did not to his knowledge see the prisoner on the day or night of the 24th ult. He was drinking in Ryan's house until about eleven o'clock, when he lay down upon the sofa, in the kitchen, and fell asleep. He never saw any bottle throve. He was awakened by some person pulling hin: ()Tr the sofa. The room was in utter darkness and he could not tell who the person was. He was kicked in the side and he was struck on the head with what he believed to be a chair. He was not sure whether he was struck more than once as he was, he believed knocked insensible by the first blow. When he" came to" he was in Widnes Accident Hospital, and he neither felt quite well nor very weak, but he had a cut on his head which was bandaged He suffered some pain during ' the nine days he was in the Accident Hospital. Afterwards he stayed in the model Lodging House, where he had formerly lived and was then taken to the Hospital at Whiston Workhouse. Here he was kept in bed for about a week. He did not know the prisoner; he had never spoken to him in his life, nor prisoner to him; though he might have seen him.—John Butler, labourer, 53, Dock-st., stated that about half past twelve on the morning of the 25th inst., he saw the prisoner come from his house and enter that of Ryan. Donovan was lying on the sofa in the kitchen. The prisoner pulled him off the sofa, and struck him on the head with his fist. He then struck him on the head with a chair, smashing the chair to pieces. Donovan cried "0 don't kill me." After he had broken the chair, the prisoner knocked Donovan from one side of the house to the other. There was a light in the kitchen and he could see all that was being done.—Corroborative evidence was given by Wm. Homy Rosevere, labourer, 20, Dick- sbn-st., James Fowler. labourer, 34, Barn-st. and James Mistler, (aged 14) of 3, High-st. These witnesses were in company of Butler.—Mary Ryan, wife of Patrick Ryan, 22; Barn-St., stated that about half-past eight on the night in question, the prisoner came to her house to in- quire for his wife. He told her hewould "put Joe. Dono- van out," and also said "he would have no bullies from the Model Lodging House there." She told him to have more sense than to create a bother, and he then left her. Donovan had been drinking in the house, and when she went to him he was lying on the sofa. She did not hear any disturbance.—Michael Conway, labourer,' 53, Moss Bank-road, said he was drinking with Donovan on the 24th ult., and he could scarcely remember what took place. About 8 o'clock, the prisoner, who was drunk and noisy, entered the house, and threatened to "clout" Donovan ; later the prisoner again entered_ the house and he (witness) believed threw a bottle at Donovan, but the missle did not strike him. Witness went home shortly afterwards. Donovan was not drunk.—John Fowler, labourer, 34, Barn-st., gave corroborative evidence.—Patrick Ryan, in whose house the attack was made' said when he went home about half past one on the Sunday morning, hefound Donovan there, bleeding profusely from wounds on the head, and he awoke his wife.—Dr. Hutchinson deposed that he was called into the house at the time and found Donovan sit- ting in a recumbent position on a stool near the fire. He was in a state of send consciousness, and had two large wounds on his head, both of which exposed the skull. The wounds appeared to have been caused by a blunt instrument. There were also some bruises upon the top of the head, and there was an effusion of blood under the scalp. A chair would cause such wounds. Donovan was very weak from loss of blood. He ordered his immediate ramoval to the Accident Hospital; where he next morning examined him. Donovan complained of pains in the head and chest. For four days the man's life was in danger, and he (the Doctor) did not think we would recover. The longest wound had not yet healed and Donovan would not be able to work for at least a month. When he visited Ryan's house the kitchen was in a state of great disorder. He noticed a broken chair and a broken bottle, and there were two indentations in ,the wall. There were splashes of wet blood on the paper and on an almanack.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Knowles, the Doctor said Donovan was a man of weak constitution.— P.C. Worsfold also described the state of the house, and said there were pools of blood upon the floor. Donovan was sitting upon a box in a state Of semi-consciousness. He washed his head and bandaged his wounds and then i sent fQr Dr. Hutchinson afterwards, the officer went to the prisoners house and as he could not gain admittance, he smashed open the door. He found the prisoner in bed. The prisoner asked him if he was "wanted for the job next door," and the constable answered "Yes." His wife said "You were not in the house were you, Dan ?" The prisoner answered "Yes, I was, you—and would have killed him if I could." Afterwards when formally charged the prisoner said "I don't know anything about it. Is he very bad ?" The prisoner was just recovering ' from the effects of drink when he was apprehended. P.S. Robinson deposed that the prisoner said "You see what she has brought me to. Its all through that model man." The prisoner was very quiet when sober but very violent when in drink.—Mr. Knowles argued that the charge should I? to one of ordinary wounding, be- cause there was no evidence of premeditation.—His wor- ship committed the prisoner to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes, _ _

.- FARNWORTII GRAMMAR SCHOOL. Under the auspices of this institution a public meeting was held in the Baths Assembly Room on Tuesday night. There was only a moderate attend- ance. The principal business of the evening was to present prizes to the scholars who had been suc- cessful at the College of Preceptors Examinations. In the absence of Mr. F. H. Gossage, JP., through indisposition, Mr. J. L. Muspratt occupied the chair, and on the platform were the Rev. J. Wright Williams and Mrs. Williams, Mr. J. Brock, J.P., and Mrs. Brock, Messrs. E. Carey, C. E. Barlow, R. Lewis, and W. A.'Watts, M.A. (the head master). Mr. Lewis read a letter from Mr. Gossage, who de- clared his " firm belief in the success of the school." Mr. Lewis then made a statement, in which he said if the schools were not a success it would not be the fault of the present Board of Governors. Mr. Watts having described the method of examina- tion and the principle tivn Which the prizes were given, the Chairman made a brief speech, Mrs. Brock afterwards distributed ite "prizes to the gficeessful students, addressing a few Words of encourage- ment to each recipient., The prizewinners were as follows R. Bate, Ist asst., honours—special certi- ficate in arithmetic and themistry ; F. N. Mercer, Ist class, honours—special certificate in chemistry and French ' • C. A. Bate, Ist class, pass division—special certificate in arithmetic; James Smith, Ist class, pass division—special certificate in chemistry; J. A. Eatock, 2nd class, Ist division; J. W. Clibborn, 2nd class, 2nd division; S. H. Tinsley, 2nd class, 2nd division; E. T. Franklin, 3rd class, Ist division; J. T. Griffiths, 3rd class, Ist division ; R. Showan, 3rd class, Ist division; A. E. Wareing, 3rd class, Ist division; W. A. Watts, 3rd class, let division, a special certificate in chemistry and physics; A. E. Barlow, 3rd class, 2nd divi- sion; E. Wigg, 3rd class, 3rd division.—Science and Art Department: Theoretical chemistry—W. A. Watts, 2nd class advanced' practical chemistry—J. R. Bate, 2nd class advanced' theoretical chemistry—J. R. Bate, Ist class elementary; thoretical chemistry—James Smith. Ist class elementary ; theoretical chemistry:—C. A. Bate, 2nd class elementary; theoretical chemistry.—J. A. Eatock, 2nd class elementary: theoretical chemeltry:—E. T. Franklin, 2nd class elementary ; theoretical chemistry —A. T. Kyle, 2nd class elementary ; theoretical chemistry —F. N. Mercer, 2nd class elementary; practical chemis- try— James Smith, Ist class elementary ; practical chemistry—w. A. Watts, Ist class elementary. Mr. Carey, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Brock for her kindaess, delivered an inspiring address to the boys. Mr. Watts seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation. Mr. Brock, in responding, said the Grammar School needed money, but it wanted that money as fees from scholars. They wanted the parents to recognise the great value of the education which the school afforded to the boys of Widnes, and to send their boys to be educa- ted there. At present there were only 23 paying boys in the school, and with this number there was a deficit of £l5O a year. Hitherto the governors had found this money, but this could not go on for ever. There was no doubt room for a high-class school of this sort in the town, and he hoped in the future it would be better ap- preciated than it appeared to have been in the past. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting.

WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH,
WARRINGTON.

• (From "Sunday Words.") Congregationalism in Warrington may be said to have taken its rise in the year 1779, when, conse- quent upon the preaching of Unitarian doctrines at Cairo-st. Chapel, a portion of the congregation with- drew; and, forming themselves into a church, erec- ted Stepney Chapel in King-street. Among the ministers who presided over the first Congregational 'Church in Warrington may be mentioned the late Rev. Alfred J. Morris, afterwards of Holloway, and Bowdon, Cheshire, the Rev.• William Owen, and the Rev. J. Brierley. For a long time things went on very satisfac- torily, but by-and-by differences arose, and ulti- mately a number of the members separated them- selves from the Church at Stepney, and in the year 1811 undertook the task of building Salem Chapel, Golbome-st. Here several pastors, with varying success, held office. Among these the late Rev. Edwin J. Hartland, afterwards of Bristol, and lat- terly of the Memorial Hall, London, is remembered by many with respectful affection. After a lapse of some years, the Congregationalists ceased to use this building, and it has now passed into the hands of the Baptists. The church which now worships in the Wycliffe Congregational Church, and with which we are at present more immediately concerned, originated in 1847, under the auspices of the Lancashire County Union, when worship was commenced in an assem- bly-room in the town, and carried on under the fre- quent ministrations of the late Drs. Vaughan. Halley, Raffles, and Rev. John Kelly. Under these auspices the cause prospered, the church increased in num- bers, and presently grew sufficiently strong to jus- tify the erection of a building suitable for public worship, and the first Wycliffe Chapel, in Bewsey- st., became an accomplished fact. This chapel was opened in 1851. with the Rev. P. A. Hampson as pastor. This gentleman was succeeded in turn by the Revs. John Kay, C. E. Palmer, R. Jessop, and George Sale Reaney, who has recently left the Stepney Meeting House, London, for an important charge at Manchester. The church stands well in a leading thorough- fare. Its services are bright and attractive, and, as might be expected. are well attended, particu- larly on Sunday evenings. Under Mr. Reaney's pas-, torate. which lasted eight years- beginning in 1868, and continuing until May, 1876—progress and de- velopment took place. So large did the congrega- tions become, that successive enlargements of the chapel and school buildings became necessary, and at length, in 1871, it became evident that no fur- ther additions could be profitably made, and it was, after due consideration, thought desirable to demol- ish the chapel, built only twenty-one years before, and erect a much larger one, with the necessary ac- commodation called for by the altered state of things, on the same site. This was done, and the present structure, which will seat about eleven hundred people, was commenced, being completed and opened in 1873. The project of erecting this new Wycliffe Church was received with favour on ' all hands, and the scheme was largely helped by generous gifts from the Laseashire and Cheshire Chapel Building Society, as well as by munificent contributions from members of the Church. With the erection of this building the names of Samuel Rigby, Esq., J.P. (now of Chester), R. W. Murray, Esq., J.P., (now of Belfast), J. G. McMinnies, Esq., J.P. (lately M.P. for Warrington), Z. Armitage, Esq. J.P, (still a (leacon of the church), will always stand honourably connected, The building is now entirely free from debt. In 1876 the Rev. G. S. Reaney accepted a call to Trinity Chapel, Reading, and after a brief interval, the Rev. John Yonge, then of Heywood, near Man- chester, who still retains the pastorate, was appoin- ted his successor. Under his ministry, the church, I notwithstanding many serious losses of some of its best supporters and workers, has continued to hold its own, and even in some respects to make encoura- ging progress. In the ten years, from 1877 to 1887 inclusive, three hundred and fifteen members have been received into church membership. The num- ber on the roll in 1877 was one hundred and seventy one; it is now two hundred and eighty. The church has raised for all purposes during this period, a sum of between fourteen and fifteen thou- sand pounds. That the religidlls training of the young occu- pies, as it alatays should do, a prominent place in the scheme of institutions connected with the church at Warrington, is plainly evidenced by the fact that in the Sunday Schools there are nearly seven hundred scholars, in addition to five hundred others who meet in a Mission School. A considerable sum is annually raised for the London Missionary Society. The other organisations include a Ladies' Dorcas and Working Society, which meets weekly, com- bining the making of garments for distribution to necessitous and deserving cases, with the making of useful and ornamental articles for sale. A Catechu- men Class was inaugurated in 1881 with the object of spiritually benefiting the young people of the congregation as they arrive at an age when they usually enter upon the active duties and responsibi- lities of life. There is also a day school with five hundred scholars in attendance, The Cockhedge Mission, hitherto under the direction of the Rev. W. R. Parry, who has just resigned to accept a call to the church at Peas- ley Cross, has been instrumental in doing good work.

It has been Mr. Yonge's custom for some years past to preach a monthly sermon to young men, which usually obtains large audiences. Popular evangelistic services, with all seats free, are held during the winter on the last Sunday evening of each month. Sankey's hymns are used, members of the choir giving a solo at each service. At the present time there seems to be a decided increase of interest and life in this church. The con- gregations are increasing; the finances, after a period of dulness, are improving. It is,hoped andbelieved that the Manchester Ship Canal will bring much new life to Warrington, in which this church may fairly expect to participate. - -

TILE REV. JOHN YONGE, the pastor of the Congregational Church at War- rington, was born in the year 1838, in the Strand, London, nearly opposite Exeter Hall. His father's family were long connected with "Old New Court," Carey-st., Lincoln's Inn, which of late years has been removed and " resurrected " at Tollington Park, Holloway. He is the nephew of the late Rev. W. C. Yonge, formerly of Brentford. and also of Mr. George Yonge, who for a great number of years was secretary to the British Society for the Propagation of the Gospel among the Jews—in which office he was succeeded by the Rev. James Dunlop. Mr. Yonge was educated for the ministry at Cheshunt College, and settled in 1862 in East Cowes, Isle of Wight, in succession to the late Rev. Joseph Waite, 8.A., who had accepted a call at Cardiff. Mr. Yonge remained there for four years, until 1866, when he resigned his charge, and accepted a call to Heywood. Manchester, where in was pastor for ten years. During his ministry n that town, a new church and school were built at a cost of six thousand pounds, and also a branch school at Cap- tain Fold, all of which he had the happiness of seeing freed from debt. The Rev. John Yonge, as has been said, succeeded the Rev. G. S. Reanev in the pastorate of the church at Warrington, and the choice of the church in selecting him to follow such a popular minister as

Mr. Reaney has been amply justified. In a flourish- ing town like Warrington—an•l, indeed, in most other place in these days—something more than the ability to preach sermons is required of a minister; I he must be the guiding power, the directing hand, to whom all the officials of the church are able to , look for counsel and guidance, as well as for practi- cal help in all their perplexities and difficulties. In this respect Mr. Yonge has proved himself emi- nently fitted for the honourable and onerous position he is called upon to occupy, and lie gentle, kindly disposition has endeared him to all with whom he. has been brought into contact. But with all the demands on his time inseparable from the charge ef an important church like the one over which he presides so capably and so well, Mr. Yonge finds time to perform the duties of at least one other office. He has been for several years the secretary of the Lancashire Congregational Union for the Liverpool district, and this year he is Presi- dent of the Manchester Congregational Board. He was also second in the ballot taken at the recent meeting of the Lancashire Congregational Union, at Blackpool, for the Chair of the Union, for which office he is well qualified,, and to which he will doubtless be elected next year.

The anniversary of Wycliffe Schools will be cele- brated to-morrow (Sunday). The Rev. J. Yonge will preach in the morning and evening, and the musical parts of these services will comprise special hymns, chants, solos, and anthems. In the after- noon there will be a children's service of praise, which will comprise, in addition to hymns, solos, &c., recitations of sacred poetry by Miss Mary Hayes, and Messrs. W. H. Wallington and J. Irish, j unr.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued frant page 6.) . WESTON.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued frant page 6.) . WESTON.

As reported last week the principal work carried on here is in the workshops. The joiners, blacksmiths, &c, are kept busily employed in the work of preparation; and hundreds of piles are lying on the wharf ready for a start in the river. Near a spot known as the "Old Folly" there is to be erected a large building in which will be made the sluice., &c., for the coffer dam that is to be constructed at the estuary of the Weaver. Large beams of timber have been deposited on the ground and a groat quantity of railway metals and sleepers have been unshipped. These are to be used in the construc- tion of a branch line to the shed mentioned, from the railway that runs from Runcorn to the docks. The huts are bemg prepared for the reception of their tenants. RUNCORN.

On this section at Norton, and near the works of Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele, the operations are i progressing n a satisfactory manner, and there is nothing of an extraordinary character to record. There are, however, indications that the important hazardous undertaking of dealing with the river bed will be com- menced in the near future. In the first place a start has been made at "No Man's Land." This spot which, notwithstanding its singular title is known to be the property of the Ship Canal Company is an island just below Runcorn Bridge on the Liverpool side, and like many a more important land mark, will be swept away by the Ship Canal. "No man's land" was not always an island. At one time it was attached to the 'mainland," but owing to its situation thecurrent of the tide was directed from the docks, which were frequently in dadger of being silted up. A cutting was therefore made through the land, and the tide in receding rushes through this gap, known locally as the "gut." and, 1 sweeping along side the dock wall, keeps a capital deep for the traffic. Covered with green herbage, No Man's Land has been a popular play ground for the boys of the neighbourhood, and in summer they could be seen dis- porting themselves in nature's garb, and plunging into the water as though it were their natural element. They will now have to find a fresh locality for their sports. On Wednesday about a score of navvies commenced the labour of removing the island from sight, and their operations were during the day watched with great interest by hundreds of townspeople.. Next day, however, the tide effectually put a stop to the navvies' exertions. The water in the river rose to a ' height of over seventeen feet, and overflowing the banks nearly covered the island, Yesterday, aided by a strong south-westerly brecte, the tide rose to a still &Ater height, and No Man's Land was covered to a depth of several feet in places. An equally high tide is expected to-day, so that the navvies will be unable to re-commence work until next Monday or Tuesday. MOORE.

The erection of six wooden cottages at the end of this section near Walton has now been completed, but the buildings are not yet tenanted. They are of a substan- tial character, well lighted and ventilated, and well able to resist severe weather. A large wooden building, 77 feet long by 35 feet wide, to. be used as offices for the engineers and officials, as well as for the purpose of a mess-room, is to be erected, but the work has not been begun yet. A smithy is in course of erection, and the building of the large engine-house has been completed. Blasting operations have this week been commenced about half-way down the. cutting. The excavator con- tinues to make satisfactory progress, and the prepara- tory work of removing the surface soil, is being quickly pushed forward. THELWALL AND LYMM.

The bridges across the river both at Thelwall and at Statham have now been completed, and an unbroken line of rails has been laid through the Whole of this length. In other respects the work is being carried on with undiminished vigour, and the smoke and noise of steam navvies and locomotives are to be heard and seen on atl 'ands within working hours. Among the wooden buildings which have been or are on the point a being completed near to Morris Brook are a large shed for locomotives, and several offices and places for the Storage of materials None of the navvies' huts are as yet inhabited, but two long rows of these temporary dwellings seem pretty near completion, while the frame- work of a third, and parallel row, is now placed in posi- tion. In compliance with a request of Mr. Walker, the contractor, the Cheshire County police authorities have told off an officer—P.C. Buchanon, lately of Heatley—to act as patrol on the Thelwall section. BARTON.

The Barton section extends from Mode Wheel to a point on the River Irwell, two miles below Barton Bridge, known as Sticking's Cut. The Canal has a straight, undeviating course right through the Trafford estate, and in several places cuts across the tortuous riverway. It is not, perhaps, generally realised that at Throstlo Nest, just below the Salford Racecourse, the Ir- well will, three or four years hence, end its course. The map maker will be called upon to alter his chart, and the schoolboy asked to sketch the features of his county will find his task somewhat the easier. From the springs on the hills above Bacup as far as Salford the Irwell will still sinuously stream on, but from thence to the sea the passage will simply be marked on the map by a deeper and perfectly straight line. The waters will empty them- selves into the Ship Canal, and the crooked, winding 1 way will from this point be blotted out all but abso- lutely. As soon as the water is turned into the Canal, at once the men will give their attention to filling up the old channel of the river. The only remnant of the old geography will be at a few points of crossing,where there will be lay-byes, places at which boats and barges may be pulled out of the canal and moored. Ex- cept, however, for these lay-byes thenday is not distant when there will be no 'more Irwell from Salford seawards. In place of the useless and puzzling waterway we shall have a splendid navigable channel, cut clean and straight from Manchester to the Mersey estuary. The running waters of the Irwell and other rivers will fill it, and their flow will give a gentle motion to the canal itself, which will always have a slight down-grade roll not unlike the most sluggish of tides. To explain how exactly the flow of water into the Ship Canal will be regulated would take too much space. It is sufficient to say that the water supply will always be ample, and that what have most to be guarded against are the periods of floods, which in the past have been the cause of so much damage in the Irwell valley. At ordinary times the water will pass over an elaborate system of sluices without regulation; when the days
A JOKE WHICH BROUGHT TEARS TO HIS EYES.

Three commercial travellers sat over their wine and cigars one day after dinner, in a comfortable inn in Devonshire. They were "jolly good fellows," knowing each other as Torn Dick, and Harry. After comparing notes on the state of trade, etc., jokes and stories went around, till, at last, Tom and Dick began chaffing Harry on the shabby condition of his head, for his hair was fast failingout, and the sparse quantity he still retained was quite gray, awl both de- clared he had deceived them concerning his age, for his scanty gray hairs proved that he had already "fallen into the sear— the yellow leaf.' Dick declared that he knew of a sure remedy. Harry innocently and anxiously inquired what it was. Dick told him: "Cut half a dozen red onions into thick slices; rub your head thoroughly with them, and—leaving the slices on your head—sit in the hot sun for three hours "Nonsense Harry objected. "Well, if you don't choose to try it, go bald I " Harry secretly resolved to try it, and did. The next day his mischievous friends spied him sitting in the sun, in the stable yard, his head plastered with onions, his eyes full of their juice, and streaming with tears. The shout they, set up told Harry that he was sold, and but for Tom's interference Dick's' head would have stood in need of a plaster. Dick apologised, and made amends by informing Harry of the admirable qualities of Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Re- storer, which never fails 0 restore the hair to its natural colour, prevents it from falling out, and gives it the luxuri- ance and silken glossiness of youth. It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the world. It should always be kept on the toilet table for dressing the hair. It is delicate and agreeable,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, _APRIL 28, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, _APRIL 28, 1888.

of flood come the sluices can be lifted, so that the navigatiol 'nay ;j3toceecl Without difficulty. In the past the low, marshy lands of this district'have been subject to periodic inundation from the river floods. Acres upon acres of fields have been covered by the waters, giving the valley the appearance of a vast inland sea, known in some neighbouring parts (Mr. Edwin Waugh says) as the " Cheshire waters. The Ship Canal will be an enormous boon to the inhabitants of this marshy country.. The company will end once and for ever, the days of floods. The greater channel to the sea will afford plenty of scope for the flood waters to run down, and even were that not the case the danger would I still be gone. The valley is to be exalted. Enormous masses of the excavated soil are to be placed on the land, so that the farmer will rejoice greatly. It is in keeping with the eternal fitness of things that a minor incident of our great scheme should be the lifting up of an entire valley.

AN INTERESTING EXPERIMENT. The Ship Canal Company made an interesting experi- ment on Tuesday. As is well known, the Warrington traffic of the conipany, which is of great extent and im- portance, is workn-1, down the Old Quay Canal. In the course of time this waterway will be absorbed in the greater undertaking of the'Ship Canal. Between War- rington and Runcorn the 'Me of the Ship Canal crosses I the Old Quay Canal several times, and then at the I works of Messrs. Vrigg Bin,. and Steele follows the same line until it enters the river at the Old Quay Docks. It would appear evident by the progress that is being made. by the." digging "operations, that the old waterway will soon have to come wan end, and the Company have therefore to face the problem of how they will deal with the traffic. Apparently they have determined to make the attempt to c-nduct it on the Mersey. On Tuesday morning the watermen were astonished at the unusu-I sight of a " Duke's Packet," passing Old Quay Docks, and proceeding in the direction of Wr.,ington, and many wee the conjectures as to the cause, which is partly explained in the above lines. The packet was the powerful puddle steamer Brackley, which was at- tempting to make the passage to Warrington. A survey of the deep had been made a few days previously, and the risk attendant on the trial trip was rendered less hazardous by the canal tug " Runcorn " drawing two fiats showing the way. The steamer successfully arri- ved at Bank Quay, Warrington, and started on the return voyage, but the tide had receded so rapidly, being aided by an east wind, that she grounded on a bank, where she had to remain until flood time, when she safely brought the flats to Run- corn. The conclusion arrived at was that a vessel of smaller dimensions would have to be employed to navi- gate the narrow and winding deep if the traffic was to be conducted on the river; but yesterday the Brackley again started on the trial trip, but the result had not transpired when this account was despatched.
DROWNING CASE AT MOORE.

Yesterday morning, the body of a youth named Richard Ledbury, who was fifteen years of age, was recovered from the Bridgewater Canal at Acton Grange. The deceased, who was in the em- ploy of Mrs. Massey, of Acton Grange, was missed from his home on Tuesday. As he did not return his friends became alarmed, and, as it became known that he had been seen on the bank of the canal, dragging was resorted to. The result was that his dead body was recovered from the canal yesterday morning by P.C. Dutton, of Moore, and Richard Massey. It is thought that, while reading a paper or book as he went along the side of the canal, he unwittingly stepped into the water. The police have communicated with the coroner, who will hold an inquiry into the circumstances of the death in due course. ,

div.head: TERRIBLE TRAGEDY NEAR HALIFAX.
div.p: TERRIBLE TRAGEDY NEAR HALIFAX.

About eleven o'clock on Wednesday forenoon a case of murder and suicide took place at the quiet little village of Luddenden, near Halifax. At a spot called Pepper Hill, Mi. Emmett, butcher and small farmer, lived with his wife. Emmott was about 60 years of age, and .his wife some seven years his junior. Mrs. Emmott was a second wife, and had been married about 18 months. She came from Manchester, where three of her daughters reside, a son being a captain in the army. It appears that Emmott and his wife had not lived comfortably to- gether. The murder must have been deliberately planned, as Emmott is said to have fetched a large knife from his shop, which is some distance from the residence. A neighbour had reasons for think- ing that all was not right, and she went td the door and called out, but got no response. She heard only a moaning noise, which proceeded front up- St airs, and she raised an alarm. On the bedroom being reached a ghastlrsight presented itself. 'Mrs. Emmott was laid on the floor in a pool of blood, with her head all but severed from her body; the husband's head was also nearly cut off, and a large knife was lying on the floor. There must have been a terrible struggle, as Mrs. Emmott's hands were badly cut. The murderer's body was lying on that of his wife.
Letter to the Obttor.
THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL AND LICENSING CLAUSES.

Sir,—l have felt inclined, the last few days more particularly, to write a few lines on the above subject, if only to thank you for the interesting and timely leaders you have inserted in the columns of the" Examiner," which I hope will have done some little service to help on our temperance friends in the neighbourhood to an increased earnestness and activity during the very critical period through which we are passing. For more reasons than one my contribution on this occasion must be brief; but I wish to urge upon our friends in this district to let these monstrous proposals of tke Government have their unqualified and determined opposition in all possible, and of course legitimate, ways. Let every Rechabite Tent, Sons of Temperance Division, Good Templar Lodge, Band of Hope, Temperance and Religious Society of every creed and denomination, at an , early meeting adopt and forward to the House of Com- mons a petition signed by the principal officers against the proposals of the Government to burden the rate- payers with a heavy tax, in order to provide ample compensation to any liquor seller whose license may not be renewed, and thus create a vested interest in licenses which previously has not been recognised either in law or custom. The licensing clauses are as bad as they well can be, and must be opposed to the uttermost, if we have to "fight like tigers." They are in no way satisfactory to temperance reformers, but according to Mr. H. M. C. Wharton, solicitor, at a meeting of "the trade," held last week, are almost entirely in th& interests of the licensed victuallers. This will at once show us the neces- sity for an active hostility. If by lukewarmness and in- difference we allow these clauses to become law, we shall find the temperance party. crippled for many years to come. "Now or never," is thq time for a determined opposition, Let temperahce and religious societies send up their petitions bX the thousand; let public meetings of ratepayers be held in every section of the constituen- cies ,• and resolutions against the clauses adopted and for- wardtd to the proper quarter. I would also urge upon every voter who has the interests and welfare of the com- munity at heart to write personally to the member of Parliament for his division, respectfully asking him to give his influence and vote in the direction above indi- cated. The traffickers are up and doing, and are in "dead earnest ; " afid if our opposition is to be in any way effec- tive, in the words of Mr. Herbert Gladstone, we must let our voices be heard "above the rest."—l am, sir, yours respectfully, LOCALITY.

div.head: QUARREL BET WEEN MOTHER AND SON AT
div.p: A QUARREL BET WEEN MOTHER AND SON AT
WIDNES.

- - -.-- At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, be- fore Messrs. J. Brock and H. Gaskell, jun., a woman named Dinah Bibby, of Farrant-st., Widnes, was summoned by her son, Samuel Hobley, for havinsz caused wilful damage to a set of china, the damage being estimated at .E 3 3s. Mr. J. W. Knowles ap- peared for the defence.—Samuel Hobley stated that he was an engine driver at Messrs. Muspmtt's chemical works, and lived at 90, Mersey-road. He kept a shop at that address. His mother came to his house on the night of the 20th int" "quietly at first," but she got quarrelsome. He had to close his shop in conse- quence of the disturbance caused. She made a claim to a set of china which he had in his kitchen, and said she would have them. The china had been given to him by his grandmother, and he had hadthem for over 12 months. He refused to let her take them, and she got them and broke them upon the floor by jumping upon them. —Cross-examined by Mr. Knowles: He had not assisted to break the articles by jumping upon them or breaking a chair over them. He had, however, broken a chair to pieces which his mother also claimed, but which he was determined she should not have.—Edith Neilson, domes- tic servant in the employ of the plaintiff, gave evidence, as to seeing the woman smash the crockery.—William I Hobley, brother to the plaintiff, stated that the articles did not belong to the plaintiff at all. They had been I left by his grandmother to his mother, who had pro- mised to give plaintiff and his brother half each. The plaintiff had seen him and offered him half a sovereign to swear falsely to the Court that he might win his ' case. It was not true that his mother had offered him a sovereign and a new coat to appear for her.—Mr. Knowles said the proper court to try the case was the ICounty Court.—The case was dismissed.

div.head: BRUTAL TREATMENT OF A HORSE AT WIDNES.
div.p: BRUTAL TREATMENT OF A HORSE AT WIDNES.

Daniel Percival, hatter's assistant, of 49, High-st., Runcorn ; John Witter, pointsman on the London and North-Western Railway, and Josiah James Evans, a fireman in the same employ, and both living at 39, Alforde-at., were summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday to answer a charge of cruelly illtreating a horse. Mr. Berry (Messrs. Bartlett and Berry), .instructed by Mr. Jesse W. Motrim secretary of the Liverpool Branch of the R.S.P.Ca., was the prosecutor, and Mr. T. J. Peters defended. According to the eyidence, Percival, who at noon on Sunday, the first April, went to the stables of Mr. J. H. Lee, in Violet-at., and engaged a horse and gig for the afternoon. He stated it was. his intention to drive his young lady to Hale, but when the giawas sent to an address which he had given in Alforde- st., the thee defendants became the occupants. About , half-past three Mr. Deakin and his wife, of the Simms Cross Hotel, were out driving, and saw a gig containing the defendants being driven along at a furious rate by Percival, who was thrashing the horse most unmerci- fully. About eight o'clock in the evening the defendants were seen by two youths named Barnett and Farley driving along Hale-road towards Ditton. The horse was galloping, and Percival was again in the act of flogging the animal. A stoppage was made at Ball Inn, Ditton, where the horse fell down exhausted. A farmer named Beasley prepared a mixture for the horse, and Mr. Lee was sent for. It was with great Idifficulty the horse was got to Widnes, and next morning it died in the stable. The animal was sold to a horse slaughterer named Rolla.son, and Mr. Robin- 'son, veterinary surgeon, made a post-mortem examina- tion. That' gentleman said there was congealed blood , under the skin and in other parts of the body, and the horse must have been grossly abused and over-driven. The immediate cause of death was congestion of the lungs, but the primary cause was over-exerdon. These facts were proved by a number of witnesses, and it was stated that the horse was in capital condition, was only about 14 years of age, and was three-parts thorough- bred. It was a " free goer," and no whip was needed. —Robert Beasley, a farmer, said the horse was 19 or 20 years of age, and it was so " fat " that he could see through it without looking round it.—Mr. peters, for the , defence, alleged that the horse was a "regular screw," 120 years of age and contended that there was no evid- ence that the defendant had severely beaten the horse. IThe indications seem by the .veterinary surgeon were probably caused by Beasley, who broke the whip stock in attempting to make the horse rise from the ground.— He called Thomas Wuswall, ostler at the Wellington Hotel, who said the horse was all right when placed in the stable on Sunday afternoon. There were no marks of ill-usage. People used to make fun of this horse, say- ing it wanted sticks putting under it to keep it up.—Mr. Brock said this appeared to the Bench a most gross ease of over-driving and cruelty, and there was practically no defence whatever. Percival appeared to be the man who had flogged the horse, and he would be fined £4, and costs £1 10s 6d, or a month's hard labour. The other defendants would be each fined £2, and costs £1 lOs 6d, or 14 days.—The money, £I2 us (id in all, was paid.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONER. THE NIGHTSOIL CONTRACT. . A special meeting of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners was held at the Town Hall last night for the purpose of considering a report of the Nuisance Inspector with regard to the unsatisfactory manner in which the nightsoil contract was being carried out. Mr. J. Meadowcroit occupied the chair, and there were present Messrs. F. A. Lake, F. Wiswall, E. Imison, J. W. Lightburn, E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor), and J. Percival (nuisance inspector.) Mr. Lightburn, chairman of the Health Committee, stated that as regarded the nightsoil contract, things were going from bad to worse.. At present there were 147 ashpits that re- quired emptying: 54 notices had been banded in this week, and 54 had been attended to A number of notices had been in the hands of the contractor for about five weeks, and a portion of the town was becoming in a filthy condition. The Health Com- mittee had adopted every possible means of persuasion and threatening to induce the contractor (Mr. Field) and his guarantors, but without avail, and it was now time that the Board should act decisively. Matters could not be carried on in the present fashion without danger to public health.—Mr. Lake said it would be better for the finances of the Board to compel Mr. Field to carry out his contract, but it would be better for the peace of the Board to put an end to the contract in the manner provided for.—ln reply to the chairman, Mr. Barker said the contract had ytt two years to run.—The Nuisance Inspector said at this time last year there were 75 notices on the books. The reason the contract was not properly carried out was that there were not sufficient men on the work.—The Secretary said the only way to effect an im- provement was to "touch the pocket" of the contrac- tor.—Mr. Imison : Let us touch it by all means, then. —After some further discussion, the following resolu- tion was adopted, on the motion of Mr. Lightburn, seconded by Mr. Wiswall :—" That the Commissioners in the first instance act upon the ninth clause of the contract and by their inspector of nuisances take posses- sion of the horses, carts, barrows, and other plant of the contractor, and employ men to do the work the contrac- tor had contracted to do, and ''' • I case the con- tractor refuses to allow the take WOpos- session of the horses, carts, , and pther plant, that the inspector of nuisances engagon behalf of the Commissioners, a sufficient number of persons, horses, carts, wheelbarrows, shovels, brooms planks, and other plant, arid properly and effectually cleanse all middens, 'cesspools, privies, ashpits, and other recep- tacles for nightsoil, dust, ashes, rubbish, and filth w:thin the limits of the district, and to remove and carry away the contents of the same, and that the costs and expenses thereby incurred should be dealt with as pro- vided by the terbts of the contract; that notice be given , to the bondsmen of the said contractor that the inspector lof nuisances certified that the contract is not being carried out in a satisfattory manner, and of the action the Board proposed to take in the matter: and further that in the opinion of the surveyor and inspector of nuis- ances, the contractor is not employing upon the work a snfficient number of horses and carts, or a sufficient quantity of other plant, to properly carryon the contract I entered into by him."

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

This Board held its fortnightly meeting on Thursday afternoon, when there were present—the Rev. T. Cham- bers. the Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. W. Middlehurst, J. Griffiths, J. Burchall, J. Birchen, J. Leatherbarrow, W. Twist, J. Ellison, J. Buckley, J. W. Wareing, J. Ken- wright, J. Ranson, R. Tuson, J. Whalley, E. Syder, J. Lowe, J. Musson, W. Tyrer, H. Hulme, R. A. Gra.ves,W. G. Ashton, T. F. EBB, C. B. Johnson, J. Fisher, W. Swift, and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk). Mr. Fisher was elected Chairman pre tem.

APPotrrntaNT Or CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.— Mr, Fisher remarked that the first business was the ap- pointment of a chairman for the ensuing twelve months. —Mr. Leatherbarrow remarked that some twelve months /Igo he had the honour and pleasure of pro- Iposing Mr. John Kenwright as the vice-chair- Allan, and as he was one of the oldest Guardians connected with the Board he now proposed his election as chairman.—Mr. Tyrer seconded the motion, which was passed unanimously, and Mr. Fisher expressed the hope that the new chairman would receive the same kindness and support with which he (Mr. gisher) had been treated during his term of office.— Mr. Kenwright acknowledged the compliment, and said he would do his best to do what was right and just in regard to the business. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. C. B. John- son afterwards moved that the Rev. T. Chambers be ap- pointed vice-chairman, and paid a compliment to that gentleman's fitness and ability.—Mr. Leatherbarrow sec- onded the motion —The Rev. T. Chambers thanked those gentlemen for their kind remarks concerning him, but declined to accept the post as he was unable to attend the meetings as he might wish, and it was his intention, if spared to the end of the present year, to withdraw from his position as a guardian. (Cries of "No, no.")— Mr. Wareing regretted that Mr. Chambers had not accepted the post, and under those circumstances he would propose that the Rev. Dean Finegan be appointed vice-chairman.—Mr. Ellison seconddd the motion which was passed, and the Rev. Dean Finegan thanked the guardians for the honour.—On the motion of Mr. Tyrer, seconded by Mr, Wareing, Mr. Hill was elected junior vice-chairman.

• THE NEW COUNTY GOVERNMENT BILL. The Clerk read a letter from the Secretary to the North-Western Poor Law conference stating that the adjourned meeting for the consideration of the Local Government Bill would be held at Manchester on Friday next. On the propo- sition of Mr. Hill. the same deputation who attended on the last ()erasion were re-appointed. THE LATE ELECTIONS.—The Clerk submitted the voting papers ,nomination papers. poll books ,Sce , used in the recent election of Guardians for Parr and Windle, and the Board decided to allow the sum of £3 3s towards the expenses in each township. This was all the business.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

TiE TRIAL OF MR. O'BRIEN, M.P.—The prosecution of Mr. W. O'Brien M.P., was resumed at Loughrea; on Friday, when Mr. Derevan, a farmer, deposed for the defence that the meeting of the Bth was not a Na- tional League meeting, but was called to deny Mr. Bal- four's statements.

The Irish Landowners's Convention met in Dublin on Friday, the Duke of Abercorn presiding. His lordship said that the recent deputation from the Convention had been courteously received by Lord Salisbury, and he believed that their firm tone would -have a good effect.

THE GOLD DISCOVERIES IN WALES.-Mr. Justice North, on Friday, granted a motion, made ex parte, restraining the defendant in the action the Attorney-General v. Morgan from removing gold, without the sanction of the Commissioner of Woods, from a mine in Merl- oneth, pending negotiations for a licence to work the mine.

A Noromous CONVICT.—On Friday, at the Old Bailey, London, " Captain " Beauchamp, the notorious con- vict, who has undergone ten and twenty years' penal' servitude for forging bank notes and post-office orders, was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude- for steal- ing a bracelet valued at £7OO, and endeavouring to in- duce a post-office employe to steall large numbers of money orders.

•M. CHAMBERLAIN'S REPORTED ENGAGEMENT.—The New • York correspondent of the "Daily News," in a telegram received from him on Thursday, states that Mr. Endacott, the mother of the lady whom Mr. Chamber- lain was said to be about to marry, indignantly denies the report cabled from London of the engagement to Mr. Chamberlain, and denounces it as an • unwarranted lib- erty with her daughter's name. The young lady is about 20 years of age. TRAGEDY IN A LONDON CAB.—The lady who shot her- self in a cab in Piccadilly Circus, on Thursday night, died in St. George's Hospital at three o'clock on Friday morning, without having recovered consciousness. The unfortunate lady was a professional vocalist, known publicly as Rosa Crossman, who had been engaged with Mr. Mapleson's company since November last. She had lived at 25, Upper Bedford-place, Russell-square, a house which is tenanted by an invalid gentleman, Captain Augustus Godbold and his wife. •

Fa°Pomp NEw RAILWW.TO4-.'.RHYL.—A deputation of landowners and traders from Flintshire has waited upon Sir Edward Watkin, chairman of the Manchester, Shef- field, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, which, in association with the Cheshire Lines, are constructing a new railway from Chester to Connah's Quay, inviting him to extend the railway to Rhyl, some 20 miles fur- ther. The landowners through whose property the rail- Way would pass are favourable to the scheme, and arrangements are now being made to have a survey of _ the whole route. _

THE SALFORD GAS SCANDAL.—It has now been defi- nitely decided that Samuel Hunter, who at the last ses- sions of the Central Criminal Court pleaded guilty to several charges of perjury and forgery, shall not come up for sentence at the present sessions. Mr. Justice Hawkins cannot attend, and the case, it is said, will not be called up until his lordship is able to appear on the bench at the Old Bailey. Hunter is detained at the Old Bailey, but an effort is at present being made to secure his removal to Strangeways prison until the May sittings of the Central Criminal Court, when, as at present arranged, sentence will be passed. THE MID-LANARK ELECTION. The polling in Mid. Lanark opened at eight o'clock on Friday morning. There was much excitement at Winshaw, and nearly 900 votes were recorded in the first hour. The polling pro- ceeded slowly at Hamilton, the miners not having come up from their work to vote. The candidates are—Mr. Robert Bousfield (Unionist), Mr. James Kier Hardie (Labour), and Mr. James Wyndford Fhillipps (Glad- stone Liberal.) Result :7

PhiliPs (Gladstonian) Bousfield (Unionist) Hardie (Labour) Bl7 THE MOSTIN MURDER.—At Manchester Assizes, on Friday, John Alfred Gell was indicted for the wilful mur- der of Mary Miller, at Mostin. The evidence showed that the prisoner lived with the debeased woman, and was violently attached to her. Owing to his long-con- tinued lack of employment, Gell was told he could no longer be allowed to live in the house, and he left early next morning.. He entered the house armed with a hat- chet with which he hacked the unfortunate woman to death and nearly killed her daughter. The defence was that the evidence was entirely circumstantial, and un- reliable, but the jury returned a verdict of guilty, and Gell was sentenced to death. THE POPE AND THE PLAN OF CAMPAIGN.—The" Free- man's Journal" publishes a special telegram from Rome stating that the Pope, through the Holy Office, condemns the Plan of Campaign—First, because it is unlawful to break voluntary contracts between landlord and tenant; secondly, because the Land Courts are open to tenants who think their rents unfair; thirdly, because the funds contributed under the Plan of Campaign have been ex- torted from those contributing to it. The practice of boycotting is condemned as against justice and charity, and having been used as an Instrument of persecution. The "Freeman "Observes that not a word is shid against the National League, and thd Plan of Campaign is no part of its programme. The decree, the Central News says, has caused considerable sensation in Irish political circles. It is contended by the Nationalists that his Holiness has been entirely misinformed by the landlord party as to recent occurrencies in Ireland; otherwise he would never have given his assent to such a decree. While unfaltering in these allegiances to the Catholic Church, and bound to submit to the authority of the Pope in matters pertaining to Church discipline and dogma, they vfill not submit to Ecclesiastical interference in political affairs.

div.head: EMPEROR FREDERICK.
div.p: THE EMPEROR FREDERICK.

The following bulletin was issued on Friday morning: —" The Emperor, after enjoying a good sleep, feels much strengthened this morning. The fever disappears in the early morning hours, but towards evening becomes manifest in a moderate degree. The general condition is slowly improving." THE QUEEN'S RETURN.

- FLI7SHING, FRIDAY.—The Queen, accompanied by Prince and Princess Henry of Battenburg arrived here by special train from Berlin at 8-2 a.m., and at once embarked on board the Royal yacht Victoria and Al- bert.
--- - FLUSHING, FRIDAY, 9-20 A.M.—The Royal Yacht, Vic- toria. and Albert, has just sailed, escorted by the yachts Osborne and Galatea.

BERLIN, FRIDAY.—The Crown Prince at half-past five yesterday afternoon, handed to the Empress Augusta a farewell letter from Queen Victoria, who had proposed taking personal leave of her Majesty at 4 o'clock. The Queen sent word two hours previously, regretting her inability to carry out her intention. FRIDAY EVENING.—The Royal yacht Victoria and Al- bert arrived at six o'clock this evening from Flushing, with the Queen, Prince and Princess Henry of Batten- berg and suite on their return from the Continent. No salutes were fired, but the war vessels in Sheerness Har- bour were dressed with flags. As the yacht passed up the harbour to Port Victoria Pier a guard of honour of Royal Marines saluted FlerMajestyfrom the decks of the flagship Duncan. The Royal special train left Port Victoria at 649 for Windsor via Waterloo. Her Majesty seemed to be in good health and spirits. BERLIN, FRICAY EVENING. The North German Gazette, in a leading article, thanks the Queen of Eng- land for her visit, which all Germans will bear in thank- ful remembrance. The visit with its personal inter- change of views, its impressions and remembrances, cannot fail to have most beneficial effect on political re- lations between Germany and England. Lord Salisbury on Friday received a private deputa- tion on the affairs of east central Africa, and promised to consider the questions brought before him. Among the associations represented were the Church of Scot- land Foreign Missions, the committee of the Anti- Slavery Society, and Royal Scottish Geographical So- ciety.

div.head: LAST MOAT'S PARLIAMENT. – HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST MOAT'S PARLIAMENT. - HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Royal assent was given by com- mission to the Army Annual Act and several private Acts. —Lord PENMAN gave notice to move for a call of the House on the second reading of the Life Peerages Bill.— Lord DELAWARE drew attention to the long hours which railway companies employed their servants, and asked Government to sanction returns to the Board of Trade of exceptional cases of overtime employment.—Earl this Low said the Government did not object to the return.—The House shortly afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at 2-8 p.m. 'GROCERS' OFF-LICENSES AND COMPENSATION.—ViSCOURt NEWARK asked the President of the Local Government Board how grocers' licenses would be dealt with as re- garded compensation under the Local Government Bill.. —Mr. Rrrcum said the new licensing authorities would have the power to refuse the renewal of licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquors. Grocers whoge licenses were refused renewal would be entitled to claim compensa- tion, and the measure of the cowpensation would be the difference between tha value of the premises with and without a license. • . .

THE DECCAN Mninso SCANDAL.—Replying to Mr. Labouchere, Mr. W. H. SMITH said the Secretary of State for India had received this morning a telegram from the Viceroy of India, stating that the Viceroy had consulted his council in reference to the Hyderabad mining con- cession, and the Government of India had no objection to the matter being fully investigated. The telegram furthet disclaimed all responsibility for the purchase of. shares by the Nizam's Government. In these circum- stances the Government would certainly offer no objec- tion to the appointment of a select committee if Mr. Labouchere would move for it.
